valley fever cases in california have risen sharply over the past decade. scientists link the increase to cycles of drought followed by heavy rain, which help the fungus grow in the soil and then spread in dust. that is why the county must pay for a public awareness campaign now. too many residents mistake valley fever for the flu and go months without a correct diagnosis. how does the author's purpose change from the first paragraph to the second? it shifts from entertaining readers to informing them about the fungus. it shifts from persuading readers to informing them about the flu and its symptoms. it shifts from describing valley fever symptoms to telling a personal story. it shifts from informing readers about rising cases to urging the county to act. paragraph 1 gives facts about the increase and its causes, which is informative. paragraph 2 says the county "must" pay for a campaign, which is persuasive.

in an editorial calling for a new crosswalk near a high school, the author writes, "twelve pedestrians have been struck at this intersection in the past three years." why does the author most likely include this statistic? to show that the intersection is dangerous and needs a crosswalk to show that drivers near the school are usually careful to inform readers about the history of the high school to entertain readers with a surprising fact a persuasive writer uses numbers as evidence. twelve people struck shows the danger and supports the call for a crosswalk. the statistic suggests the opposite of careful drivers, and it has nothing to do with the school's history or entertainment.

at last, families in huron won't have to drive an hour to see a doctor. the new clinic, opening in may, is a long-overdue victory for our community. which word best describes the author's attitude toward the new clinic? skeptical enthusiastic indifferent disappointed "at last" and "a long-overdue victory" show that the author is excited and pleased. skeptical means doubtful, indifferent means not caring, and disappointed means let down; none of these fit.

"join the valley blood drive this saturday! one donation can save up to three lives. free snacks and a t-shirt for every donor!" what is the author's main purpose? to inform readers about the date of a blood drive to explain how one donation saves three lives to persuade readers to donate blood to advertise free snacks and t-shirts exclamation points, a benefit (saving lives) and incentives (snacks, t-shirt) all push readers to donate, so the purpose is to persuade.

"i remember the night my grandmother was rushed to the hospital. the nurse who stayed with us explained every step in spanish and held my mother's hand. that night, i decided i would become a nurse." from which point of view is the passage written? first person second person third person limited third person omniscient the narrator uses "i," "my," and "us," which signals first person.

a pamphlet from a company that sells water filters states that "most tap water in the region is unsafe." why should a reader be cautious about this claim? the company profits if readers believe the claim. pamphlets are never accurate sources of health information. "unsafe" is an opinion that no test could check. tap water in every region meets safety standards. the company has a financial interest in convincing readers that tap water is unsafe, so the claim should be checked against an independent source such as the local water report.

"clinical rotations taught me more than any textbook. yes, there were 5 a.m. alarms and long drives to visalia, but each patient showed me something no lecture could." what is the author's attitude toward clinical rotations? appreciative despite the challenges resentful because of the early mornings regretful about the time spent on the road doubtful that textbooks have any value the author admits the hardships ("yes, there were...") but stresses what each patient taught, so the attitude is appreciation.

before the first day of kindergarten, make sure your child's shots are up to date, including dtap, polio, mmr, hepatitis b and chickenpox. bring the yellow shot record to registration, along with proof of your home address. who is the intended audience of this notice? parents of children starting kindergarten kindergarten teachers preparing for the year school nurses who give the vaccines children who are entering kindergarten the notice says "your child's shots" and asks the reader to bring a shot record and proof of address. those are tasks for a parent or guardian.

assess the incision every 4 hours for erythema, edema and purulent drainage. document findings in the wound flowsheet and notify the surgeon of any signs of infection. for which audience was this text most likely written? patients caring for their own incisions at home surgeons deciding where to make an incision nurses caring for patients after surgery students learning the definitions of medical terms medical terms are used without definitions, and the reader is told to document in a flowsheet and notify the surgeon. those are nursing tasks in a hospital.

what is the main purpose of the last paragraph? to persuade readers to skip cna training and go straight into a registered nursing program to describe the daily duties of licensed vocational nurses to argue that four-year nursing degrees are a waste of time and money for most students to admit the path's drawbacks while explaining why it still appeals to some students "climbing slowly has costs" names the drawbacks; "yet" turns to the benefit of earning while moving up. the paragraph does not tell readers to skip steps, does not describe lvn duties, and does not attack four-year degrees.

what is the author's main purpose in the passage? to show readers what a night shift is like for a hospital nurse to persuade readers that night-shift nurses should be paid more to explain step by step how to assess a patient's pain to entertain readers with a series of jokes about hospitals the passage follows one nurse through a 12-hour night, describing typical tasks and moments. it makes no argument about pay, gives no step-by-step pain instructions, and is not humorous.

what is the writer's main purpose? to inform readers about the history of the clinic to entertain readers with stories about clinic patients to persuade the board to keep the clinic open to explain how the county creates its budget the writer says "i am writing to urge you" and ends with "please vote no on the proposal to close the clinic."

the author of passage 2 mentions that a family could pay "hundreds of dollars more a year" mainly to emphasize how heavily the tax could burden some families show that the tax would raise a great deal of money for schools prove that families drink less soda after a tax explain how the tax would be collected the detail supports passage 2's argument that the tax "falls hardest on low-income families." passage 2 opposes the tax, so it is not praising the money raised or explaining how to collect it.

what is the main purpose of the memo? to persuade students that the flu vaccine is safe and effective to tell students how this year's flu shot clinic will be different to explain why the clinic was so crowded and slow last year to remind students to upload a copy of their student id the memo opens by saying it is "making three changes" and then lists them: two days, a new room and online sign-up.

why does the passage stress using level teaspoons? heaping spoonfuls dissolve too slowly to be useful. extra salt can make dehydration worse. level spoonfuls make the solution taste sweeter. level spoonfuls keep the container from overflowing. the "important" note says too much salt can make dehydration worse, so careful measuring matters.

why does the author include the father's "recipe" for reaching a goal? to show how hernández's parents earned a living picking crops each season to explain the method hernández later followed to become an astronaut to argue that working in the fields is harder than studying in school to describe the foods the family cooked while traveling between jobs after the recipe, the passage shows hernández doing exactly that: he measured how far he was from nasa's standards and built a road map (pilot's license, scuba, russian).

why does the author most likely tell readers to keep the upper arm at heart level? to make the cuff easier to wrap to keep the reading accurate to prevent the patient from talking to speed up the measurement the passage introduces every step as part of getting "an accurate reading." arm position is one of those accuracy steps.

why does the author include the detail about the children and the wooden beam? to show that children invented the stethoscope to show where laennec got the idea that solids carry sound to prove that wood carries sound better than paper to describe how children played in nineteenth-century paris right after remembering the children, laennec applies the same idea with a paper tube. the detail explains the source of his insight.

why does the author describe the sore arm and low fever as signs the immune system is responding? to warn readers that vaccine side effects are dangerous and should be avoided to reassure readers that common side effects are expected and short-lived to argue that booster doses are unnecessary for people who had side effects to explain how memory cells fade over time after a vaccine the author says such side effects "usually last a day or two" and connects them to the immune response, which helps readers interpret them calmly.

what is thanh's main purpose in writing the email? to complain that the college's tuition costs have gone up for spring to ask why the spring grant is missing and request an extension to ask the office to change the enrollment from 9 units to 12 units to ask for help completing the fafsa for the first time thanh explains that the spring grant hasn't appeared and asks two questions: whether documents are missing and whether an extension is possible.

which word best describes the tone of the email? polite and specific angry and demanding casual and joking confused and disorganized thanh uses respectful phrases ("could you please," "thank you") and gives specific dates, an id number and an attachment.

why does thanh mention changing from 9 units to 12 units? to show that classes may be dropped if payment is late because the change may affect the amount of the grant to ask the office for permission to change enrollment to explain why the fafsa was submitted late in the year thanh says the change "should increase my grant," which may explain a delay while the grant is recalculated.

what is the author's purpose in the final paragraph? to argue that walking more than 7,500 steps a day is a waste of time to encourage readers who can't reach 10,000 steps to still walk more to recommend that readers buy a fitness tracker with a step counter to explain how pedometers and fitness trackers count each step the paragraph says people "should not give up" and that adding 1,000 to 2,000 steps may help.

what is the main purpose of the flyer? to persuade people to come get a free flu shot to inform readers about who is at high risk from flu to report how many residents were hospitalized to tell families about free books for children the flyer gives the time and place, removes excuses (free, no appointment, 15 minutes) and ends with a call to action, "see you saturday!" its purpose is to persuade.

why does the writer mention that many hospitalized residents had skipped their shot because they were "too busy"? to show that busy people are most at risk from the flu to raise a common excuse and then answer it to criticize residents for not taking the flu seriously to prove that flu shots prevent hospitalization the next sentence says getting protected now takes only 15 minutes with no appointment. the writer raises the "too busy" excuse so the flyer can knock it down.

which group of readers does the flyer especially try to reach with the detail about interpreters? people who speak spanish, hmong or punjabi adults over 65, pregnant women and young children children younger than six months families without health insurance listing interpreters tells people who are more comfortable in spanish, hmong or punjabi that they will be understood. that widens the audience.

from whose point of view is the passage told? a patient recovering from heart surgery a nurse who works the night shift a hospital manager hiring new nurses a nursing student writing a report the writer says "i" walked onto the cardiac unit, has worked nights for six years, and talks with patients at 3 a.m. it's first person, from a night-shift nurse.

what is the author's main purpose? to persuade new nurses that night shift can be rewarding to describe what a typical night on a cardiac unit is like to warn new nurses about the hardships of night shift to compare night shift with day shift in detail the essay shares personal experiences and ends by speaking directly to new nurses: "don't let anyone tell you the night is second best."

why does the author include the paragraph about blackout curtains and missed birthday parties? to warn readers that night shift harms nurses' health to show that the night crew replaces her real family to explain why most nurses prefer day shifts to give a balanced picture by admitting the drawbacks "night shift is not easy" introduces honest downsides. admitting them makes the writer's overall recommendation more believable.

which word best describes the author's tone in the last paragraph? defensive and annoyed nostalgic and wistful confident and encouraging cautious, careful and balanced the author speaks firmly ("don't let anyone tell you") and warmly ("for the right person, it is the best").

why does the author compare 17 hours without sleep to a blood alcohol level of 0.05%? to suggest that some nurses drink before work to prove that 12-hour shifts cause medication errors to help readers understand how serious fatigue is to argue that fatigue is worse than drinking alcohol the comparison turns tiredness into something readers already know is dangerous (impaired reaction time), making the point vivid.

the nurse noticed that the patient was lethargic ; he could barely keep his eyes open, and he answered questions slowly. based on the context, what does lethargic mean? sluggish and drowsy anxious and restless talkative and cheerful feverish and sweaty the clues "could barely keep his eyes open" and "answered questions slowly" describe someone sluggish and drowsy. restless and talkative are close to the opposite, and nothing in the sentence mentions fever.

because the mountains around the san joaquin valley trap air like the sides of a bowl, pollution from cars, trucks, and farms builds up over cities such as fresno and bakersfield. as a result, the region has some of the worst air quality in the nation, and children here have higher rates of asthma. which best describes how the passage is organized? compare and contrast chronological order cause and effect problem and solution signal words "because" and "as a result" link a cause (trapped air) to effects (poor air, more asthma). nothing is compared, no timeline is given, and no solution is offered.

both type 1 and type 2 diabetes cause high blood sugar. in type 1, the body makes little or no insulin, so patients must take insulin every day. in type 2, the body makes insulin but does not use it well, and many patients can manage the disease at first with diet, exercise, and pills. which best describes how the passage is organized? cause and effect compare and contrast chronological order problem and solution "both" shows a similarity, and the descriptions of type 1 versus type 2 show differences. showing how two things are alike and different is compare and contrast.

a nurse wants to describe, in a positive way, a patient who asks many questions about his treatment. which word should she choose? nosy pushy demanding curious "curious" has a positive connotation: interested and eager to learn. "nosy," "pushy," and "demanding" all carry negative feelings.

the nurse asked the patient to rate his pain on a scale of 0 to 10. in which sentence is the word scale used with the same meaning as in the sentence above? the nurse carefully weighed the newborn on the scale in the nursery. on a scale of 1 to 5, how satisfied were you with your visit? the hikers had to scale the steep granite wall. the fish's silver scales shone in the bright afternoon sunlight. in the original sentence, a scale is a range of numbers used to rate something. the other sentences use different meanings: a weighing device, to climb, and the plates on a fish's skin.

many patients forget to take their medicines on time. to help, some pharmacies now offer blister packs labeled with the day and time of each dose, and others send text-message reminders. which best describes how the passage is organized? compare and contrast chronological order description problem and solution the first sentence states a problem (forgetting doses), and the second gives ways to solve it.

unlike her gregarious roommate, who loved crowded parties, lily preferred quiet evenings alone. what does gregarious most likely mean? sociable and outgoing shy and quiet studious and serious rude and unkind "unlike" signals a contrast: lily likes quiet evenings, so her roommate is the opposite. someone who loves crowded parties is sociable and outgoing. "shy and quiet" describes lily, not the roommate.

the cut on the child's knee was superficial , so the nurse simply cleaned it and applied a bandage; no stitches were needed. as used in the sentence, what does superficial mean? badly infected and swollen deep and serious on the surface; not deep very painful to touch because the cut needed only cleaning and a bandage, not stitches, it was shallow. superficial (super- = above, -ficial from "face" or surface) means on the surface.

in 1918, influenza spread across the world in three waves. the first, in the spring, was fairly mild. the second, which arrived in the fall, was far deadlier and killed many healthy young adults. by the summer of 1919, the third wave had faded. which best describes how the passage is organized? compare and contrast problem and solution order of importance chronological order the passage moves through time (1918 spring, fall, then 1919 summer) to describe the three waves in order.

two newspapers described the same speech by a city council member. one said she explained her housing plan to the audience. the other said she lectured the audience about her plan. how does the word lectured change the meaning? it suggests she spoke clearly and helpfully to the audience. it suggests she was preachy and talked down to the audience. it suggests that she works as a teacher at a local college. it suggests that the audience agreed with every part of her plan. "explained" is neutral, but "lectured" has a negative connotation of scolding or talking down to people. it does not mean she is a teacher, and it hints the audience may not have liked it.

many older adults take several prescription medicines at the same time, a situation known as polypharmacy . based on the sentence, what does polypharmacy mean? taking many medicines at once working at several pharmacies refusing to take medicine buying medicine without a prescription the sentence defines the term directly: polypharmacy is the situation of taking several medicines at the same time. the root poly- means "many," which also points to the answer.

after a 12-hour shift, rosa's feet were blocks of lead. what does the author mean? rosa's feet were very cold. rosa was wearing heavy work boots. rosa's feet felt very heavy and tired. rosa had injured her feet at work. this is a metaphor: lead is a heavy metal, so her feet felt heavy after a long shift. the sentence is figurative. rosa's feet are not literally made of lead, and no injury or boots are mentioned.

acute pain begins suddenly, after a cut, a burn, or surgery, and usually fades as the body heals. chronic pain, by contrast, lasts for months or even years. as used in the passage, acute most nearly means sudden and short-term sharp and intense mild and dull permanent and lasting the passage defines acute pain as beginning suddenly and fading with healing, and contrasts it with long-lasting chronic pain. "sharp and intense" is another common meaning of acute, but it is not the meaning used here.

the patient's compliance with her treatment plan was poor: she skipped doses, missed two appointments, and never started the walking program her doctor recommended. as used in the sentence, compliance means understanding payment following instructions agreement with a diagnosis the examples after the colon (skipped doses, missed appointments) describe not following the plan. so compliance means following instructions or the plan as directed.

the western side of the san joaquin valley is arid . rain is scarce, sometimes less than six inches a year, and without irrigation the land would support little more than dry grasses and scrub. which phrases are context clues for the meaning of arid ? select all that apply. "rain is scarce" "less than six inches a year" "dry grasses and scrub" "the western side" "san joaquin valley" scarce rain, very little rainfall, and dry plants all point to the meaning of arid: very dry. the location phrases tell where, not what arid means.

the patient's fever had not come down after two doses of acetaminophen. ______, the nurse notified the provider. which transition best fits the blank? however as a result for example similarly the nurse called the provider because the fever did not come down, so a cause-and-effect transition fits. "however" shows contrast, "for example" introduces an example, and "similarly" shows a likeness.

the landlord made the repairs only after months of stalling. which word in the sentence suggests that the writer disapproves of the landlord? landlord repairs months stalling "stalling" means delaying on purpose, which has a negative connotation. the other words are neutral.

the doctor told mr. chen that his biopsy results were negative , and he smiled with relief. as used in the sentence, negative means the news was bad the result was a number less than zero the test did not find the disease the doctor was pessimistic in medicine, a negative test result means the condition being tested for was not found. mr. chen's relief is a clue that the news was good, so "bad news" is the everyday-meaning trap.

put these sentences in the most logical order to form a paragraph. a vaccine introduces a harmless piece or weakened form of a germ into the body. the immune system responds by making antibodies and memory cells. later, if the real germ enters the body, the memory cells recognize it. the body then fights off the germ quickly, often before the person feels sick. the paragraph follows a cause-and-effect chain: the vaccine goes in, the body responds, the memory cells recognize the real germ later, and the body fights it off. words like "responds," "later," and "then" help show the order.

which pair of words has nearly the same denotation but different connotations? doctor / physician hot / cold nurse / patient thrifty / cheap thrifty and cheap both mean careful with money, but "thrifty" sounds positive and "cheap" sounds negative. doctor and physician share both meaning and neutral feeling; hot/cold are opposites; nurse/patient are different people.

use context clues. click the word that means "became less strong." after she moved away from the smoke, she "could speak in full sentences again," so the cough got weaker. subsided means became less strong. exacerbated means the opposite: made worse. the smoke made the cough worse. moved and entrance don't describe a change in strength.

first, the virus attaches to a cell. next, it injects its genetic material. then the cell begins making new viruses. finally, the cell bursts and releases them. how is this text organized? compare and contrast sequence problem and solution cause and effect signal words first, next, then and finally show a sequence of steps.

type 1 diabetes usually appears in childhood, and the body makes little or no insulin. type 2 diabetes is more common in adults, and the body makes insulin but cannot use it well. both types raise blood sugar. how is this paragraph organized? chronological order compare and contrast problem and solution spatial order the paragraph shows differences (age, insulin production) and a similarity (both raise blood sugar).

the nurse explained that the medication was contraindicated for the patient because it could dangerously interact with her heart medicine. what does contraindicated mean? strongly recommended not advised given in a lower dose likely to cause side effects the medication "could dangerously interact" with her heart medicine, so it should not be used: not advised. "contra-" means against, as in contradict.

many students struggle to find time to study. one solution is to break study sessions into 25-minute blocks with short breaks. another is to study during "dead time," such as bus rides. which structure does the author use? problem and solution cause and effect chronological order description the paragraph names a problem (finding time) and offers solutions.

the night before her teas exam, ana lay awake while her thoughts raced like cars on highway 99. which type of figurative language does the phrase "raced like cars on highway 99" use? metaphor simile personification hyperbole a simile compares two unlike things using "like" or "as." her thoughts are compared to speeding cars using "like."

during a week of staffing shortages, the new charge nurse was a rock for the unit. when everyone else was frantic, she kept the shifts covered and the patients safe. in this context, what does the metaphor "a rock" suggest about the charge nurse? she was stubborn and refused to change plans. she was quiet and rarely spoke to the staff. she was strong enough to lift patients alone. she was steady and dependable under pressure. the next sentence gives the clue: while others were frantic, she kept everything running. a rock here means something solid that others can lean on.

by 2 p.m. the august sun hung over the vineyard like a heavy blanket, and the heat pressed down on the pickers' shoulders. "i've drunk a gallon of water every ten minutes," luis joked, "and i'm still a raisin." which phrase is an example of hyperbole, and what does it suggest? "like a heavy blanket": the heat feels thick and smothering "the heat pressed down": the heat seemed to push on the workers "a gallon of water every ten minutes": he is extremely thirsty "i'm still a raisin": luis has actually become dehydrated and wrinkled hyperbole is deliberate exaggeration. no one could drink a gallon every ten minutes; luis overstates it to show how thirsty the heat makes him.

as used in paragraph 1, the word rung most nearly means a telephone call a level or stage a type of college degree a hospital department the paragraph compares a career to a ladder, so the "next rung" is the next step or level. "a telephone call" confuses rung with rang.

in the last paragraph, the word bone-tired means suffering from sore bones bored with the work cold from the early morning air extremely tired "bone-tired" is an expression meaning tired all the way through, which fits the end of a 12-hour shift. it is not about actual bones, and the word "but" shows she felt satisfied, not bored.

based on paragraph 1, the word miasma refers to a type of microorganism found in water an underground system for carrying waste bad-smelling air once blamed for disease water from shallow, polluted wells the sentence defines it directly: "a foul-smelling 'bad air' that rose from rotting garbage and filth."

as used in the section "when sleep runs short," the word chronic most nearly means continuing over a long time severe, painful, and serious sudden and unexpected rare and unusual the phrase "over months and years" signals that chronic means long-lasting. it is contrasted with "one night of poor sleep" in the sentence before.

how is paragraph 3 mainly organized? it lists groups at higher risk and gives a reason for each. it tells events in the order in which they happened. it compares two competing scientific theories about how sweat works. it describes a problem and then offers a solution. paragraph 3 names older adults, young children, people on certain medicines, and outdoor workers, and explains each group's risk. there is no timeline, no pair of theories, and no solution in this paragraph; solutions come in the last paragraph.

as used in the passage, the word "loop" most nearly means a knot tied in a rope a repeated circular route a short break between jobs a mistake in planning the family drove "a loop between mexico and california" each year as the seasons changed, a route they repeated.

which best describes how the first paragraph is organized? problem and solution compare and contrast cause and effect chronological order of historical events the paragraph explains what happens when the body can't release heat (cause) and the symptoms and damage that follow (effects). signal words: "when...," "as a result," "if..."

as used in the passage, the word "acclimatize" most nearly means to get sick from heat to adjust to new conditions to take a break in the shade to follow safety rules the passage defines it right after the word: "to acclimatize, or adjust, to working in heat."

how is the second paragraph mainly organized? it compares laennec's paper tube with the children's wooden beam. it narrates events in the order they happened. it lists reasons why doctors should stop listening with the ear. it defines the medical terms stethoscope and auscultation. the paragraph moves step by step: he remembered the children, rolled the paper, placed it, and heard the heartbeat.

based on the passage, "auscultation" most nearly means cutting open and studying a body after death listening to body sounds to detect disease rolling paper into a tube pressing on the chest to feel the heartbeat the passage says laennec's book taught doctors "to listen for specific sounds of disease, a method called auscultation."

what does the first sentence of the passage mainly do? warns visitors that they may be asked to leave the unit explains the reason for the rules in a reassuring way lists the hours when visiting is allowed gives medical information about icu patients "we know that family support helps patients heal" signals that the hospital values visits and that the rules exist to protect patients, which sets a welcoming tone.

in passage 2, the phrase "check a box" most nearly means mark the correct answer on a written cpr skills test meet a requirement on paper without reaching its goal inspect cpr practice kits and medical equipment count how many students have been trained each year the author worries a one-time lesson lets schools say the requirement is done "without building lasting skills."

how is most of the second paragraph organized? compare and contrast sequence (step by step) problem and solution cause and effect signal words like "begins," "next," "when they arrive" and "then" walk through the cold chain in order.

as used in the passage, the word fragile most nearly means likely to shatter easily damaged short-lived hard to find the next sentences explain that vaccines lose strength if they get too warm or too cold: they are easily damaged.

which statement is an opinion? the new hospital wing has 120 patient beds and four operating rooms. the new hospital wing is the most beautiful building in visalia. the new hospital wing opened in march. the new hospital wing has a helicopter pad on its roof for emergencies. "most beautiful" is a personal judgment that people could disagree about. the number of beds, the opening date, and the helicopter pad can all be checked.

which statement is a fact? the human heart has four chambers. nursing is the most rewarding career a person can choose. hospital food tastes terrible. everyone should get a flu shot every year. the number of heart chambers can be verified in any anatomy textbook. "most rewarding" and "tastes terrible" are judgments, and "should" signals a recommendation, which is an opinion.

(1) the city's new bike lanes opened in april. (2) since then, the number of cyclists counted on blackstone avenue has doubled. (3) the bike lanes are the smartest investment the city has made in decades. (4) the project cost $2.1 million. which sentence states an opinion? sentence 1 sentence 2 sentence 3 sentence 4 "the smartest investment" is a judgment that cannot be proven. the opening date, the cyclist count, and the cost could all be checked in records.

an article praising a new weight-loss supplement was written by a doctor who is paid by the company that sells it. what should a careful reader conclude? the article must be accurate because a doctor wrote it. the supplement is definitely dangerous. the article is a neutral, reliable source. the article may be biased in favor of the supplement. when an author earns money from a product, he has a reason to present it favorably, so the article may be biased. being a doctor does not remove a conflict of interest, and bias alone does not prove the product is dangerous.

which statement is a stereotype? some teenage drivers take dangerous risks. drivers under 20 have higher crash rates than middle-aged drivers. all teenagers are careless drivers. many teens take a driver's education course. a stereotype applies a fixed idea to every member of a group, as in "all teenagers are careless." "some" and "many" are limited statements, and crash rates are data, not stereotypes.

the council's reckless budget cuts will gut the city's only free clinic. which words in the sentence reveal the writer's bias? select all that apply. reckless gut council's budget clinic "reckless" (careless and dangerous) and "gut" (destroy from the inside) are loaded words that show the writer's strong disapproval. "council's," "budget," and "clinic" are neutral nouns.

which sentence states a fact that could be verified? the clinic's staff are the kindest and most caring people in the entire county. the clinic's annual report shows it served a record number of patients in 2025. the clinic should receive more funding next year. patients probably prefer the clinic to the hospital because the waits are shorter. a reader could check the annual report to confirm the number of patients served. "kindest" is a judgment, "should" is a recommendation, and "probably prefer" is a guess.

studies show that people who eat breakfast tend to have more energy in the morning. clearly, skipping breakfast is the worst habit a student can have. the author uses the word clearly mainly to present an opinion as though it were an obvious fact introduce a statistic from a study of student habits name the source of the information about breakfast signal a contrast with the idea in the first sentence "clearly" makes the claim sound certain, but "the worst habit a student can have" is an opinion that the study does not prove. no statistic or source follows the word, and it does not signal contrast the way "however" would.

a student is researching whether a new diabetes medicine is safe. which source is likely to be the least biased? a study by researchers who got no money from the drug's maker a television commercial paid for by the company that makes the drug a blog by a person who sells herbal remedies that compete with the drug a press release from the company that makes and sells the new drug researchers with no financial ties to the drug have the least reason to favor or attack it. the commercial and press release come from the maker, and the blogger profits from a competing product.

the statement "sacramento is the capital of california" is an opinion, because not everyone agrees a fact only because it appears in textbooks an opinion, because an expert said it a fact, because it can be checked a fact can be proven true with reliable sources, such as a map or a state government website. whether something is a fact does not depend on who says it or where it is printed.

which statement would be the most difficult to prove? at sea level, water boils at 100 °c. the best way to relax is to listen to music. the clinic opens at 8 a.m. on weekdays. merced is located in the san joaquin valley. "the best way" is a judgment; people relax in different ways, so it cannot be proven. the boiling point, clinic hours, and location can all be checked.

a brochure for sunny meadows assisted living highlights its rose garden, weekly outings, and chef-prepared meals. it does not mention the facility's staffing levels or the results of its most recent state inspection. what can a careful reader conclude? sunny meadows must have failed its most recent state inspection, or it would say so. the brochure is an objective source of information about the facility. the brochure shows only the positives, so the reader should check other sources. sunny meadows does not have enough staff to care for all of its residents safely. leaving out important information is a form of bias; the brochure shows only the positives. the missing information does not prove a failed inspection or low staffing; it means the reader should look elsewhere.

our town needs a dog park. (1) dog owners here deserve better. (2) the nearest dog park is 14 miles away. (3) a dog park would make our town the friendliest in the valley. (4) everyone loves dogs. which numbered sentence states a fact? sentence 1 sentence 2 sentence 3 sentence 4 the distance to the nearest dog park can be measured. "deserve better," "the friendliest," and "everyone loves dogs" are opinions or overgeneralizations.

which word most often signals an opinion? measured recorded according to best superlatives like "best" usually express a judgment. "measured," "recorded," and "according to" point to evidence or sources.

a website that sells herbal tea states, "doctors agree that our tea cures anxiety." what is the main problem with this claim? it proves that herbal tea is dangerous for people with anxiety. it is a fact, because doctors are the experts on health and anxiety. it gives no named doctors or evidence, and it comes from the seller. it is an opinion only because it is about a food rather than a medicine. "doctors agree" is vague: no doctors, studies, or numbers are given, and the seller profits from the claim. the problem is lack of support, not proof of danger. expert words still need evidence.

which revision turns the opinion "the new urgent care center has terrible wait times" into a statement of fact? the average wait at the new urgent care center last month was 74 minutes. the new urgent care center has awful, frustrating wait times. everyone hates waiting so long at the new urgent care center down the street. the new urgent care center should hire more staff. a measured average wait time can be checked, so it is a fact. "awful" and "frustrating" are still judgments, "everyone hates" is an overgeneralization, and "should" is a recommendation.

a health blog states, "drinking eight glasses of water a day is the only way to stay healthy." this statement is best described as a fact supported by data an opinion presented as a fact a definition of a medical term a set of step-by-step directions the statement sounds certain, but "the only way" is an exaggeration that cannot be proven. no data are given, nothing is defined, and there are no steps.

as a lifelong farmer, i can tell you that the proposed groundwater fees will destroy family farms across the valley. these fees are nothing more than a tax on the people who feed america. which best describes the author's bias? the author strongly opposes the fees and writes as a farmer who would pay them. the author supports the fees as a way to protect the valley's groundwater supply. the author presents both sides of the groundwater issue fairly and equally. the author is biased in favor of city residents who use less groundwater. the author identifies as a farmer and uses strong words such as "destroy" and "nothing more than a tax." only one side is presented, and city residents are never mentioned.

which statements are opinions? select all that apply. nursing school is harder than medical school. california has 58 counties. night shifts are more interesting than day shifts. the teas includes a reading section. every nurse should learn spanish. "harder," "more interesting," and "should" express judgments that people may disagree with. the number of counties and the sections of the teas can be checked.

a survey found that 7 out of 10 patients rated the clinic "excellent." the clinic is therefore the best in the county. which part of the passage is a fact? the claim that the clinic is the best in the county the idea that every patient likes the clinic the survey result about patient ratings the idea that the clinic should expand the survey result can be checked against the survey data. "the best in the county" is an opinion that the survey does not prove. the last two choices are not in the passage.

click the sentence that states an opinion rather than a fact. a fact can be checked and proven. an opinion is a belief or judgment. "friendliest" is a judgment. people could disagree, and there is no way to prove it. the opening year, the number of rooms and the hours could all be checked.

which statement is an opinion? the clinic's waiting room was remodeled last year. the new waiting room is the nicest in town. patients waited an average of 12 minutes last month. the clinic is the largest in town, with six exam rooms. "nicest" is a judgment that people could disagree with; no measurement could prove it.

which statement is a fact? nursing is the most rewarding career in health care. california rns must pass the nclex-rn. twelve-hour shifts are too long for nurses to work safely. the nclex-rn is harder than any exam in nursing school. the nclex-rn licensing requirement can be verified with the state board of nursing. the other statements contain judgment words (most rewarding, too long, harder).

"our energy drink is the only way to stay alert during finals. don't be the student who fails because you were too tired!" which persuasive technique does this ad use? bandwagon appeal fear and exaggeration personal testimonial logical appeal with evidence "only way" is an exaggeration, and "don't be the student who fails" appeals to fear.

an article about a new diet is written by the owner of the company that sells the diet's meal plans. what is the most likely concern about the article? it may rely too heavily on scientific studies. the author may lack formal nutrition training. its information about the diet may be out of date. the author's profit motive may bias it. an author who profits from a product has a conflict of interest that may bias the article toward it.

which sentence from the passage expresses an opinion? "in the 1850s, investigations of cholera outbreaks pointed to contaminated drinking water rather than bad air." "they dug sewers to carry waste away from homes and built reservoirs to store cleaner water." "public health workers deserve far more credit than they usually receive." "beginning in the early 1900s, many cities also treated their drinking water with sand filters and chlorine." "deserve far more credit" is a judgment about what people should think. the other sentences report historical events that can be checked in records.

which statement from the letter is an opinion? "the people who work at eastside are the most dedicated health workers in the valley." "the clinic serves about 9,000 patients a year." "the nearest alternative will be a hospital emergency room six miles away." "some board members have said that the county simply cannot afford the clinic's $1.8 million yearly budget." "the most dedicated" is a judgment that cannot be measured or proven. patient numbers, distance, and what board members said can all be checked.

which detail suggests that the writer may have a personal bias in favor of the clinic? the clinic serves about 9,000 patients a year. she has been a patient at the clinic for eleven years. the nearest emergency room is six miles away. the county published a health report about the clinic. as a longtime patient, the writer has a personal stake in keeping the clinic open. the other choices are facts about the clinic and county, not about the writer's own connection.

which sentence from the passage expresses an opinion? "every city in the valley should open cooling centers on any day above 100 °f." "infants and young children heat up faster than adults do." "when the air is humid, sweat evaporates slowly, so it cools the body less." "the human body works best at a core temperature near 98.6 °f (37 °c)." "should" signals a recommendation, which is an opinion others might disagree with. the other sentences are scientific facts that can be checked.

which statements from the passage are facts that could be checked? select all that apply. the american academy of pediatrics recommended in 2014 that schools start no earlier than 8:30 a.m. those concerns deserve attention, but they are problems of scheduling. california law requires most public high schools to start no earlier than 8:30 a.m. any parent who has tried to wake a sixteen-year-old at 6 a.m. already knows the answer. our schools should keep the later start. the aap recommendation and the california law can be checked in published sources. the other statements are the author's judgments and opinions.

which statements from the advertisement are facts that could be checked? select all that apply. each tablet contains 500 mg of vitamin c. immunoboost max is the most powerful immune supplement on the market. these statements have not been evaluated by the food and drug administration. busy nurses, teachers, and parents everywhere trust immunoboost max. the offer for a free second bottle ends sunday. the amount of vitamin c, the fda disclaimer and the deadline of the offer can each be verified. "most powerful" and "trust ... everywhere" are opinions and exaggerations that cannot be measured.

what is the main purpose of the testimonial from dana r.? to give scientific proof that the product prevents colds to persuade readers using one customer's experience to explain the ingredients in each tablet to warn readers about side effects a testimonial is a persuasive technique. one person's experience isn't scientific evidence; she might have avoided colds for other reasons.

which phrase is meant to create a sense of urgency? "made in a facility that follows good manufacturing practices" "500 mg of vitamin c" "hurry: this offer ends sunday!" "not intended to diagnose, treat, cure, or prevent any disease" a deadline ("hurry," "ends sunday") pressures readers to buy quickly instead of comparing products.

which sentence from the flyer is an appeal to emotion rather than a plain fact? this year, getting protected takes about 15 minutes. nurses from the county health department will give the shots. protect yourself. protect your family. kids who get their shots will receive a free book and a sticker. "protect yourself. protect your family." pulls on the reader's feelings about keeping loved ones safe. the other choices state things you could check.

which statement from the letter is a fact that could be checked? closing it would be the worst decision this board has ever made. the clinic served 11,400 patient visits last year. anyone with common sense knows what will happen. board members have probably never set foot in our neighborhood. the visit count comes from the county's annual report, so it can be checked. the other choices are opinions or guesses.

the phrase "anyone with common sense knows" is an example of which technique? appeal to authority using statistics as evidence implying that opponents lack sense appeal to fear of a child's illness it implies that anyone who disagrees with the writer lacks common sense, instead of offering evidence. this is a persuasive technique, not proof.

which detail shows the writer's personal connection to the issue, which may affect her point of view? she cites the county's own annual report. she knows the bus ride to the next clinic takes over an hour. she has lived there 30 years; its nurses treated her family. she questions whether board members have ever visited the area. her family has used the clinic for years. this makes her well informed, but also personally invested, which readers should consider.

who wrote this blog post? an independent medical researcher the marketing team of the company that sells rushfuel a pre-nursing student named jenna a newspaper health reporter the byline says it was posted by the marketing team at rushfuel beverages, the company that profits from sales.

why should a reader be cautious about the claims in this post? the writers profit when readers buy the drink. the post admits energy drinks have been linked to heart problems. rushfuel has much more caffeine than coffee. blog posts are never reliable sources. because the authors earn money when people buy rushfuel, they are likely to present only information that favors the product. that is a source of bias.

what kind of support is jenna's quotation? a scientific study a personal testimonial a government statistic an expert opinion from a doctor jenna gives a single personal statement about her own experience. testimonials can be persuasive but are not strong evidence.

our campus should offer free flu shots to all students. last winter, flu outbreaks caused hundreds of missed classes, and many students could not afford to see a doctor. what is the author's main claim? flu outbreaks caused hundreds of missed classes. the campus should offer free flu shots to all students. many students could not afford to see a doctor. flu shots have serious side effects. the claim is the position the author wants readers to accept: the campus should offer free flu shots. missed classes and doctor costs are evidence that support the claim. side effects are never mentioned.

which evidence best supports the claim that later school start times improve students' health? many students say they enjoy eating breakfast at home with their families before school. most teachers in one survey said they prefer an early start so they can leave school sooner in the afternoon. school buses are expensive to operate, especially for districts that cover large rural areas. after one district started school an hour later, students slept more and saw the school nurse less. only the district example connects a later start time with a health result (more sleep, fewer nurse visits). the other choices are about breakfast habits, teacher preference, and cost, not student health.

a school claims that its new reading program raised third graders' test scores. which fact, if true, would most weaken this claim? teachers in the school said they enjoyed using the new program. the program cost the school about $10 per student each year to run. average scores rose by 12 points in the year after the program began. the state made the test easier in the same year the program began. if the test got easier, scores could have risen without any help from the program, so another explanation exists. teacher enjoyment and cost don't affect the claim, and a 12-point rise would support it.

"dr. gomez is an excellent heart surgeon, so her advice about which stocks to buy must be right." what is the flaw in this reasoning? surgeons are not allowed to give their patients advice of any kind. her skill in surgery does not make her an expert on investing. the statement relies on too many statistics. the statement attacks dr. gomez's character. this is a false appeal to authority: expertise in one field is used to support a claim in an unrelated field. the statement praises her, it does not attack her, and it contains no statistics.

the county clinic should stay open on weekends. (1) many patients work monday through friday and cannot come during the week. (2) the emergency room is crowded on weekends with patients who do not have emergencies. (3) the clinic building was painted blue last year. (4) during a trial, weekend appointments filled within hours. which sentence is not relevant to the argument? sentence 1 sentence 2 sentence 3 sentence 4 the color of the building has nothing to do with whether weekend hours are needed. patients' work schedules, er crowding, and fast-filling weekend appointments all support opening on weekends.

"my neighbor felt sick the day after his flu shot, so flu shots make people sick." what is the main flaw in this reasoning? it relies on the opinion of a medical expert. it attacks the character of people who get flu shots. it draws a broad conclusion from a single example. it offers only two choices when there are more. one person's experience is not enough evidence for a claim about everyone. this is a hasty generalization. no expert, personal attack, or either-or choice appears in the statement.

since the clinic began sending text-message reminders in january, patients have missed far fewer appointments. therefore, the text reminders are what reduced missed appointments. which assumption does this argument depend on? nothing else changed at the same time that could explain the drop. patients dislike receiving text messages from the clinic. the clinic also mails reminder cards to patients. most other clinics in the area do not send any appointment reminders. the argument says the texts caused the drop, which assumes there is no other explanation, such as a new bus route or easier scheduling. disliking texts would weaken the argument, mailed cards would be another explanation, and other clinics are irrelevant.

according to a recent survey of 1,200 california nurses, 40 percent said they planned to leave their jobs within five years. what type of evidence does the author use? a personal anecdote an expert's opinion statistics an analogy a survey result given as a percentage is statistical evidence. an anecdote is a personal story, and an analogy compares two different things.

claim: planting shade trees in south fresno neighborhoods would reduce heat-related illness. which evidence would most strengthen this claim? in a similar city, shadier blocks were up to 10 °f cooler and had fewer heat-related er visits. trees provide shade and homes for many kinds of birds and insects in the city. some residents say they would prefer palm trees to oak trees on their streets. young trees must be watered often during hot summers, which can raise water bills for residents. this evidence connects trees to both lower temperatures and fewer heat illnesses, which is exactly what the claim says. birds, tree preferences, and watering needs have nothing to do with heat illness.

some argue that limiting nurses to shifts of 12 hours or less would cause staffing shortages. however, research on fatigue shows that error rates rise sharply after 12 hours of work, and the cost of treating patients harmed by errors is far greater than the cost of hiring extra staff. how does the author respond to the counterargument? by agreeing that shift limits would cause too many staffing problems by arguing that fatigue-related errors cost more than extra staff by attacking the character of the people who disagree with the author by changing the subject to how much nurses are paid for overtime the author states the opposing view, then uses "however" to give evidence that errors are more costly than extra staff. the author does not agree with the opposing side, does not insult anyone, and does not discuss pay.

(1) seat belts cut the risk of death in a crash nearly in half for front-seat passengers. (2) yet some drivers skip buckling up on short trips. (3) many crashes happen close to home. (4) therefore, everyone should wear a seat belt on every trip, no matter how short. which sentence states the author's conclusion? sentence 1 sentence 2 sentence 3 sentence 4 "therefore" signals the conclusion, which is drawn from the facts in sentences 1–3.

"either we close the hospital's maternity ward, or the entire hospital will go bankrupt." what is the main flaw in this statement? it attacks the character of the people who disagree. it relies on a single personal example. it cites an expert from an unrelated field. it presents only two choices when other options may exist. this is a false dilemma (either-or reasoning): there may be other ways to save money, such as cutting other costs or finding grants.

which piece of evidence is strongest for the claim that a new asthma inhaler reduces emergency room visits? a patient who says that the new inhaler has completely changed her life for the better a company website that calls the inhaler "clinically proven" and "doctor recommended" a randomized study of 2,000 patients that found 30 percent fewer er visits with the new inhaler a doctor who says she likes prescribing the new inhaler to many of her patients with asthma a large, randomized study that measures er visits directly is the strongest kind of evidence. one patient's story, a seller's slogan, and a doctor's preference are weaker and may be biased.

councilmember reyes argues that the city needs more cooling-center space. last july, the city's two cooling centers turned away 140 people because they were full. heat-related visits to the county hospital's emergency room doubled during the july heat wave. reyes also notes that she grew up without air conditioning. the current centers offer free wi-fi. which statements from the passage provide evidence that the city needs more cooling-center space? select all that apply. the two centers turned away 140 people because they were full. heat-related er visits doubled during the heat wave. reyes grew up without air conditioning. the current centers offer free wi-fi. reyes is a member of the city council. people being turned away shows the centers are too small, and doubled er visits show many residents needed relief from the heat. reyes's childhood, the wi-fi, and her job title do not show a need for more space.

"this textbook is reliable because it says it is the most trustworthy textbook available." what is the flaw in this reasoning? it uses the claim itself as its own proof. it draws a conclusion from one example. it presents only two choices. it attacks the author of a different textbook. this is circular reasoning: the book's reliability is "proven" only by the book's own statement about itself.

students should eat breakfast before morning exams. in one study, students who ate breakfast scored higher on morning tests than students who skipped it. which statement is the evidence in this argument? students should eat breakfast before morning exams. morning exams cause many students a great deal of stress and worry. breakfast is the most important meal of the day for growing students. in one study, breakfast eaters scored higher on morning tests. the study result is the support offered for the claim. "students should eat breakfast" is the claim itself, and the other choices do not appear in the passage.

"we shouldn't listen to ms. tran's plan for the clinic. she drives an old car and can't even keep her lawn mowed." what is the flaw in this reasoning? it relies on statistics that are out of date. it attacks the person instead of responding to her plan. it offers only two possible choices when there are more. it uses the claim itself as the proof for the claim. this is an ad hominem attack: her car and lawn have nothing to do with whether her clinic plan is good.

all patients on the cardiac unit wear a heart monitor. mr. kim is wearing a heart monitor. based only on these statements, what can be concluded? mr. kim is on the cardiac unit. mr. kim is not on the cardiac unit. every patient with a heart monitor is on the cardiac unit. it cannot be determined whether mr. kim is on the cardiac unit. the statements say cardiac patients wear monitors, not that only cardiac patients wear them. patients on other units, such as the er, may also wear monitors, so mr. kim's unit cannot be determined.

our town of 3,000 people needs a pharmacy. the nearest one is 20 miles away, and the county bus runs only twice a day. older residents sometimes go days without their medicine because they cannot get a ride. which sentence, if added, would most strengthen the argument? 60 percent of older residents in a survey had missed doses because they could not reach a pharmacy. pharmacists earn some of the highest salaries in health care, so the job would easily attract workers. the town already has two grocery stores, a gas station, and a small public library downtown. some residents enjoy driving 20 miles to the city to shop and see a movie on weekends. the survey adds hard numbers that show how often the distance causes missed medicine. salaries and grocery stores are irrelevant, and residents who enjoy driving weakens rather than strengthens the case.

put the parts of this argument in the most logical order, from the claim to the conclusion. our college should add an evening section of anatomy. last semester, 85 students were on the waiting list for the only evening section. some may say that no instructors are available to teach at night. however, two part-time instructors have already offered to teach the class. adding the section would help working students stay on track for nursing school. a strong argument usually moves from claim, to evidence, to a counterargument, to a rebuttal ("however..."), to a conclusion. the counterargument must come before the "however" sentence that answers it.

click the sentence that gives evidence for the writer's claim, rather than just repeating the claim. evidence is specific information, such as data, a study or an example, that can be checked. the study result (injuries dropped by 20%) is evidence. the other sentences are claims or opinions. they tell you what the writer believes, but not why.

"the city should add bike lanes on shaw avenue. last year, 14 cyclists were injured there, and cities that added protected lanes saw injuries fall." what evidence does the author give? a personal story about an injured cyclist injury counts and other cities' results a traffic engineer's recommendation data on how many cyclists use shaw avenue the author cites 14 injuries on shaw avenue and falling injuries in cities that added protected lanes.

"everyone in my study group passed the exam after using flashcards, so flashcards guarantee a passing score." what is the main weakness in this argument? it attacks students who study differently. it appeals to emotion instead of reason. it overgeneralizes from one small group. it contradicts the example it gives. one study group is too small to prove that flashcards "guarantee" success, and the group may have passed for other reasons.

an author claims that walking 30 minutes a day improves mood. which evidence would best support this claim? the author enjoys walking and feels happier after every walk. a study of 2,000 adults linking daily walks to less depression a study showing that walkers have lower blood pressure a survey finding that most adults walk less than experts advise a large study that measures mood in daily walkers directly supports the claim. evidence must match the claim's exact topic.

"students who eat breakfast earn higher grades. therefore, the school should provide free breakfast to every student." which assumption does this argument depend on? eating breakfast itself causes the higher grades. every student at the school already eats breakfast. students with higher grades tend to eat breakfast. free breakfast would cost the school too much. the argument assumes eating breakfast causes better grades, not just that the two go together. if grades were higher for another reason, free breakfast might not help.

which detail from the passage best supports the claim that heavy groundwater pumping has a "hidden cost"? surface water is plentiful and relatively cheap in wet years. farmers reach groundwater by drilling wells. much of the valley receives less than 12 inches of rain a year. some small household wells go dry, and in some places the land sinks. the hidden cost is the harm that over-pumping causes, and dry wells and sinking land are examples of that harm. the other details describe water sources and rainfall, not costs of pumping.

which evidence from the passage best supports the claim that sleep helps strengthen memories? the body releases growth hormone and repairs its tissues during deep sleep. students who slept after learning words remembered more than students who stayed awake. in mice, the spaces between brain cells widen during sleep so that waste can wash away. bright evening light can delay the release of melatonin. the word-list experiment directly measured memory after sleep versus after staying awake. growth hormone relates to tissue repair, the brain-cell spaces relate to waste removal, and melatonin relates to falling asleep.

how does the writer respond to the argument that the county cannot afford the clinic? she cites a county report showing the clinic cuts costly er visits, so closing it will cost more. she agrees with the board and suggests that the clinic cut its hours to save money instead. she attacks the character of the board members who want to close it. she ignores the cost argument and talks only about how dedicated the clinic's staff members are. she acknowledges the concern ("i understand that the county faces hard choices"), then answers it with evidence from the county's own report. she never suggests cutting hours, never insults board members, and directly addresses the cost argument.

which new fact would most weaken the argument in passage 1? programs that use a lottery graduate a more diverse group of nurses. many applicants work full-time jobs while they take prerequisite courses. in one study, lottery admits failed out at twice the rate of ranked admits. test-prep courses cost more than many working families can afford. passage 1 claims that students who meet the minimum can succeed and the extra points matter little. evidence that lottery students fail out far more often challenges that claim directly.

what is the author's main claim? teenagers should go to bed earlier on school nights. schools should keep later start times for teenagers. after-school sports should be moved to the weekend. school buses should run more often in the morning. the author argues throughout, and concludes, that "our schools should keep the later start."

how does the author respond to critics in the third paragraph? by ignoring the critics' concerns completely by agreeing that later start times should be reversed by admitting the concerns are real but solvable by proving that buses and jobs are not affected the author says the concerns "deserve attention" but are "problems of scheduling, not reasons to ignore students' health." this is a counterargument followed by a rebuttal.

which sentence offers the weakest support for the author's claim? during puberty, the body's internal clock shifts later, so teens can't fall asleep early. districts that moved their start times have reported better attendance. studies have linked adequate sleep to fewer car crashes among teen drivers. any parent who has tried to wake a sixteen-year-old at 6 a.m. already knows the answer. the last-paragraph sentence appeals to common experience rather than evidence. the other choices are based on biology, district reports or studies.

which statement best evaluates the advertisement's claim that the product helps you "feel unstoppable this flu season"? it is well supported because each tablet contains vitamin c, zinc and vitamin d. it is well supported because a customer reported not getting a single cold all winter. it is weakly supported; the fine print says it isn't meant to prevent disease. it is proven, because the food and drug administration has approved the product. the ad offers only a testimonial and a list of ingredients, and its own disclaimer says the fda has not evaluated the statements and the product is not meant to prevent disease.

which claim is supported by evidence in the second paragraph? walking 10,000 steps a day is required for good health at every age. in one study, the benefit leveled off near 7,500 steps a day. walking more than 7,500 steps a day can be harmful for older women. younger adults need fewer daily steps than older adults to benefit. the study of older women found the benefit grew with steps but leveled off at about 7,500.

which statement, if true, would most strengthen the author's final point? most fitness trackers still set 10,000 steps as their default daily goal. another study found adding 2,000 daily steps to a low baseline cut heart problems. the word manpo-kei is still used in japan to describe a pedometer. some very active people walk more than 15,000 steps on a typical day. the final point is that small increases from a low baseline can help. a study showing benefit from adding 2,000 steps supports it directly.

which piece of information would most strengthen the writer's argument that closing the clinic won't really save money? a survey showing that westside residents want the clinic to stay open proof that the $1.2 million savings estimate is accurate er cost data from another county after a similar clinic closed patient testimonials praising the clinic's nurses her key claim is that skipped care leads to expensive er visits. real cost data from a similar closure would directly support it.

which statement is the best evaluation of how the post handles news stories about heart problems? it proves energy drinks are completely safe. it ignores the heart-problem stories altogether. it answers the concern with data from several medical studies. it mentions the concern, then dismisses it without evidence. the post mentions the heart-problem stories and then claims they "usually" involve heavy use, without citing any data. it downplays a counterargument instead of answering it with evidence.

what is the author's main claim? hospitals should rethink 12-hour shifts because of fatigue. 12-hour shifts give nurses more days off and fewer handoffs. tired nurses make more medication errors than rested ones. hospitals should ban all shifts longer than 8 hours. the author presents research on burnout, errors and fatigue, then proposes more 8-hour shifts, overtime caps and true breaks.

which evidence best supports the claim that long shifts can affect patient safety? nurses get four days off each week. medication-error risk rose in the last hours of long shifts. there are fewer handoffs between shifts. nurses working shifts of 10 hours or longer reported more burnout. rising medication errors late in long shifts directly links shift length to patient safety.

which statement, if true, would most weaken the author's argument? a large study found equal error rates on 8- and 12-hour shifts. many nurses say they prefer 12-hour shifts because of the days off. hiring replacement nurses is expensive. some nurses on 8-hour shifts also report burnout. the argument depends on long shifts causing more errors. a large study finding no difference would undercut that key link.

which phrase from the passage is the weakest evidence? 72% of students said they liked vegetables more. the salad bar "seemed busier." 180 students answered the survey. larger studies have found garden programs can increase vegetable eating. "seemed busier" is a vague impression with no count or measurement, so it is the weakest evidence.

why do the researchers question the principal's conclusion? it measured neither actual eating nor a no-garden school. only 180 students answered the survey. the garden program lasted only one year. larger studies found that garden programs have no effect at all. without before-and-after measurements or a comparison group, it's impossible to know whether the garden itself caused any change.

which conclusion is best supported by all of the information in the passage? the garden proves that gardening makes children eat healthier. the survey shows students' eating habits did not change. garden programs only work while the program is running. the garden may have helped, but the evidence isn't conclusive. the survey is encouraging, but the researchers' cautions and the larger studies point to a modest, uncertain effect. a careful reader wouldn't go beyond that.

which detail best supports the idea that insulin dramatically changed the outlook for patients? before the 1920s, type 1 diabetes was a death sentence. leonard thompson, near death, lived 13 more years. the extract lowered blood sugar in diabetic dogs. thompson's first dose was too impure to help much. thompson went from near death to living 13 more years, a vivid example of the change from "death sentence" to treatable condition.

an article about sleep includes the table below. survey of college students daily screen time after 9 p.m. average sleep (hours) less than 30 minutes 7.8 30–60 minutes 7.1 1–2 hours 6.5 more than 2 hours 5.9 which statement best describes the relationship shown in the table? as late-night screen time increases, average sleep decreases. as late-night screen time increases, average sleep increases. late-night screen time has no relationship to sleep. students with the most screen time sleep about 7.8 hours. moving down the table, screen time goes up while sleep goes down (7.8 to 5.9 hours): a negative relationship. 7.8 hours goes with the least screen time.

health guidelines suggest limiting added sugars to less than 10 percent of daily calories. for a 2,000-calorie diet, that is about 50 grams of added sugar per day. maya drinks one cola and one sports drink in a day. drink (12 fl oz) added sugars (g) cola 39 sweet tea 32 sports drink 21 sparkling water 0 based on the passage and the table, which statement is true? maya's drinks contain 60 g of added sugar, which is under the limit. maya's drinks contain 39 g of added sugar, which is under the limit. maya's drinks contain 60 g of added sugar, which is over the limit. maya's drinks contain exactly 50 g of added sugar. cola 39 g + sports drink 21 g = 60 g. 60 g is more than the suggested 50 g limit, even before she eats any food.

ty works every day and can study only after his shift ends at 5:30 p.m. day library hours monday–thursday 8 a.m.–8 p.m. friday 8 a.m.–5 p.m. saturday 10 a.m.–2 p.m. sunday closed on which days can ty study at the library after his shift? monday through friday saturday and sunday every day except sunday monday through thursday the library is open after 5:30 p.m. only monday–thursday (until 8 p.m.). it closes at 5 p.m. on friday, at 2 p.m. on saturday, and is closed sunday.

most newborns lose a little weight in their first few days, but they usually return to their birth weight by about 2 weeks of age. infant weight checks age weight (lb) birth 7.5 2 weeks 7.8 1 month 9.0 2 months 11.2 is this infant's growth consistent with the passage? no; the infant did not lose any weight after birth. yes; by 2 weeks the infant weighed more than at birth. no; the infant weighed less at 2 weeks than at birth. yes; the infant doubled its birth weight by 1 month. at 2 weeks the infant weighed 7.8 lb, above the birth weight of 7.5 lb, which matches "return to birth weight by about 2 weeks." the table does not show the first few days, so we cannot say the infant never lost weight. 9.0 lb is not double 7.5 lb.

one morning, jess drinks 4 fl oz of brewed coffee, 16 fl oz of black tea, 8 fl oz of an energy drink, and 16 fl oz of green tea. approximate caffeine content drink (per 8 fl oz) caffeine (mg) brewed coffee 95 energy drink 80 black tea 47 green tea 28 put the drinks in order from the most caffeine jess got to the least. black tea energy drink green tea brewed coffee adjust each drink for the amount: coffee 4 oz = ½ × 95 = 47.5 mg; black tea 16 oz = 2 × 47 = 94 mg; energy drink 8 oz = 80 mg; green tea 16 oz = 2 × 28 = 56 mg. most to least: black tea (94), energy drink (80), green tea (56), coffee (47.5). coffee has the most per 8 oz, but jess drank only half a serving.

a state grant will go to the county with the lowest rate of health insurance. county residents with health insurance county a 88% county b 92% county c 85% county d 90% which county will receive the grant? county c county b county a county d county c has the lowest insured rate, 85%. county b has the highest rate, the opposite of what the grant requires.

the table shows asthma visits at a clinic. click the row for the month with the largest increase from the month before. find each month's change from the month before: feb 38 − 42 = −4, mar 51 − 38 = +13, apr 70 − 51 = +19, may 47 − 70 = −23. the largest increase is april (+19). april also has the most visits, but the question asks about the change, not the total. may has the biggest change, but it is a decrease.
according to the table, which activity burns the most calories in 30 minutes? walking bicycling swimming running running (360) is the largest value in the table.

why is the asterisk note important when using this table? it shows that the values are averages for all adults. it explains how the calories were measured. it tells which activity is best for losing weight fastest. the values are for a 155-lb person; others will differ. the note says the values are for a 155-lb person; people who weigh more or less burn different amounts, so the numbers can't be applied to everyone.

a graph shows the number of measles cases in a county by month. cases rise sharply in march and fall back to near zero by june. which statement is supported by the graph? measles cases peaked in spring and then declined. measles was eliminated from the county after june. measles cases rose steadily all year. measles cases reached their peak in june. cases rose sharply in march and fell to near zero by june, so the peak was in spring.

which program gives a qualified applicant the best chance of getting a seat? college a college b college c all programs give the same chance. seats ÷ applicants: a = 40/200 = 20%, b = 60/180 ≈ 33%, c = 30/210 ≈ 14%. college b has the best odds.

a reader finds this table of reported valley fever cases in one county for a single year. season winter spring summer fall reported cases 80 70 110 190 do the data support the passage's statement about when cases peak? no; the most cases were reported in the summer. no; cases were about the same in every season. yes; the most cases were reported in the fall. yes; the most cases were reported in the winter. the passage says cases often peak in the fall. fall has the highest count in the table (190). summer (110) is second, and winter and spring are the lowest.
