which statement is supported by both the passage and the table? in a dry year, extra pumping replaces most, but not all, of the lost surface water. in a dry year, the district has more total water available than it has in a wet year. in a dry year, surface water supplies most of the district's water. the district pumps about the same amount of groundwater in wet years and dry years. surface water drops by 300,000 − 60,000 = 240,000 acre-feet. groundwater rises by 280,000 − 100,000 = 180,000 acre-feet. 180,000 replaces most of the 240,000 lost, but the total still falls from 400,000 to 340,000. in a dry year, surface water is only 60,000 of 340,000, and groundwater use clearly changes.

ana plans to apply in february 2027. her teas results are shown below. attempt test date total score 1 november 2024 58% 2 january 2025 66% based on the directions and the table, can ana use her teas score for this application? yes, because her second score is above 62 percent. no, because her passing score will be more than two years old. no, because she took the test more than once. yes, because she waited more than the required 30 days to retest. her only passing score (66%) is from january 2025. scores are valid for two years, so it expires in january 2027. by february 2027 the score is more than two years old, so she must retest. retesting is allowed, so taking the test twice is not the problem.

which statement is supported by the table? er visits were highest on wednesday, in the middle of the week. er visits stayed about the same all week, whatever the temperature. friday had more er visits than tuesday, even though it was cooler. er visits rose with the high temperature and peaked on thursday. the hottest day, thursday (109 °f), had the most visits (22), and visits generally rose and fell with temperature. wednesday had 17 visits, fewer than thursday; friday had 7, fewer than tuesday's 9.

how long does the bus take to travel from the downtown transit center to the medical center? 8 minutes 21 minutes 35 minutes 45 minutes each trip leaves downtown and reaches the medical center 35 minutes later (for example, 6:10 → 6:45).

a student must be at the medical center by 8:00 a.m. for a clinical shift. what is the latest time she can catch the bus at main st & 5th? 6:48 a.m. 7:18 a.m. 7:48 a.m. 8:33 a.m. the 7:18 bus from main st & 5th reaches the medical center at 7:45, before 8:00. the next one (7:48) arrives at 8:15, which is too late.

based on the schedule notes, when should the next bus leave the downtown transit center after the 8:25 a.m. bus? 8:55 a.m. 9:10 a.m. 9:25 a.m. 9:40 a.m. the note says buses run every 45 minutes after 7:40 a.m. 8:25 + 45 minutes = 9:10.

which statements are supported by the schedule? select all that apply. buses leave every 30 minutes from 6:10 to 7:40 a.m. a student with a valid id pays no fare. the bus runs on saturdays. the bus waits at each stop until all riders board. the college library is 14 minutes from the medical center. the first four buses leave 30 minutes apart. students with id ride free. the notes say route 28 runs monday through saturday. 6:31 → 6:45 is 14 minutes. the notes say buses do not wait for late riders.
how many grams of added sugars are in the whole container? 9 g 11 g 54 g 66 g each bar has 9 g of added sugars, and there are 6 bars: 9 × 6 = 54 g.
based on the label's guide, which nutrient in one bar is closest to being "high"? sodium dietary fiber added sugars total fat 20% dv or more is high. added sugars are at 18%, the closest to 20%.

what is the purpose of the asterisk (*) after "% daily value"? it marks the nutrient the company most wants you to notice. it points to a note explaining what % daily value means. it shows that the values were not tested. it marks the nutrients that are high. the asterisk links to the note at the bottom, which explains % dv, the 2,000-calorie basis and the low/high guide.

a student eats 3 bars in one day. what percent of the daily value for saturated fat does that provide? 7.5% 13% 26% 39% one bar gives 13% dv of saturated fat. three bars give 3 × 13% = 39%. (label percents are rounded, so working from grams gives a slightly different 37.5%; use the %dv on the label.)
in which year were child asthma ed visits the lowest? 2019 2020 2022 2023 the visit column is lowest in 2023, at 62 per 10,000 children.

by how many days did the number of unhealthy air days change from 2020 to 2023? it decreased by 28 days. it decreased by 13 days. it increased by 28 days. it decreased by 18 days. 46 days (2020) − 18 days (2023) = 28 fewer days.

which statement best explains why 2020 does not follow the same pattern as the other years? wildfires in 2020 did not affect the county's air quality in any measurable way. families avoided eds that year, so visits undercount asthma problems. the department stopped counting ed visits partway through 2020 because of the closures. fewer children in the county had asthma in 2020 than in any other year. 2020 had the most unhealthy days but relatively few ed visits. the note explains that families avoided eds except for serious problems during the closures.

which conclusion is best supported by the table and notes? air pollution is the only cause of childhood asthma in valley county. over most years, fewer unhealthy air days came with fewer child asthma ed visits. every neighborhood in the county has about the same level of air pollution. child asthma ed visits will keep falling and reach zero by 2025. leaving out the unusual year 2020, the two years with the fewest unhealthy days (2022 and 2023) also had the fewest visits, and the two worst years (2019 and 2021) had the most. the match isn't perfect year by year. the data show a pattern (association), not proof of cause.
according to the chart, in which month were the most heat-related illness reports made? june july august september july's bar is the tallest, at 61 reports.
about how many more reports were there in july than in may? 14 38 47 61 july had 61 and may had 14: 61 − 14 = 47 more reports.

click the plane that divides the body into right and left portions. a sagittal plane runs vertically from front to back, so it splits the body into right and left parts. the midsagittal plane passes straight down the middle of the body from front to back. notice the dark line where it cuts the body's midline: it makes equal right and left halves. the horizontal sheet is the transverse plane (upper and lower parts). the sheet that runs from one shoulder to the other is the frontal plane (front and back parts).

a radiology student needs an image that separates the front of the body from the back. click the plane that makes this division. front and back means anterior and posterior. the plane that separates them is the frontal (coronal) plane. the frontal plane runs from one side of the body to the other, through both shoulders and hips, so the face and chest are on one side and the back is on the other. a sagittal plane would make right and left parts, and a transverse plane would make upper and lower parts.

the plane labeled c divides the body into which portions? anterior and posterior superior and inferior right and left proximal and distal plane c is horizontal, so it is the transverse (horizontal) plane. a horizontal cut separates an upper (superior) part from a lower (inferior) part. ct images are usually transverse "slices" like this. anterior/posterior is made by the frontal plane (b), right/left by the sagittal plane (a). proximal and distal describe positions along a limb, not a plane.

in the side view the person faces to the right. which letter marks the arrow that points in the anterior (ventral) direction? e f g d anterior (ventral) means toward the front of the body, the side the face and belly are on. the person faces right, so the arrow pointing right, d, points anterior. e points toward the back (posterior), f points up (superior), and g points down (inferior).

click the body cavity that holds the urinary bladder, the rectum, and the internal reproductive organs. the urinary bladder, rectum, and internal reproductive organs sit low in the trunk, inside the bony pelvis. that space is the pelvic cavity, the lowest part of the ventral body cavity, just below the abdominal cavity. the abdominal cavity, just above it, holds organs such as the stomach, liver, and most of the intestines.

which of the lettered structures are parts of the ventral body cavity? select all that apply. a b c d e f the ventral cavity is on the front (belly) side of the trunk. it includes the thoracic cavity (c), the abdominal cavity (e), and the pelvic cavity (f). a (cranial cavity) and b (vertebral cavity) form the dorsal cavity, which protects the brain and spinal cord. d is the diaphragm. it is a muscle that separates the thoracic cavity from the abdominal cavity. it is not a cavity itself.

based on the diagram, which statement about the thoracic cavity is correct? it is part of the dorsal body cavity, along with the cranial and vertebral cavities. it is inferior to the abdominal cavity. it is superior to the abdominal cavity and separated from it by the diaphragm. it is continuous with the cranial cavity through the neck. the thoracic cavity (chest) sits above the abdominal cavity, so it is superior to it. the dome-shaped diaphragm forms the wall between the two cavities. the thoracic cavity is part of the ventral cavity, not the dorsal cavity. the cranial cavity connects to the vertebral cavity, not to the thoracic cavity.

in anatomical position, the wrist is ______ to the elbow. proximal distal superior deep proximal and distal compare positions along a limb: proximal = closer to where the limb attaches to the trunk, distal = farther away. the wrist is farther from the shoulder than the elbow is, so the wrist is distal to the elbow. "superior" is wrong: in anatomical position the arms hang down, so the wrist is below the elbow.

which plane divides the body into anterior (front) and posterior (back) portions? frontal (coronal) plane sagittal (lateral) plane transverse (horizontal) plane midsagittal plane a frontal (coronal) plane runs side to side, like a crown headband, separating front from back. sagittal and midsagittal planes divide left from right; a transverse plane divides superior from inferior.

a ct scan shows a "slice" of the abdomen that separates the body into upper and lower portions. which plane is this? frontal (coronal) plane midsagittal (median) plane oblique plane transverse (horizontal) plane a transverse plane runs horizontally and divides the body into superior and inferior parts. most ct and mri images of the trunk are viewed as transverse (cross-sectional) slices.

the heart and lungs are located in which body cavity? abdominal cavity pelvic cavity thoracic cavity cranial cavity the thoracic (chest) cavity is the part of the ventral cavity above the diaphragm. it contains the lungs (in pleural cavities) and the heart (in the pericardial cavity within the mediastinum).

a patient at a visalia urgent care has fever and pain that began near the navel and has moved to the lower right abdomen. appendicitis is suspected. in which abdominopelvic quadrant is the appendix located? left lower quadrant right lower quadrant right upper quadrant left upper quadrant the appendix hangs from the cecum, the first part of the large intestine, in the right lower quadrant (rlq). right and left always refer to the patient's right and left, not the viewer's.

what is the smallest level of organization that can carry out all the functions of life? cell molecule tissue organ molecules (like dna or proteins) are not alive by themselves. the cell is the smallest living unit; tissues and organs are built from many cells.

put these levels of structural organization in order from simplest (smallest) to most complex. chemical (atoms and molecules) cell tissue organ organ system atoms and molecules form cells. similar cells working together form a tissue. two or more tissue types form an organ, and organs working together form an organ system.

which tissue type covers body surfaces, lines body cavities and hollow organs, and forms glands? connective tissue muscle tissue nervous tissue epithelial tissue epithelial tissue forms sheets that cover and line surfaces (skin epidermis, lining of the gi tract) and forms glands. connective tissue supports and binds; muscle contracts; nervous tissue conducts signals.

which of the following are types of connective tissue? select all that apply. blood bone adipose (fat) tissue epidermis of the skin cardiac muscle connective tissues have cells scattered in an extracellular matrix: blood (liquid plasma matrix), bone (mineralized matrix), and adipose tissue are all connective tissue. the epidermis is epithelial tissue, and cardiac muscle is muscle tissue.

the walls of the alveoli (air sacs) in the lungs are made of simple squamous epithelium. which feature of this tissue best explains why it is found there? many stacked layers of cells protect the lungs from abrasion cilia on the cells sweep mucus and trapped dust out of the lungs a single layer of thin, flat cells allows rapid diffusion of gases tall columnar cells secrete large amounts of mucus into the sacs "simple" means one cell layer and "squamous" means flat cells, so the barrier is extremely thin. a thin barrier lets o₂ and co₂ diffuse quickly between air and blood. stacked (stratified) layers protect areas like the skin; ciliated and mucus-secreting cells line the larger airways, not the alveoli.

which of the following is an example of negative feedback? oxytocin release that strengthens uterine contractions during labor sweating when body temperature rises above normal activated platelets attracting more platelets to a forming clot milk release that increases as an infant continues to nurse negative feedback reverses a change and brings a variable back toward its set point. sweating cools the body, reversing the rise in temperature. the other three are positive feedback: the response amplifies the original change until an event (birth, clot, feeding) ends it.

during labor, stretching of the cervix triggers release of a hormone that makes uterine contractions stronger, which stretches the cervix even more. which hormone and which type of feedback does this describe? oxytocin; positive feedback oxytocin; negative feedback prolactin; positive feedback progesterone; negative feedback the hormone that stimulates uterine contractions is oxytocin, released from the posterior pituitary. the response (stronger contractions) increases the original stimulus (cervical stretch), so it is positive feedback; it stops when the baby is delivered. prolactin stimulates milk production, and progesterone actually helps keep the uterus quiet during pregnancy.

in a homeostatic feedback loop, which component detects a change in the internal environment? control center effector set point receptor (sensor) the receptor senses the change and sends information to the control center. the control center compares the value to the set point, and the effector (a muscle or gland) carries out the response.

a phlebotomist draws blood from a vein in the antecubital region. where is this? the back (posterior) of the knee the armpit (axillary region) the front (anterior) of the elbow the groin (inguinal region) antecubital means "in front of the elbow" (ante = before, cubitus = elbow). the back of the knee is the popliteal region, the armpit is the axillary region, and the groin is the inguinal region.

a nurse checks for a pulse in the hollow behind the knee. which pulse is this? femoral pulse popliteal pulse brachial pulse radial pulse the popliteal region is the posterior knee, where the popliteal artery can be felt. the femoral pulse is in the groin, the brachial pulse is in the arm near the elbow, and the radial pulse is at the thumb side of the wrist.

which of the following organs are located in the abdominopelvic cavity? select all that apply. liver urinary bladder small intestine lungs thyroid gland the abdominopelvic cavity lies below the diaphragm. the liver and small intestine are in the abdominal portion; the urinary bladder is in the pelvic portion. the lungs are in the thoracic cavity, and the thyroid gland is in the neck, outside the ventral body cavity.

the ventral body cavity is divided into the thoracic cavity and the abdominopelvic cavity by a dome-shaped muscle called the ______. the diaphragm separates the chest (thoracic) cavity above from the abdominopelvic cavity below. it is also the main muscle of breathing.

which serous membrane is attached directly to the outer surface of each lung? visceral pleura parietal pleura visceral pericardium parietal peritoneum visceral layers cover organs (viscera); parietal layers line the cavity walls. "pleura" refers to the lungs, "pericardium" to the heart, and "peritoneum" to the abdominal cavity. so the membrane on the lung surface is the visceral pleura.

which statement uses a directional term incorrectly for a person in anatomical position? the sternum is medial to the arms. the skin is superficial to the skeletal muscles. the nose is anterior to the ears. the knee is proximal to the hip. the hip is closer to the trunk than the knee, so the knee is distal to the hip, not proximal. the sternum is near the midline (medial), the skin is closer to the surface (superficial), and the nose is in front of (anterior to) the ears, so those statements are correct.

homeostasis is best described as keeping every body variable at one exact value at every moment of the day the body's repair response that occurs only after an injury or infection keeping internal conditions within a stable range despite outside changes the steady growth of new cells to replace old, worn-out ones homeostasis means keeping internal conditions (temperature, blood glucose, ph) within a narrow normal range. values fluctuate around a set point; they are not frozen at one exact number.

the spinal cord is protected within which body cavity? thoracic (chest) cavity vertebral (spinal) cavity pelvic (hip) cavity pericardial (heart) cavity the dorsal body cavity has two parts: the cranial cavity (brain) and the vertebral cavity (spinal cord). the thoracic, pelvic, and pericardial cavities are all parts of the ventral body cavity.

a patient's chart says a wound is located on the "plantar" surface. where should the nurse look? the sole of the foot the palm of the hand the back of the hand the top of the head plantar refers to the sole of the foot (think "planting" your foot on the ground). the palm is the palmar surface, the back of the hand is dorsal, and the top of the head is the cranial or parietal region.

click the plane that divides the body into upper (superior) and lower (inferior) parts. a transverse (horizontal) plane cuts straight across the body. everything above it is superior and everything below it is inferior. ct scans are usually viewed as a stack of transverse 'slices.'

in the side view, click the arrow that points in the posterior (dorsal) direction. posterior (dorsal) means toward the back of the body. the person in the side view faces right, so the arrow pointing left, toward her back, is posterior. the arrow pointing right is anterior, the one pointing up is superior and the one pointing down is inferior.

a wound on the knee is described as "inferior to the hip." in the side view, click the arrow that shows the inferior direction. inferior means below, or toward the feet. the knee is lower on the body than the hip, so it is inferior to the hip. superior is the opposite direction, toward the head.

click the body cavity that protects the brain. the cranial cavity is formed by the bones of the skull and holds the brain. it is part of the dorsal body cavity, along with the vertebral cavity. the ventral cavities (thoracic, abdominal, pelvic) are in the front of the trunk.

click the body cavity that holds the heart and lungs. the thoracic cavity is the chest cavity, above the diaphragm. it contains the heart (in the mediastinum) and both lungs (in the pleural cavities). the abdominal cavity is below the diaphragm.

click the dome-shaped muscle that separates the thoracic cavity from the abdominal cavity. the diaphragm is a sheet of skeletal muscle under the lungs. when it contracts it flattens and moves down, making the thoracic cavity larger so air flows in. it forms the floor of the thoracic cavity and the roof of the abdominal cavity.

a lumbar puncture (spinal tap) draws fluid from around the spinal cord. click the cavity the needle enters. the spinal cord and the fluid around it sit in the vertebral (spinal) cavity. this cavity runs through the openings in the stacked vertebrae and is continuous with the cranial cavity. together, the cranial and vertebral cavities make up the dorsal body cavity.

click the part of the loop that compares body temperature with its set point and decides what to do. the control center receives information from the receptors, compares it with the set point (about 37 °c), and sends commands out. for body temperature, the control center is the hypothalamus in the brain. receptors only detect the change, and effectors only carry out the response.

in this loop, what role do the sweat glands play? receptor control center effector stimulus effectors are the muscles or glands that carry out the control center's commands. sweat glands release sweat, and evaporation cools the skin. dilated skin blood vessels also release heat. both are effectors. thermoreceptors are the receptors, and the hypothalamus is the control center.

during childbirth, the baby's head stretches the cervix, which triggers oxytocin release, which makes contractions stronger, which stretches the cervix even more, until the baby is born. how does this differ from the loop in the diagram? it is positive feedback: the response makes the original change bigger instead of reversing it. it is also negative feedback, because the loop eventually stops. it has no control center, so it is not a feedback loop. it is negative feedback, because oxytocin is a hormone. in the diagram (negative feedback), the response cancels the stimulus: rising temperature leads to cooling, so the body returns to its set point. in childbirth, the response (stronger contractions) increases the stimulus (more stretch). that is positive feedback, and it keeps building until an event (birth) ends it. positive feedback is rare in the body; other examples are blood clotting and breastfeeding (milk let-down). most of homeostasis uses negative feedback.

a patient points to pain right around the navel (belly button). tap that abdominopelvic region. the navel sits in the center square, the umbilical region (umbilicus = navel). the nine regions are made by two vertical lines and two horizontal lines, like a tic-tac-toe board over the abdomen.

appendicitis classically causes pain in the patient's lower right abdomen. the figure is a front view of the patient. tap that region. the appendix hangs off the large intestine in the patient's right iliac (inguinal) region. in a front view, the patient's right side is on your left, so it's the lower-left square on the screen. this left-right flip is one of the most common teas traps.

most of the liver and the gallbladder lie in which lettered region? a c b e the liver sits under the right ribs, so it fills mostly the patient's right hypochondriac region (a) and extends into the epigastric region (b). "hypo-" (below) + "chondr-" (cartilage) = below the rib cartilages. the spleen sits on the other side, in the left hypochondriac region (c).

click the chamber that pumps oxygen-rich blood out to the whole body. oxygen-rich blood (red) comes back from the lungs to the left side of the heart. the left ventricle pumps that blood into the aorta, which carries it to the body. its thick muscular wall gives it the force to do this. the left atrium also holds oxygen-rich blood, but it only passes blood down to the left ventricle. it does not pump blood to the body.

click the valve that blood passes through as it leaves the right atrium. blood in the right atrium flows down into the right ventricle. the valve between them is the tricuspid valve (right atrioventricular valve). it has three flaps. the pulmonary valve is the next valve on the path. blood passes through it when it leaves the right ventricle.

a patient has a narrowed (stenotic) valve. because of it, the left ventricle must work harder to push blood into the aorta. click that valve. blood leaves the left ventricle through the aortic valve and enters the aorta. if the aortic valve is narrowed, the left ventricle must squeeze harder to push blood through the smaller opening. over time its wall thickens. the mitral valve lets blood into the left ventricle, not out of it. the pulmonary valve is on the right side of the heart.

the vessel labeled j carries: oxygen-rich blood from the left ventricle to the body oxygen-poor blood from the right ventricle to the lungs oxygen-rich blood from the lungs to the left atrium oxygen-poor blood from the body to the right atrium j is the pulmonary trunk. it leaves the right ventricle and splits into the right and left pulmonary arteries. it carries oxygen-poor blood (blue) to the lungs to pick up o₂. the aorta (i) carries blood to the body, the pulmonary veins (m) bring blood back from the lungs, and the venae cavae (k, l) bring blood back from the body.

when the left ventricle contracts, which lettered valve closes so that blood does not flow back into the left atrium? e g f h the valve between the left atrium and the left ventricle is the mitral (bicuspid) valve, f. when the ventricle contracts, the rising pressure snaps the mitral valve shut, so blood can only leave through the aortic valve (h). e is the tricuspid valve (right side), and g is the pulmonary valve.

a red blood cell has just left the superior vena cava. put these structures in the order it passes through them, first to last. right atrium tricuspid valve right ventricle pulmonary valve pulmonary trunk the superior vena cava empties oxygen-poor blood into the right atrium. from the right atrium, blood passes through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle. the right ventricle pumps it through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk, which carries it toward the lungs.

using the diagram, which vessels carry oxygen-rich blood? select all that apply. aorta pulmonary veins pulmonary trunk superior vena cava inferior vena cava the pulmonary veins bring freshly oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium. the aorta carries that same oxygen-rich blood from the left ventricle to the body. the pulmonary trunk carries oxygen-poor blood to the lungs. the superior and inferior venae cavae return oxygen-poor blood from the body. the common trap is thinking all veins carry oxygen-poor blood. the pulmonary veins are the exception in adults.

put these structures in the order that oxygen-poor blood passes through them on its way from the body to the lungs. superior and inferior venae cavae right atrium tricuspid valve right ventricle pulmonary valve oxygen-poor blood from the body returns through the venae cavae into the right atrium. it passes the tricuspid (right av) valve into the right ventricle. the right ventricle pumps it through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk and arteries toward the lungs.

put these structures in the order that oxygen-rich blood passes through them, starting from the lungs. pulmonary veins left atrium mitral (bicuspid) valve left ventricle aorta oxygen-rich blood returns from the lungs through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium. it flows through the mitral (bicuspid) valve into the left ventricle. the left ventricle pumps it through the aortic valve into the aorta and out to the body.

which vessel carries oxygen-poor blood from the heart to the lungs? pulmonary vein aorta pulmonary artery superior vena cava arteries carry blood away from the heart, even when that blood is low in oxygen. the pulmonary arteries take oxygen-poor blood from the right ventricle to the lungs; the pulmonary veins bring oxygen-rich blood back.

which chamber of the heart has the thickest muscular wall? right ventricle left ventricle left atrium right atrium the left ventricle pumps blood through the entire systemic circulation, which has much higher resistance than the lungs. it needs the most muscle (myocardium) to generate that pressure. the right ventricle pumps only to the nearby lungs, and the atria just push blood into the ventricles.

which structure is the heart's natural pacemaker? sinoatrial (sa) node atrioventricular (av) node purkinje fibers bundle of his the sa node in the wall of the right atrium fires on its own fastest, so it sets the heart rate. the av node, bundle of his, and purkinje fibers conduct the signal it starts.

put the parts of the cardiac conduction system in the order the electrical impulse travels through them. sa node av node bundle of his (av bundle) right and left bundle branches purkinje fibers the impulse starts at the sa node and spreads across the atria, which contract. the av node briefly delays it so the ventricles can fill. it then travels down the bundle of his, the bundle branches, and the purkinje fibers, which make the ventricles contract from the apex upward.

which valve is located between the left atrium and the left ventricle? tricuspid (right av) valve aortic (semilunar) valve pulmonary (semilunar) valve mitral (bicuspid) valve the left atrioventricular valve has two cusps, so it is called the bicuspid or mitral valve. the tricuspid valve is on the right side; the aortic and pulmonary valves are semilunar valves at the exits of the ventricles.

exchange of oxygen, nutrients, and wastes between the blood and body tissues takes place across the walls of which vessels? arteries veins capillaries arterioles capillary walls are a single layer of endothelial cells, thin enough for substances to diffuse through. arteries, arterioles, and veins have thicker walls and mainly serve to carry blood.

which of the following are formed elements (cells or cell fragments) of the blood? select all that apply. erythrocytes (red blood cells) leukocytes (white blood cells) platelets albumin water formed elements are the cells and cell fragments: red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets (fragments of megakaryocytes). albumin (a plasma protein) and water are parts of plasma, the liquid portion of blood.

a patient with a very low platelet count is at greatest risk for which problem? frequent bacterial infections excessive bleeding and bruising low blood oxygen levels dangerously high blood pressure platelets (thrombocytes) form a plug at an injury and help start clotting. too few platelets means bleeding is hard to stop. frequent infections suggest low white blood cells; low oxygen suggests too few red blood cells (anemia).

a patient has left-sided heart failure, meaning the left ventricle cannot pump blood forward effectively. fluid will most likely back up into which organs first? lungs liver and abdomen ankles and feet kidneys blood returning from the lungs enters the left side of the heart. if the left ventricle fails, blood backs up into the pulmonary veins and lungs, causing pulmonary congestion and shortness of breath. swelling of the ankles, feet, and liver is typical of right-sided failure, because blood backs up into the systemic veins.

a patient's blood pressure is 128/82 mm hg. what does the 128 represent? pressure in the arteries when the ventricles relax (diastolic) the number of times the heart beats per minute the pressure inside the right atrium of the heart pressure in the arteries when the ventricles contract (systolic) the top number is systolic pressure: the peak arterial pressure during ventricular contraction (systole). the bottom number (82) is diastolic pressure, during ventricular relaxation. heart rate is measured separately in beats per minute.

why do many veins in the legs contain valves? to raise blood pressure in the veins above arterial pressure to allow gas exchange with surrounding tissues to prevent blood from flowing backward away from the heart to pump blood the way the heart does blood pressure in veins is low, and blood in the legs must return to the heart against gravity. one-way valves keep blood moving toward the heart while skeletal muscles squeeze the veins. valves do not pump on their own; the surrounding muscle contractions provide the push.

a blockage in a coronary artery most directly deprives which tissue of oxygen? the lung tissue (alveoli) the myocardium (heart muscle) the brain (cerebral cortex) the inner lining of the aorta the coronary arteries branch off the aorta and supply the heart muscle itself. a blocked coronary artery causes a myocardial infarction (heart attack), in which heart muscle cells die from lack of oxygen.

a patient's heart rate is 75 beats per minute and the stroke volume is 70 ml per beat. what is the cardiac output in liters per minute? (cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume.) cardiac output = 75 beats/min × 70 ml/beat = 5,250 ml/min. convert to liters: 5,250 ml ÷ 1,000 = 5.25 l/min. a normal resting adult cardiac output is about 5 l/min, so this answer is reasonable.

which blood type is considered the universal donor for red blood cells? o negative ab positive a negative b positive type o negative red blood cells have no a, b, or rh (d) antigens on their surface. with no antigens to react to, they can be given to nearly any recipient in an emergency. ab positive is the universal recipient, the opposite idea.

a patient has type a blood. which antibodies are normally present in this patient's plasma? anti-a antibodies only both anti-a and anti-b antibodies no abo antibodies anti-b antibodies only type a red blood cells carry a antigens. the plasma contains antibodies against the antigen the person does not have, so type a blood has anti-b antibodies. if this patient received type b blood, the anti-b antibodies would attack the donor cells.

which statements about arteries are correct? select all that apply. they carry blood away from the heart. they have thicker muscular walls than veins. they always carry oxygen-rich blood. they contain one-way valves along their length. they carry blood at higher pressure than veins. arteries carry blood away from the heart under high pressure, so they have thick, muscular, elastic walls. not all arteries carry oxygen-rich blood: the pulmonary arteries carry oxygen-poor blood to the lungs. valves along the vessel are a feature of veins, not arteries.

what is the name of the double-layered sac that surrounds the heart? pleura peritoneum pericardium myocardium the pericardium encloses the heart; fluid between its layers reduces friction as the heart beats. the pleura surrounds the lungs, the peritoneum lines the abdominal cavity, and the myocardium is the heart muscle itself.

the first heart sound ("lub") is caused by which event? closing of the aortic and pulmonary (semilunar) valves closing of the tricuspid and mitral (av) valves contraction of the atria opening of the av valves when the ventricles begin to contract, pressure rises and snaps the av valves shut, producing "lub." "dub" is the second sound, when the semilunar valves close as the ventricles relax. valve opening is normally silent.

in adults, where are red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets produced? red bone marrow spleen liver lymph nodes and thymus hematopoiesis (blood cell formation) in adults takes place in red bone marrow, found in bones such as the hip bones, sternum, and vertebrae. the spleen removes old red blood cells, the liver makes plasma proteins, and lymph nodes house lymphocytes but do not make all blood cells.

the hepatic portal vein carries nutrient-rich blood from the stomach and intestines directly to which organ? heart kidneys spleen liver after a meal, absorbed nutrients travel in the hepatic portal vein to the liver before reaching the rest of the body. this lets the liver process nutrients, store glucose as glycogen, and detoxify drugs and toxins first.

click the chamber that receives oxygen-poor blood returning from the body. blood from the body returns through the superior and inferior venae cavae. both veins empty into the right atrium. the left atrium receives oxygen-rich blood from the lungs instead.

click the vessel that carries oxygen-poor blood from the heart toward the lungs. the right ventricle pumps blood into the pulmonary trunk. the pulmonary trunk splits into the right and left pulmonary arteries, which lead to the lungs. it is an artery (it carries blood away from the heart) even though its blood is oxygen-poor.

click the largest artery in the body, which carries oxygen-rich blood to the body. the aorta leaves the left ventricle and arches over the heart. its branches carry oxygen-rich blood to every part of the body except the lungs' air sacs. the pulmonary trunk is the other great artery, but it goes to the lungs.

click the valve that keeps blood from flowing back into the right ventricle after it has been pumped toward the lungs. the pulmonary valve sits between the right ventricle and the pulmonary trunk. when the right ventricle relaxes, the valve snaps shut so blood cannot fall back in. the tricuspid valve is the valve between the right atrium and right ventricle.

a patient has mitral valve prolapse, so blood leaks backward when the ventricle contracts. click the chamber the leaking blood flows back into. the mitral (bicuspid) valve sits between the left atrium and the left ventricle. if it does not close well, contraction of the left ventricle pushes some blood back up into the left atrium. this backflow (mitral regurgitation) can enlarge the left atrium over time.

click the vessels that bring oxygen-rich blood from the lungs back to the heart. the pulmonary veins carry freshly oxygenated blood from the lungs. they empty into the left atrium. they are the main exception to the idea that veins carry oxygen-poor blood.

click the heart's natural pacemaker, the structure that starts each heartbeat. the sinoatrial (sa) node is a small cluster of special muscle cells in the wall of the right atrium, near where the superior vena cava enters. it fires on its own about 60–100 times a minute, so it sets the normal heart rate (normal sinus rhythm). the av node, lower down, is the second stop. it only fires on its own if the sa node fails, and more slowly.

click the structure that briefly delays the electrical signal so the atria can finish emptying into the ventricles. the av (atrioventricular) node sits low in the right atrium near the tricuspid valve. it slows the signal for about 0.1 second. that pause lets the atria contract and push their blood down before the ventricles contract. on an ecg, this delay is part of the flat stretch between the p wave and the qrs complex.

a nursing student nicks a finger while cutting tape. put the steps of hemostasis (stopping the bleeding) in the order they happen. vascular spasm: the injured blood vessel constricts a platelet plug forms at the break in the vessel wall coagulation: fibrin threads form a solid clot clot retraction: the clot tightens and pulls the vessel edges together fibrinolysis: the clot is dissolved after the vessel heals first the vessel constricts (vascular spasm), which slows blood loss right away. platelets stick to the damaged wall and to each other to form a plug; then the clotting cascade turns fibrinogen into fibrin threads that trap cells and make a solid clot. the clot then shrinks (retracts) to draw the edges together, and once the tissue is repaired, plasmin breaks the clot down (fibrinolysis).

a patient's sa node stops firing, and a heart monitor shows a slow, steady rhythm of about 50 beats per minute. which lettered structure is most likely now acting as the pacemaker? a b d e when the sa node (a) fails, the next structure in line, the av node (b), takes over as the pacemaker. the av node's own rate is slower, about 40–60 beats per minute, which matches the monitor. cells further down (bundle branches, purkinje fibers) can also fire on their own, but even more slowly, about 20–40 per minute.

on the middle heartbeat, click the part of the ecg that shows the ventricles depolarizing (the signal that makes them contract). ventricular depolarization makes the tall, sharp qrs complex. the ventricles have much more muscle than the atria, so this wave is the biggest. the small bump before it (p wave) is the atria depolarizing. the rounded wave after it (t wave) is the ventricles repolarizing (resetting). atrial repolarization happens at the same time as the qrs, so it is hidden inside it.

on this ecg, the distance from one r peak (top of qrs) to the next is 3 large boxes. each large box is 0.20 s. what is the heart rate in beats per minute? time between beats: 3 large boxes × 0.20 s = 0.60 s per beat. beats per minute = 60 s ÷ 0.60 s per beat = 100 beats per minute. quick rule nurses use: heart rate ≈ 300 ÷ (number of large boxes between r peaks) = 300 ÷ 3 = 100.

before birth, much of the blood entering a fetus's right atrium passes straight into the left atrium through the foramen ovale. why is this shortcut useful in the fetus? it lets blood bypass the fluid-filled fetal lungs. it sends extra blood to the fetal lungs so they can pick up more oxygen from the amniotic fluid. it keeps oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor blood from ever mixing in the heart. it carries blood from the heart directly to the placenta. a fetus gets oxygen from the placenta, not its lungs, which are fluid-filled and do not exchange gases yet. the foramen ovale (between the atria) and the ductus arteriosus (between the pulmonary trunk and the aorta) both route blood around the lungs. at birth, the lungs inflate and pressure in the left atrium rises, which pushes the foramen ovale's flap closed.

a patient's lab report shows a hematocrit of 42%. what does this value measure? the percentage of red blood cells that carry oxygen the percentage of blood volume that is red blood cells the percentage of blood volume made up of plasma the percentage of hemoglobin in each red blood cell hematocrit is the fraction of whole blood volume taken up by red blood cells; normal adult values are roughly 37–52%, higher in males. plasma makes up most of the rest, with a thin layer of white blood cells and platelets.

a patient with iron-deficiency anemia feels tired and short of breath. which explanation is best? iron is needed for platelets, so the blood clots poorly. iron is needed to help oxygen dissolve directly in the plasma. iron is needed to make white blood cells that carry oxygen. less iron means less hemoglobin to carry oxygen. each hemoglobin molecule has four heme groups, and each heme has an iron atom that binds one o₂ molecule. without enough iron, the body makes less hemoglobin, so the blood carries less oxygen, leading to fatigue and shortness of breath.

click the trachea (windpipe). the trachea is the tube that runs from the larynx down into the chest, where it splits into the two primary bronchi. c-shaped rings of cartilage (the stripes in the drawing) hold it open. the esophagus lies behind the trachea and carries food, not air.

click the flap of cartilage that covers the opening of the larynx during swallowing, so food goes into the esophagus instead. the epiglottis is a leaf-shaped flap of elastic cartilage at the top of the larynx. when you swallow, the larynx rises and the epiglottis folds down over its opening. food and drink slide back into the esophagus. if this fails, food or liquid can be aspirated into the airway. nurses watch for this in patients with swallowing problems (dysphagia).

click the tiny air sac where gas exchange with the blood takes place. gas exchange happens in the alveoli. these are tiny, thin-walled air sacs at the ends of the bronchioles. each alveolus is wrapped in capillaries. o₂ diffuses from the alveolus into the blood, and co₂ diffuses from the blood into the alveolus. the capillary is a blood vessel, not an air sac.

which lettered structure contains the vocal cords? d b c e the vocal cords (vocal folds) are inside the larynx, or voice box, labeled d. b is the pharynx (throat), which carries both food and air. c is the epiglottis, which covers the larynx during swallowing. e is the trachea, below the larynx.

air has just entered the nasal cavity. put these structures in the order the air passes through them on the way to the alveoli. pharynx larynx trachea primary bronchus bronchioles from the nasal cavity, air moves back into the pharynx (throat), then down through the larynx (voice box). next comes the trachea, which branches into the right and left primary bronchi. the bronchi keep branching into smaller and smaller bronchioles, which end at the alveoli.

in the close-up, blood in capillary i picks up gases from alveolus h. compared with the blood arriving at the alveolus, the blood leaving it has: less o₂ and more co₂ more o₂ and more co₂ about the same o₂ and co₂ more o₂ and less co₂ gases diffuse from high concentration to low concentration. air in the alveolus has more o₂ than the blood arriving from the body, so o₂ moves into the blood. the blood has more co₂ than the alveolar air, so co₂ moves out of the blood. the blood leaves with more o₂ and less co₂. this oxygen-rich blood returns to the heart through the pulmonary veins.

in pulmonary edema, fluid builds up in and around the alveoli. why does this lower the patient's blood oxygen level? the fluid thickens the barrier between alveolus and capillary, so o₂ diffuses more slowly. the fluid collects in the trachea and bronchi and blocks air from reaching the lungs. the fluid makes the diaphragm contract harder, which pushes air back out of the alveoli. the fluid reacts with o₂ in the alveoli and changes it into co₂. o₂ reaches the blood by diffusing across the very thin wall between the alveolus and the capillary. diffusion is fastest when that barrier is thin. fluid makes the distance thicker, so less o₂ crosses in the same amount of time, and blood oxygen drops. edema fluid collects in the alveoli and the lung tissue, not in the trachea. the diaphragm pulls air in when it contracts. fluid cannot change one gas into another.

put these structures in the order inhaled air passes through them, starting at the nose. nasal cavity pharynx larynx trachea primary bronchi air enters the nasal cavity, where it is warmed, moistened, and filtered. it passes through the pharynx (throat) and larynx (voice box) into the trachea. the trachea splits into the right and left primary bronchi, one to each lung.

put these airways in order from largest to smallest as air moves deeper into the lung. trachea primary bronchus secondary (lobar) bronchus bronchiole alveolus the trachea branches into primary bronchi, which branch into secondary (lobar) bronchi, one per lobe. bronchi keep branching into tiny bronchioles, which end in clusters of alveoli where gas exchange occurs.

which muscle does most of the work during quiet breathing? pectoralis major rectus abdominis trapezius diaphragm the diaphragm is the primary muscle of inspiration; the external intercostals help. abdominal muscles assist only with forced exhalation, and the pectoralis major and trapezius move the arm and shoulder.

gas exchange between the lungs and the blood takes place in tiny air sacs called ______. the alveoli are thin-walled sacs surrounded by capillaries. oxygen diffuses from the alveoli into the blood, and carbon dioxide diffuses from the blood into the alveoli.

which change occurs during normal inspiration (inhalation)? the diaphragm relaxes and domes upward, decreasing the volume of the thoracic cavity air pressure inside the lungs rises above the atmospheric pressure outside the diaphragm contracts and flattens, increasing the volume of the thoracic cavity the external intercostal muscles relax, and the ribs move downward and inward when the diaphragm contracts it moves downward, and the external intercostals lift the ribs, so the chest cavity gets bigger. bigger volume means lower pressure in the lungs (boyle's law), so air flows in from the higher-pressure atmosphere. the other choices describe exhalation.

which structure folds over the opening of the larynx during swallowing to keep food out of the airway? uvula epiglottis vocal cords pharyngeal tonsil the epiglottis is a flap of elastic cartilage that covers the laryngeal opening (glottis) when you swallow. the uvula and soft palate close off the nasal cavity, not the larynx.

a baby born at 28 weeks of gestation struggles to keep the alveoli from collapsing after each breath. a deficiency of which substance is most likely the cause? surfactant hemoglobin mucus cilia surfactant is made by type ii alveolar cells and lowers surface tension inside the alveoli. without enough surfactant, alveoli collapse at the end of each exhalation, making breathing exhausting. the lungs do not make enough surfactant until late in pregnancy, so premature infants are at risk.

oxygen moves from the alveoli into the pulmonary capillary blood by which process? active transport by atp-powered membrane pumps osmosis through the respiratory membrane filtration driven by capillary blood pressure diffusion down its partial pressure gradient alveolar air has a higher partial pressure of oxygen than the blood arriving at the lungs. oxygen therefore diffuses down its gradient across the thin respiratory membrane; no atp is needed. osmosis refers to the movement of water, not gases.

in a healthy person, which change is the strongest chemical stimulus to increase the rate and depth of breathing? a small drop in blood oxygen level a rise in blood glucose level a rise in blood carbon dioxide level a drop in core body temperature chemoreceptors in the medulla and in the carotid and aortic bodies are most sensitive to co₂ and the h⁺ (lower ph) it forms. even a small rise in co₂ quickly increases ventilation. oxygen must fall quite low before it becomes the main drive in a healthy person.

which part of the brain contains the main centers that set the basic rhythm of breathing? cerebellum medulla oblongata occipital lobe thalamus respiratory centers in the brainstem, especially the medulla oblongata (with help from the pons), set the breathing rhythm. the cerebellum coordinates movement, the occipital lobe processes vision, and the thalamus relays sensory information.

how is most of the carbon dioxide carried in the blood from the tissues to the lungs? as bicarbonate ions (hco₃⁻) in plasma bound to the iron atoms in hemoglobin as dissolved carbon dioxide gas in plasma attached to the surface of platelets about 70% of co₂ reacts with water inside red blood cells (sped up by carbonic anhydrase) to form carbonic acid, which becomes h⁺ and hco₃⁻. the bicarbonate moves into the plasma and is carried to the lungs. smaller amounts travel bound to hemoglobin's protein part (not the iron, where o₂ binds) or dissolved as gas.

which structure is known as the "voice box" because it contains the vocal cords? pharynx trachea bronchus larynx the larynx sits on top of the trachea and contains the vocal folds, which vibrate to produce sound. the pharynx is the throat; the trachea is the windpipe.

the right lung has three lobes, but the left lung has only two. what is the best explanation? the liver sits directly beneath the left lung and compresses it the left primary bronchus is wider and shorter than the right one the heart takes up space on the left side of the thoracic cavity the left lung does not take part in gas exchange with the blood the heart tilts toward the left, so the left lung is smaller and has an indentation called the cardiac notch. the liver lies under the right side of the diaphragm, and both lungs exchange gases. in fact, the right primary bronchus is the wider, more vertical one.

smoking damages the ciliated cells that line the trachea and bronchi. which function is most directly impaired? exchanging oxygen and carbon dioxide across the alveolar walls sweeping mucus and trapped particles out of the airways producing surfactant to keep the alveoli open contracting the diaphragm during each inhalation the airways are lined with cells whose cilia beat to push mucus (and trapped dust and microbes) up toward the pharynx, where it is swallowed or coughed out. when cilia are damaged, mucus builds up, causing "smoker's cough" and more infections.

during an asthma attack, which change is the main reason air flow is reduced? bronchiole smooth muscle contracts, narrowing the airways the alveoli fill with blood and stop exchanging gases the diaphragm becomes paralyzed and cannot contract the cartilage rings of the trachea soften and collapse asthma involves inflammation and spasm of the smooth muscle in bronchiole walls (bronchoconstriction), plus extra mucus. narrower airways increase resistance, causing wheezing and difficulty exhaling. rescue inhalers work by relaxing this smooth muscle (bronchodilation).

a longtime smoker from merced is diagnosed with emphysema, in which the walls between alveoli are destroyed. why does this reduce oxygen uptake? the airways become lined with extra cilia that block airflow the blood loses its ability to carry carbon dioxide the alveoli make so much surfactant that they stick shut less surface area is available for gas exchange breaking down the walls between alveoli merges many small sacs into fewer large ones. fewer, larger sacs have much less total surface area, so less oxygen can diffuse into the blood. the lungs also lose elastic recoil, so air gets trapped and exhaling is difficult.

which structure is a shared passageway for both food and air? larynx trachea pharynx esophagus the pharynx (throat) carries air to the larynx and food to the esophagus. the larynx and trachea carry only air, and the esophagus carries only food.

tidal volume is best defined as the maximum amount of air that can be exhaled after a deep breath the volume of air moved in or out in one normal, quiet breath the air that remains in the lungs after a forced exhalation the number of breaths a person takes per minute at rest tidal volume is the normal resting breath, about 500 ml in an adult. the maximum exhaled after a maximum inhale is vital capacity, the air left over is residual volume, and breaths per minute is respiratory rate.

which are functions of the nasal cavity? select all that apply. warming incoming air moistening (humidifying) incoming air trapping dust and microbes in mucus exchanging oxygen with the blood producing surfactant the nasal cavity's mucous membrane and rich blood supply warm and moisten air, and hairs and mucus filter it. gas exchange happens only in the alveoli, and surfactant is made by alveolar cells.

a student having a panic attack breathes very rapidly and deeply (hyperventilates). what happens to the blood? co₂ decreases and ph rises (more basic) co₂ increases and ph falls (more acidic) co₂ decreases and ph falls (more acidic) co₂ increases and ph rises (more basic) hyperventilation exhales co₂ faster than the body makes it, so blood co₂ falls. less co₂ means less carbonic acid and fewer h⁺ ions, so ph rises: respiratory alkalosis. this can cause dizziness and tingling in the fingers and lips.

what is the main function of the pleural fluid between the two pleural membranes? exchanging oxygen and carbon dioxide with the blood producing antibodies against inhaled microbes moving mucus toward the pharynx reducing friction as the lungs expand and recoil the visceral and parietal pleurae are separated by a thin film of serous fluid. the fluid lets the lungs glide smoothly against the chest wall and also helps the membranes cling together so the lungs follow the chest wall as it expands.

which events occur during normal, quiet exhalation? select all that apply. the diaphragm relaxes and moves upward the volume of the thoracic cavity decreases air pressure in the lungs rises slightly above atmospheric pressure the external intercostal muscles contract the abdominal muscles contract forcefully quiet exhalation is passive: the diaphragm and external intercostals relax, and the elastic lungs recoil. thoracic volume shrinks, so lung pressure rises above atmospheric pressure and air flows out. contracting the external intercostals is part of inhalation, and forceful abdominal contraction happens only in forced exhalation (like coughing).

click the voice box, which holds the vocal cords. the larynx (voice box) sits at the top of the trachea. air passing over the vocal folds inside it makes them vibrate, producing sound. the epiglottis is a flap at its top that covers it during swallowing.

click the passage shared by both air and food. the pharynx (throat) carries air from the nose and mouth and also carries food to the esophagus. below the pharynx, air goes forward into the larynx and food goes back into the esophagus. the epiglottis helps send each to the right place.

click the space that warms, moistens and filters air as it is breathed in through the nose. the nasal cavity is lined with mucous membrane and many blood vessels. mucus traps dust and germs, and the warm lining heats and humidifies the air. breathing through the mouth skips this conditioning step.

click the main muscle used for breathing in. the diaphragm is a dome-shaped muscle under the lungs. when it contracts it moves down, the chest cavity gets bigger, pressure drops and air flows in. when it relaxes, it moves back up and air flows out.

a peanut that is inhaled usually lodges in the right lung, because the right airway leaving the trachea is wider and more vertical. click the airways that branch off the trachea into each lung. the trachea splits into the right and left primary bronchi. the right primary bronchus is shorter, wider and more vertical than the left, so inhaled objects tend to fall into it. each bronchus keeps branching into smaller bronchi and then bronchioles.

in the close-up, click the blood vessel where oxygen enters the blood. pulmonary capillaries wrap around each alveolus. oxygen diffuses from the air in the alveolus across two thin walls into the blood in the capillary. co₂ diffuses the opposite way, from the blood into the alveolus.

how much air did the patient with asthma breathe out in the first second? 1.6 l 3.2 l 3.5 l 2.4 l read the orange dashed line at 1 second: about 1.6 l. the healthy adult blew out about 3.2 l in that same second, twice as much.

the patient's total exhaled volume is close to normal, but the air comes out much more slowly. what best explains this pattern? the bronchioles are narrowed, so airflow out of the lungs is slowed. the lungs are much smaller than normal, so they hold less air. the alveoli cannot exchange o₂ and co₂. the diaphragm is pulling air into the lungs during the exhale. in asthma, smooth muscle around the bronchioles tightens and the lining swells and makes mucus, which narrows the airways. narrow airways resist airflow, so it takes longer to push air out: a low volume in the first second (fev₁), even though the lungs still hold nearly the usual amount. a disease that shrinks the lungs (restrictive disease) would lower the total volume instead.

a patient with severe copd cannot exhale co₂ effectively and breathes slowly and shallowly (hypoventilation). which acid–base imbalance is most likely? respiratory alkalosis metabolic acidosis metabolic alkalosis respiratory acidosis co₂ that is not exhaled builds up and combines with water to form carbonic acid, which releases h⁺. more h⁺ lowers blood ph (acidosis), and because the cause is a breathing problem, it is respiratory acidosis.

click the organ where most chemical digestion and nutrient absorption take place. the small intestine (duodenum, jejunum, ileum) is where most chemical digestion is finished and most nutrients are absorbed. enzymes from the pancreas and bile from the liver and gallbladder are added in the duodenum, and folds, villi, and microvilli give it a huge surface for absorption. the stomach starts protein digestion, but it absorbs very little. the large intestine mainly absorbs water and electrolytes.

click the organ that stores and concentrates bile. the gallbladder is the small sac tucked under the liver. it stores bile and concentrates it until a fatty meal arrives. then it contracts and squeezes bile into the duodenum, where the bile emulsifies fats. trap: the liver makes bile, but the gallbladder stores it.

click the muscular tube that carries swallowed food from the throat to the stomach. the esophagus connects the pharynx (throat) to the stomach. waves of muscle contraction called peristalsis push food along it. that is why you can swallow even lying down. no digestion or absorption happens in the esophagus. it only moves food.

organ f releases digestive enzymes into the small intestine and releases insulin into the blood. what is organ f? gallbladder liver pancreas stomach f is the pancreas, which lies behind and below the stomach, with its head inside the curve of the duodenum. it is both an exocrine gland (enzymes and bicarbonate sent through a duct to the duodenum) and an endocrine gland (insulin and glucagon released into the blood). the gallbladder (d) stores bile, the liver (c) makes bile, and the stomach (e) makes acid and pepsin. none of these makes insulin.

a patient is diagnosed with hepatitis, which is inflammation of the liver. which letter marks the affected organ? d c e f "hepat-" means liver, and "-itis" means inflammation. the liver is c, the large organ in the upper right of the abdomen (on the viewer's left in a front view). d is the gallbladder, e is the stomach, and f is the pancreas.

accessory digestive organs help digestion by making or storing substances, but they lie outside the alimentary canal, so food does not pass through them. which lettered organs are accessory organs? select all that apply. c d e f g c (liver) makes bile, d (gallbladder) stores bile, and f (pancreas) makes digestive enzymes. ducts carry these to the duodenum, but food never travels through these organs. e (stomach) and g (small intestine) are parts of the gi tract (alimentary canal). food passes right through them. the salivary glands are also accessory organs, and the teeth and tongue are accessory structures in the mouth.

put these parts of the gi tract in the order that food passes through them, first to last. esophagus stomach small intestine large intestine rectum after swallowing, food goes down the esophagus to the stomach. from the stomach it moves into the small intestine (duodenum first), then into the large intestine (colon). waste is stored in the rectum before it leaves through the anus.

put these organs in the order food passes through them, from first to last. mouth esophagus stomach small intestine large intestine food is chewed in the mouth, swallowed through the pharynx and esophagus, and churned in the stomach. most digestion and absorption finish in the small intestine, and the large intestine absorbs water and forms feces.

put these regions of the intestines in the order that food residue passes through them. duodenum jejunum ileum cecum ascending colon the small intestine runs duodenum → jejunum → ileum ("dow jones industrial"). the ileum empties through the ileocecal valve into the cecum, the first part of the large intestine. from the cecum, material moves up the ascending colon, then across the transverse colon and down the descending colon.

in which organ does most absorption of nutrients take place? small intestine stomach large intestine esophagus the small intestine is long and has a huge surface area, so it absorbs most nutrients. the stomach absorbs only a few substances (such as alcohol), and the large intestine mainly absorbs water and electrolytes.

what is the main purpose of the villi and microvilli that line the small intestine? to produce bile for fat digestion to push food along the tract by peristalsis to store food in the intestine until it is digested to increase the surface area for absorption villi are finger-like projections of the lining (which also has large circular folds), and microvilli are tiny projections on each absorptive cell (the "brush border"). together they multiply the surface area, so more nutrients can be absorbed. peristalsis is done by smooth muscle layers, and bile is made by the liver.

which statement about bile is correct? it is produced by the gallbladder and stored in the liver it is produced by the pancreas and stored in the gallbladder it is produced by the liver and stored in the gallbladder it is produced by the stomach and stored in the duodenum liver cells (hepatocytes) make bile continuously. the gallbladder stores and concentrates bile, then releases it into the duodenum when fatty food arrives.

what is the main role of bile in digestion? breaking down proteins into amino acids emulsifying fats into smaller droplets digesting starch into glucose neutralizing the stomach's acid in the stomach itself bile salts break large fat globules into tiny droplets (emulsification), the way dish soap breaks up grease. this gives lipase much more surface area to work on. bile has no digestive enzymes of its own.

chemical digestion of starch (carbohydrate) begins in which location? the mouth, by salivary amylase the stomach, by pepsin the small intestine, by lipase the large intestine, by bacteria salivary glands release amylase, which starts breaking starch into smaller sugars while you chew. pepsin digests protein, and lipase digests fat. pancreatic amylase continues starch digestion in the small intestine.

chemical digestion of protein begins in which organ? mouth large intestine esophagus stomach chief cells in the stomach release pepsinogen, which hydrochloric acid converts into the active enzyme pepsin. pepsin begins breaking proteins into smaller peptides; pancreatic enzymes finish the job in the small intestine.

which enzyme breaks down dietary fats (triglycerides)? amylase pepsin lipase lactase "lip-" refers to lipids (fats), so lipase digests fats into fatty acids and monoglycerides. amylase digests starch, pepsin digests protein, and lactase digests the milk sugar lactose.

peristalsis is best described as the chemical breakdown of food by digestive enzymes wavelike smooth muscle contractions that move food along the absorption of nutrients through the intestinal wall chewing and grinding food into smaller pieces rings of smooth muscle contract behind a food mass and relax ahead of it, squeezing it forward. peristalsis moves food down the esophagus and through the stomach and intestines; it does not chemically digest food.

what is the main function of the large intestine? absorbing water and electrolytes and forming feces producing bile and most digestive enzymes absorbing most of the nutrients from digested food beginning the chemical digestion of protein by the time material reaches the large intestine, most nutrients have already been absorbed. the large intestine reabsorbs much of the remaining water and electrolytes, compacting the residue into feces. this is why problems that speed material through the colon cause watery diarrhea.

a patient had her gallbladder removed (cholecystectomy). which type of meal is she most likely to have trouble digesting comfortably? a meal high in starch a meal high in lean protein a meal high in fiber a large, high-fat meal the gallbladder stores concentrated bile and releases a large amount when fatty food enters the duodenum. without it, bile trickles in continuously from the liver, so there may not be enough at once to emulsify a large fatty meal. starch and protein digestion depend mainly on enzymes, not bile.

bacteria living in the large intestine produce a vitamin needed to make blood clotting factors. a patient on long-term antibiotics may become deficient in which vitamin? vitamin c vitamin a vitamin k vitamin d normal gut bacteria in the colon synthesize vitamin k, which the liver uses to make several clotting factors. long antibiotic courses can kill these bacteria, lowering vitamin k and increasing bleeding risk. vitamin d is made in the skin with sunlight, not by gut bacteria.

a patient has frequent heartburn because stomach acid flows back into the esophagus (gerd). weakness of which structure is most likely responsible? pyloric sphincter (stomach exit) lower esophageal (cardiac) sphincter ileocecal valve (small-to-large intestine) internal anal sphincter the lower esophageal sphincter at the stomach's entrance normally keeps acidic stomach contents out of the esophagus. the pyloric sphincter is at the stomach's exit, and the ileocecal valve and anal sphincter are much farther down the tract.

which structure controls the passage of chyme from the stomach into the duodenum? pyloric sphincter lower esophageal sphincter ileocecal valve epiglottis the pyloric sphincter is a ring of smooth muscle at the bottom (pylorus) of the stomach. it releases small amounts of chyme at a time so the duodenum is not overwhelmed.

which is a function of the hydrochloric acid (hcl) secreted in the stomach? it emulsifies dietary fats into droplets so lipase can digest them it absorbs water from food it digests starch into maltose it activates pepsin and kills many swallowed microbes hcl makes the stomach very acidic (ph about 2). this acid converts inactive pepsinogen into pepsin and destroys many bacteria in food. bile emulsifies fat, and amylase digests starch.

which of the following are functions of the liver? select all that apply. producing bile detoxifying drugs and alcohol storing glucose as glycogen secreting insulin absorbing most nutrients from digested food the liver makes bile, breaks down drugs, alcohol, and toxins, and stores glucose as glycogen (it also makes plasma proteins like albumin). insulin is secreted by beta cells of the pancreas, and most nutrient absorption occurs in the small intestine.

the semi-liquid mixture of partly digested food and gastric juice that leaves the stomach is called ______. the stomach churns food with gastric juice into a soupy mixture called chyme. chyme passes through the pyloric sphincter into the duodenum. (do not confuse it with chyle, the fatty lymph in lacteals.)

pancreatic juice contains bicarbonate (hco₃⁻). what is its main role? emulsifying fats into small droplets activating pepsin so it can digest proteins in the stomach neutralizing acidic chyme as it enters the duodenum killing bacteria in the large intestine chyme leaving the stomach is very acidic. bicarbonate from the pancreas neutralizes it, protecting the intestinal lining and providing the near-neutral ph that pancreatic enzymes need.

which of the following are accessory digestive organs, meaning food does not pass through them? select all that apply. liver pancreas gallbladder stomach esophagus accessory organs help digestion by making or storing secretions (bile, enzymes) that flow into the gi tract through ducts. the stomach and esophagus are part of the alimentary canal (gi tract) itself, so food passes through them.

a patient's skin and the whites of the eyes appear yellow (jaundice) because of a buildup of bilirubin. which organ is most likely involved? stomach liver large intestine small intestine bilirubin comes from the breakdown of old red blood cells and is normally processed by the liver and excreted in bile. liver disease (such as hepatitis or cirrhosis) or a blocked bile duct lets bilirubin build up in the blood, turning tissues yellow.

carbohydrates must be digested into which form before they can be absorbed by the small intestine? monosaccharides, such as glucose amino acids fatty acids and glycerol disaccharides, such as sucrose only single sugars (monosaccharides like glucose, fructose, and galactose) can be absorbed. brush-border enzymes such as sucrase and lactase split disaccharides into monosaccharides first. amino acids come from protein, and fatty acids come from fat.

click the organ that makes bile. the liver makes bile, which breaks fat into small droplets (emulsifies it). bile is stored and concentrated in the gallbladder and released into the small intestine. the liver also stores glycogen and filters drugs and toxins from the blood.

click the organ that churns food with hydrochloric acid and the enzyme pepsin. the stomach's muscular wall mixes food with gastric juice. hydrochloric acid kills many germs and activates pepsin, which begins protein digestion. the partly digested mixture (chyme) then moves into the small intestine.

click the organ that absorbs most of the remaining water and forms feces. the large intestine (colon) absorbs water and electrolytes from undigested material. its bacteria also make some vitamins, such as vitamin k. most nutrient absorption already happened in the small intestine.

a patient with type 1 diabetes has lost the cells that make insulin. click the organ where those cells are found. insulin is made by beta cells in the pancreatic islets (islets of langerhans). the pancreas is both an endocrine gland (insulin, glucagon) and an exocrine gland (digestive enzymes). it lies behind the stomach and sends its enzymes into the small intestine.

use the table. which enzyme begins the digestion of proteins in the stomach? lipase pepsin salivary amylase lactase find the row where "works in" is stomach and "breaks down" is proteins: pepsin. pepsin works best in the very acidic stomach (ph about 2). trypsin from the pancreas continues protein digestion in the small intestine.

use the table. a patient has had most of the pancreas removed. digestion of which nutrients would be most affected? starch, proteins and fats in the small intestine only proteins in the stomach only lactose starch in the mouth the pancreas makes pancreatic amylase, trypsin and lipase, which digest starch, proteins and fats in the small intestine. losing the pancreas means poor digestion of all three. patients often take pancreatic enzyme capsules with meals. fat digestion is hit hardest, causing greasy stools. pepsin (stomach), salivary amylase (mouth) and lactase (intestinal lining) don't come from the pancreas.

a visalia patient eats a fatty fast-food meal. when the fatty chyme reaches the duodenum, which hormone signals the gallbladder to contract and the pancreas to release digestive enzymes? gastrin cholecystokinin (cck) secretin insulin fats and proteins in the duodenum trigger the release of cholecystokinin (cck). cck makes the gallbladder contract to push bile into the duodenum and stimulates the pancreas to secrete enzyme-rich juice.

when acidic chyme enters the duodenum, the small intestine releases secretin. what does secretin mainly cause? the stomach to secrete more hydrochloric acid the liver to store more glycogen the gallbladder to store bile the pancreas to release bicarbonate secretin travels in the blood to the pancreas, which releases juice rich in bicarbonate (hco₃⁻). the bicarbonate neutralizes stomach acid so the intestinal enzymes can work and the duodenal lining is protected.

which letter marks the part of the neuron that receives signals from other neurons? g d e a dendrites (a) are the short, branched extensions that receive incoming signals and carry them toward the cell body. d is the axon, which carries the impulse away from the cell body. g marks the axon terminals, which send the signal on to the next cell. e is the myelin sheath.

in the synapse close-up, click the gap where neurotransmitter molecules diffuse from one neuron to the next. when an impulse reaches the axon terminal, synaptic vesicles release neurotransmitter by exocytosis. the neurotransmitter diffuses across the synaptic cleft, the narrow gap between the two cells, and binds to receptors on the receiving neuron. the vesicles store the neurotransmitter. the cleft is the space it crosses.

in multiple sclerosis (ms), the immune system damages structure e. what is the most direct effect on the neuron? the cell body can no longer make proteins. synaptic vesicles can no longer store or release neurotransmitter. dendrites can no longer receive any signals from other neurons. impulses travel more slowly along the axon, or fail to get through. e is the myelin sheath, the fatty insulation wrapped around the axon. myelin lets the impulse jump from node to node (saltatory conduction), which makes it fast. when myelin is damaged, conduction slows or is blocked. this causes ms symptoms such as weakness, numbness, and vision problems. ms damages the myelin. it does not directly stop protein synthesis, neurotransmitter storage, or dendrite function.

click the part of the brain that coordinates balance and smooth, precise movements. the cerebellum ("little brain") sits below the occipital lobe at the back of the head. it compares planned movements with what the body is actually doing, keeping movements smooth and balanced. damage to it causes ataxia: a wide, unsteady gait and clumsy movements. that is why a field sobriety test checks balance, since alcohol impairs the cerebellum.

after a brain injury, a patient's heart rate, blood pressure, and basic breathing rhythm become unstable. click the region that contains the control centers for these vital functions. the medulla oblongata is the lowest part of the brainstem, just above the spinal cord. it contains the cardiac, vasomotor (blood pressure), and respiratory rhythm centers, so injury here can be life-threatening. the pons, just above it, helps adjust breathing. but the centers for heart rate and blood pressure are in the medulla. the cerebellum controls coordination, not vital functions.

which lettered lobe processes visual information from the eyes? a c b d vision is processed in the occipital lobe, c, at the back of the cerebrum. a (frontal) handles planning, decisions, and voluntary movement. b (parietal) handles touch and body position. d (temporal) handles hearing and memory. a hard hit to the back of the head can cause "seeing stars" or vision loss because it injures the occipital lobe.

click the layer of the eye that contains the photoreceptors (rods and cones). the retina is the inner layer lining the back of the eye. its rods (dim light) and cones (color) change light into nerve signals. these signals leave the eye through the optic nerve. the sclera is the tough white outer layer, and the choroid (the dark layer between them) is full of blood vessels. neither one detects light.

put these structures in the order light passes through them on its way to the photoreceptors, first to last. cornea pupil lens vitreous humor retina light first passes through the clear cornea, which does most of the bending (refraction). it goes through the pupil, the opening in the iris, and then through the lens, which fine-tunes the focus. it crosses the gel-like vitreous humor and lands on the retina, where rods and cones detect it.

which lettered structure changes shape to focus light from near or far objects onto the retina? a b f d d is the lens. when the ciliary muscle contracts, the suspensory ligaments slacken and the lens rounds up for near vision. when the muscle relaxes, the ligaments pull the lens flatter for distance vision. this is called accommodation. a (cornea) bends light even more than the lens does, but its shape is fixed. b (iris) changes the size of the pupil to control how much light enters. f (retina) detects the light.
