what is the basic functional cell of the nervous system that transmits electrical signals? nephron neuron neuroglia (glial cell) osteocyte neurons generate and conduct electrical impulses. glial cells support and protect neurons, a nephron is the kidney's functional unit, and an osteocyte is a bone cell.

put these parts in the order a signal travels through a neuron, from where it is received to where it is passed on to the next cell. dendrites cell body axon axon terminals dendrites receive incoming signals and pass them to the cell body. the impulse travels down the axon to the axon terminals, which release neurotransmitter onto the next cell.

a nurse taps a patient's patellar tendon and the leg kicks. put the parts of this reflex arc in order. sensory receptor in the muscle sensory (afferent) neuron integration center in the spinal cord motor (efferent) neuron effector (quadriceps muscle) a stretch receptor detects the stimulus and a sensory neuron carries the signal to the spinal cord. the signal is processed in the spinal cord (for the knee-jerk, the sensory neuron synapses directly on the motor neuron). a motor neuron carries the command to the effector, the quadriceps, which contracts.

what is the main function of the myelin sheath that wraps many axons? it increases the speed of nerve impulse conduction it produces neurotransmitters for the synapse it receives incoming signals from other neurons it stores calcium ions needed for muscle contraction myelin is a fatty insulating layer formed by schwann cells (pns) and oligodendrocytes (cns). impulses jump from one gap in the myelin (node of ranvier) to the next, which is much faster than in unmyelinated axons. in multiple sclerosis, loss of cns myelin slows or blocks signals.

a patient with damage to the cerebellum would most likely have trouble with which function? understanding and producing spoken language regulating body temperature seeing colors and recognizing faces balance and coordination of movement the cerebellum compares intended movements with actual movements and fine-tunes them, so damage causes clumsy, unsteady movements. language is handled mainly in the cerebral cortex, temperature by the hypothalamus, and vision by the occipital lobe.

during a summer heat wave in fresno, which brain region detects the rising body temperature and triggers sweating? cerebellum occipital lobe hypothalamus medulla oblongata the hypothalamus is the body's thermostat; it also regulates hunger, thirst, and the pituitary gland. when blood temperature rises, it signals sweat glands to secrete and skin blood vessels to dilate.

a stroke damaging the occipital lobe of the cerebrum would most likely affect which function? hearing vision smell balance the occipital lobe at the back of the brain contains the primary visual cortex. hearing is processed in the temporal lobe, and balance relies on the cerebellum and inner ear.

which response is caused by the sympathetic ("fight-or-flight") division of the autonomic nervous system? pupils dilate and heart rate increases digestion speeds up and salivation increases pupils constrict and heart rate slows the bladder contracts to empty sympathetic activation prepares the body for emergencies: faster heart rate, dilated pupils and bronchioles, and more glucose released into the blood. digestion, salivation, pupil constriction, and bladder emptying are "rest-and-digest" parasympathetic responses.

which of the following are effects of the parasympathetic nervous system? select all that apply. slowing the heart rate stimulating digestion constricting the pupils dilating the bronchioles releasing glucose from the liver the parasympathetic division ("rest and digest") slows the heart, increases digestive activity, and constricts the pupils. dilating the bronchioles and raising blood glucose are sympathetic (fight-or-flight) effects.

which of the following are part of the peripheral nervous system (pns)? select all that apply. cranial nerves spinal nerves ganglia (clusters of neuron cell bodies outside the cns) spinal cord cerebellum the cns is the brain (including the cerebellum) and the spinal cord. everything outside them, including cranial nerves, spinal nerves, and ganglia, belongs to the pns.

during depolarization of a neuron's membrane in an action potential, which ion movement occurs? potassium ions (k⁺) rush into the cell chloride ions (cl⁻) rush out of the cell calcium ions (ca²⁺) are pumped out of the cell sodium ions (na⁺) rush into the cell when voltage-gated na⁺ channels open, na⁺ flows into the cell, making the inside more positive (depolarization). repolarization follows when k⁺ channels open and k⁺ flows out of the cell. the na⁺/k⁺ pump later restores the resting ion distribution.

which neurotransmitter is released by motor neurons at the neuromuscular junction to stimulate skeletal muscle? dopamine serotonin acetylcholine insulin motor neurons release acetylcholine (ach), which binds receptors on the muscle fiber and triggers an action potential. dopamine and serotonin act mainly in the brain, and insulin is a hormone, not a neurotransmitter.

which layer of the eye contains the light-sensitive photoreceptor cells? cornea retina iris sclera the retina at the back of the eye contains rods and cones that convert light into nerve signals. the cornea bends incoming light, the iris controls pupil size, and the sclera is the tough white outer coat.

which photoreceptors are responsible for color vision and sharp detail in bright light? cones rods hair cells ganglion cells cones work best in bright light and come in types sensitive to different wavelengths, allowing color vision. rods are more sensitive in dim light but see only shades of gray. hair cells are receptors in the inner ear.

put these structures in the order that sound vibrations travel through them on the way to the brain. external auditory canal tympanic membrane (eardrum) ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes) cochlea cochlear branch of the vestibulocochlear nerve sound waves travel down the ear canal and vibrate the eardrum. the three ossicles of the middle ear amplify the vibration and pass it to the oval window. fluid waves in the cochlea bend hair cells, which trigger signals in the cochlear nerve to the brain.

a patient reports severe dizziness and a spinning sensation when turning her head. which inner-ear structures detect rotation of the head? cochlea ossicles eustachian (auditory) tube semicircular canals the three semicircular canals are filled with fluid that moves when the head rotates, bending hair cells that signal the brain. the cochlea is for hearing, the ossicles transmit sound, and the eustachian tube equalizes middle-ear pressure.

which structure of the eye changes shape to focus light on the retina for near or distant objects? iris pupil lens optic nerve ciliary muscles adjust the curvature of the lens (accommodation) to focus images on the retina. the iris and pupil control how much light enters, and the optic nerve carries signals to the brain.

which colored, muscular part of the eye controls the size of the pupil? retina iris cornea lens the iris contains smooth muscle that constricts or dilates the pupil to control how much light enters. the pupil is the opening; the iris is the colored ring around it.

the narrow region between the axon terminal of one neuron and the next cell, across which neurotransmitters diffuse, is called the synaptic ______. a synapse is the junction between a neuron and another cell. the narrow space within the synapse is the synaptic cleft; neurotransmitter diffuses across it and binds receptors on the next cell.

a patient has a stroke that damages the motor cortex in the left cerebral hemisphere. where would muscle weakness most likely appear? on the right side of the body on the left side of the body on both sides of the body equally only in the muscles of the eyes most motor pathways cross to the opposite side (decussate) in the brainstem. so the left hemisphere controls voluntary movement on the right side of the body, and vice versa.

what is a main function of cerebrospinal fluid (csf)? carrying oxygen to the bones of the skull producing myelin for axons transmitting nerve impulses between neurons at synapses cushioning and protecting the brain and spinal cord csf fills the ventricles of the brain and the space around the brain and spinal cord. it acts as a shock absorber, makes the brain buoyant, and carries nutrients and wastes. a lumbar puncture (spinal tap) collects csf to test for infections such as meningitis.

which neurons carry information from sensory receptors toward the central nervous system? motor (efferent) neurons interneurons sensory (afferent) neurons schwann cells afferent neurons "arrive" at the cns with sensory information. efferent (motor) neurons "exit" the cns to muscles and glands, and interneurons connect neurons within the cns. schwann cells are glial cells, not neurons.

click the branches that receive signals from other neurons. dendrites are short, branching extensions of the cell body. receptors on them pick up neurotransmitters released by other neurons. the signal then travels toward the cell body and down the axon.

click the fatty covering that insulates the axon and speeds up the impulse. the myelin sheath is made of wrapped glial cell membranes. it insulates the axon so the impulse jumps from gap to gap instead of moving slowly along every point. diseases like multiple sclerosis damage myelin and slow nerve signals.

in saltatory conduction, the impulse jumps from one gap in the insulation to the next. click one of those gaps. the gaps between segments of myelin are called nodes of ranvier. ion channels are packed at the nodes, so the action potential is regenerated there and seems to jump from node to node. this is why myelinated axons conduct impulses much faster than unmyelinated ones.

in the synapse close-up, click the small sacs that store neurotransmitter. synaptic vesicles are tiny membrane sacs inside the axon terminal. when an impulse arrives, calcium enters and the vesicles fuse with the membrane, releasing neurotransmitter into the cleft. the neurotransmitter then binds to receptors on the receiving neuron.

click the lobe that processes vision. the occipital lobe is at the back of the brain. signals from the eyes travel through the optic nerves and tracts to the visual cortex in this lobe. damage here can cause vision loss even if the eyes are healthy.

after a stroke, a patient has trouble planning, making decisions and moving the right arm on purpose. click the lobe most likely affected. the frontal lobe handles planning, judgment, personality and voluntary movement. its primary motor cortex, just in front of the central sulcus, controls voluntary muscle movement. each side of the brain controls the opposite side of the body.

click the lobe that processes hearing. the temporal lobe sits on the side of the brain, at about ear level. its auditory cortex processes sound, and nearby areas help with memory and understanding language. the parietal lobe processes touch and body sensation.

click the lobe that receives touch, temperature and pain information from the skin. the parietal lobe lies behind the central sulcus. its primary somatosensory cortex maps sensations from every part of the body. the frontal lobe, in front of the central sulcus, handles voluntary movement instead.

click the colored muscle that controls how much light enters the eye. the iris is a ring of smooth muscle with pigment that gives the eye its color. it widens or narrows the pupil: in bright light the pupil gets smaller, and in dim light it gets larger. the pupil is the opening, not the muscle.

click the structure that fine-tunes focus by changing its shape for near or far objects. the lens is a clear, flexible disk behind the iris. ciliary muscles change its shape (accommodation) to focus light on the retina. with age the lens stiffens, which is why many adults need reading glasses.

click the clear front layer of the eye that does most of the bending (refraction) of light. the cornea is the clear, curved window at the front of the eye. because of its curve, it bends light more than the lens does, but its shape cannot change. lasik surgery reshapes the cornea to correct vision.

click the nerve that carries visual signals from the eye to the brain. the optic nerve leaves the back of the eye. it carries signals from the retina's rods and cones to the brain. the spot where it leaves has no photoreceptors, which causes a blind spot.

click the snail-shaped structure that contains the receptors for hearing. the cochlea is the coiled, snail-shaped part of the inner ear. hair cells inside it bend when fluid waves pass by, and they turn those vibrations into nerve signals. the semicircular canals, right next to it, look like three loops. they sense balance, not sound.

a child with a cold has ear pain because pressure can't equalize in the middle ear. click the tube that normally equalizes middle-ear pressure. the auditory (eustachian) tube runs from the middle ear down to the throat (nasopharynx). it opens when you swallow or yawn, which equalizes air pressure on both sides of the eardrum. that's the "pop" on an airplane. a cold can swell the tube shut. in young children the tube is short and nearly level, so germs travel up it easily, which is one reason middle ear infections (otitis media) are common.

put these structures in the order sound vibrations reach them, first to last. auricle external auditory canal tympanic membrane ossicles cochlea the auricle collects sound and funnels it down the external auditory canal. sound waves make the tympanic membrane vibrate, and the three ossicles (malleus → incus → stapes) pass and amplify the vibration. the stapes pushes on the oval window of the cochlea, setting its fluid in motion. hair cells then send signals along the vestibulocochlear nerve.

a patient feels dizzy and loses balance whenever she turns her head, but her hearing is normal. which lettered structure is most likely affected? c d e f e points to the semicircular canals. fluid moving inside them when the head rotates tells the brain about head movement and balance. hearing depends on the eardrum (c), ossicles (d) and cochlea (f). since her hearing is normal, those are probably working. balance problems with normal hearing point to the vestibular parts of the inner ear: the semicircular canals and vestibule.

tap the longest and strongest bone in the body, the bone of the thigh. the femur runs from the hip joint to the knee. it is the longest, heaviest and strongest bone in the body. the tibia and fibula are in the lower leg, below the knee. the humerus is the long bone of the upper arm.

which bone is labeled h? ulna humerus radius fibula h points to the forearm bone on the thumb side (lateral side, with palms facing forward). that bone is the radius. the ulna (g) is the other forearm bone, on the little-finger side. the humerus (e) is in the upper arm, and the fibula (m) is in the lower leg.

a patient at a fresno clinic fell on an outstretched hand and has a fracture of the forearm bone on the thumb side, just above the wrist. tap the bone that is broken. in anatomical position (palms forward), the thumb side of the forearm is the lateral side. the lateral forearm bone is the radius. a fall on an outstretched hand very often breaks the distal radius, near the wrist. the ulna is the medial (little-finger side) forearm bone, so it is the trap answer.

the axial skeleton forms the central axis of the body. which of the labeled bones belong to the axial skeleton? select all that apply. skull sternum ribs clavicle pelvic girdle (hip bones) the axial skeleton is the skull, vertebral column, ribs and sternum (plus small bones like the hyoid). the clavicle is part of the pectoral (shoulder) girdle, and the hip bones form the pelvic girdle. girdles attach the limbs, so they belong to the appendicular skeleton.

in an adult long bone, red bone marrow that makes blood cells is found mainly in the region labeled: h d c g g points to spongy bone in the epiphysis. the spaces between its thin plates of bone hold red marrow, which makes blood cells. h is the medullary cavity of the diaphysis. in adults it is filled mostly with yellow marrow (fat). d is dense compact bone, and c is the periosteum, the membrane that covers the outside of the bone.

what is the job of the articular cartilage shown at the ends of the bone? it makes red blood cells and platelets for the body it gives a smooth, slippery surface that reduces friction in the joint it anchors tendons and ligaments firmly to the outer shaft of the long bone it stores fat as an energy reserve inside the bone articular cartilage is a thin layer of hyaline cartilage covering the ends of bones where they meet in a joint. its smooth surface lets bones glide past each other with little friction and helps absorb shock. red marrow makes blood cells, the periosteum anchors tendons and ligaments, and yellow marrow stores fat.

a 10-year-old's x-ray shows a band of cartilage in the place where this adult bone has the epiphyseal line. what happens at that band of cartilage in the child? blood cells are made and released into the blood the bone grows in diameter by adding layers under the periosteum the bone grows in length calcium is removed from the bone to raise blood calcium in children, the epiphyseal (growth) plate is a layer of hyaline cartilage between the epiphysis and diaphysis. new cartilage forms and is replaced by bone, so the bone gets longer. when growth stops after puberty, the plate turns to bone and leaves the epiphyseal line seen in adults. growth in width happens at the periosteum, not at the growth plate.

compare the relaxed and contracted sarcomeres. which region stays the same length when the muscle contracts? h zone i band sarcomere (z line to z line) a band the a band is the full length of the thick (myosin) filaments. filaments do not shorten, so the a band stays the same length. thin (actin) filaments slide toward the m line, which pulls the z lines closer together. the sarcomere, the i band and the h zone all get shorter. in the diagram, the myosin rows are the same length in both sarcomeres, but the z lines are much closer together when contracted.

tap a thick filament, the protein whose heads grab and pull the thin filaments during contraction. thick filaments are made of myosin. myosin heads bind actin, pivot (the power stroke) and pull the thin filaments toward the center of the sarcomere. this pulling uses atp and requires calcium to expose binding sites on actin. the thin filaments attached to the z lines are actin.

how many bones are in the typical adult human skeleton? 106 270 206 312 the adult skeleton has 206 bones. newborns have about 270 bony parts, but many fuse together (for example, in the skull and sacrum) during growth.

which type of muscle tissue is striated and involuntary? skeletal muscle cardiac muscle smooth muscle both skeletal and smooth muscle cardiac muscle has striations (stripes) like skeletal muscle but is controlled involuntarily. skeletal muscle is striated and voluntary; smooth muscle is non-striated and involuntary.

smooth muscle is found mainly in which location? the walls of hollow organs, such as the stomach attached to bones of the skeleton by tendons only in the walls of the heart chambers in the tongue and the muscles of facial expression smooth muscle lines hollow organs: the gi tract, blood vessels, bladder, uterus, and airways. skeletal muscle attaches to bones (and forms the tongue and facial muscles), and cardiac muscle is found only in the heart.

a soccer player at fresno state twists her ankle and is told she has a sprain. which structure is injured? a tendon a bone skeletal muscle fibers a ligament a sprain is a stretched or torn ligament; ligaments connect bone to bone at a joint. a strain is an injury to a muscle or tendon (tendons connect muscle to bone), and a fracture is a broken bone.

put these events of skeletal muscle contraction in order, from first to last. a motor neuron releases acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction an action potential spreads along the muscle fiber membrane calcium ions are released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum myosin heads bind to actin, forming cross-bridges thin filaments slide toward the center of the sarcomere acetylcholine binds receptors on the muscle fiber, starting an action potential that travels along the membrane and into the t-tubules. this signals the sarcoplasmic reticulum to release ca²⁺, which binds troponin and moves tropomyosin off actin's binding sites. myosin heads attach to actin and pull (power stroke), sliding thin filaments inward and shortening the sarcomere.

during skeletal muscle contraction, calcium ions bind to which protein, allowing myosin to reach the binding sites on actin? myosin collagen troponin hemoglobin at rest, tropomyosin covers the myosin-binding sites on actin. calcium binds troponin, which shifts tropomyosin out of the way so cross-bridges can form.

after death, muscles become stiff (rigor mortis). what is the best explanation? without calcium, actin and myosin cannot bind without atp, myosin heads cannot detach from actin acetylcholine is released continuously after death the bones lose calcium and lock the joints in place myosin needs a fresh molecule of atp to release from actin after each power stroke. after death, atp production stops, so cross-bridges stay locked and muscles stiffen. calcium actually leaks into the cytoplasm after death, which allows binding; it does not prevent it.

the thick filaments in a sarcomere are made mainly of which protein? myosin actin keratin collagen thick filaments are myosin, whose heads form cross-bridges. thin filaments are mainly actin (with troponin and tropomyosin). keratin is in skin and hair, and collagen is in connective tissues.

which bone cells break down bone tissue, releasing calcium into the blood? osteoblasts osteocytes chondrocytes osteoclasts osteoclasts dissolve (resorb) bone matrix. osteoblasts build new bone, osteocytes are mature bone cells that maintain the matrix, and chondrocytes are cartilage cells.

which of the following are characteristics of skeletal muscle tissue? select all that apply. striated (striped) appearance under voluntary control long cells with many nuclei found in the walls of blood vessels cells joined by intercalated discs skeletal muscle fibers are long, multinucleated, striated cells that we control voluntarily. smooth muscle lines blood vessel walls, and intercalated discs join cardiac muscle cells.

which bone is part of the axial skeleton? femur scapula sternum clavicle the axial skeleton forms the body's central axis: skull, vertebral column, ribs, and sternum. the femur (limb), scapula, and clavicle (pectoral girdle) belong to the appendicular skeleton.

which type of joint allows the widest range of motion, including rotation in many directions? hinge joint, such as the elbow ball-and-socket joint, such as the shoulder pivot joint, such as between the first two vertebrae suture, such as between skull bones in a ball-and-socket joint, the rounded head of one bone fits into a cup of another, allowing movement in all planes. hinge joints move in one plane, pivot joints allow rotation around one axis, and sutures are essentially immovable.

the sutures that join the bones of an adult skull are classified as fibrous, immovable joints synovial, freely movable joints cartilaginous, slightly movable joints ball-and-socket joints sutures are fibrous joints in which bones are bound by dense connective tissue and essentially do not move (synarthroses). synovial joints have a fluid-filled cavity and move freely; cartilaginous joints like the intervertebral discs move slightly.

an older woman is diagnosed with osteoporosis after a hip fracture. which imbalance best describes what has been happening in her bones? bone building by osteoblasts has exceeded bone breakdown by osteoclasts cartilage has gradually replaced compact bone red bone marrow has replaced all of the yellow marrow bone breakdown by osteoclasts has exceeded bone building by osteoblasts bone is constantly remodeled; in osteoporosis, resorption outpaces formation, so bones lose mass and become porous and fragile. after menopause, falling estrogen allows osteoclast activity to increase, which is why older women are at higher risk. weight-bearing exercise, calcium, and vitamin d help maintain bone density.

bending the elbow so the hand moves toward the shoulder is an example of which movement? extension abduction flexion rotation flexion decreases the angle between two bones at a joint. straightening the elbow is extension, abduction moves a limb away from the midline, and rotation turns a bone around its own axis.

raising your arm out to the side, away from the midline of the body, is called adduction abduction flexion supination abduction moves a body part away from the midline (think "abducted" = taken away). adduction brings it back toward the midline (you "add" it back to the body). supination turns the palm to face up or forward.

which vitamin is needed for the intestine to absorb calcium, supporting healthy bones? vitamin d vitamin c vitamin b12 vitamin a active vitamin d (calcitriol) increases calcium absorption from the small intestine. without enough vitamin d, bones become soft (rickets in children, osteomalacia in adults). vitamin c is needed for collagen, but it does not control calcium absorption.

which of the following are functions of the skeletal system? select all that apply. supporting the body and protecting internal organs storing calcium and phosphate producing blood cells in red bone marrow producing most of the body's heat secreting digestive enzymes bones support and protect (the skull protects the brain, the ribs protect the heart and lungs), store minerals, and house red marrow that makes blood cells. most body heat comes from contracting skeletal muscle, and digestive enzymes come from digestive glands.

bone-forming cells that secrete new bone matrix are called ______. osteoblasts build bone by laying down collagen and helping it mineralize. once surrounded by matrix, an osteoblast becomes an osteocyte.

when the biceps brachii contracts to flex the elbow, the triceps brachii relaxes. in this movement, the triceps is acting as the prime mover (agonist) synergist fixator antagonist the prime mover (here the biceps) is mainly responsible for the movement. the antagonist (the triceps) opposes that movement and must relax for it to happen; it is the prime mover for elbow extension.

the diaphragm is made of which type of muscle tissue? smooth muscle cardiac muscle skeletal muscle dense connective tissue only the diaphragm is a skeletal muscle controlled by the phrenic nerves. breathing usually happens automatically, but you can also control it voluntarily (holding your breath), which fits skeletal muscle.

osteoarthritis, common in older adults, mainly involves the wearing away of which tissue? red bone marrow articular cartilage covering the ends of bones the periosteum covering the shaft of the bone the tendons and skeletal muscles that cross the joint in synovial joints, smooth hyaline (articular) cartilage covers the bone ends and reduces friction. in osteoarthritis this cartilage breaks down, so bone rubs on bone, causing pain and stiffness.

tap the kneecap. the patella (kneecap) is a sesamoid bone inside the tendon of the quadriceps muscle. it protects the knee joint and gives the quadriceps better leverage. the femur is above it and the tibia is below it.
tap the bone of the upper arm. the humerus runs from the shoulder to the elbow. at the elbow it meets the radius and ulna of the forearm. at the shoulder it fits into a socket on the scapula.

tap the larger, weight-bearing bone of the lower leg (the shin bone). the tibia is the shin bone, on the big-toe side of the lower leg. it carries most of the body's weight from the femur to the ankle. the fibula is the thin bone beside it and bears little weight.

cpr compressions are done on the center of the chest. tap the bone the hands press on. chest compressions are done on the lower half of the sternum (breastbone). the sternum connects to the ribs through costal cartilage, so pressing it squeezes the heart between it and the spine. pressing too low, on the tip (xiphoid process), can injure the liver.

tap the bone that is the most commonly broken bone in a fall onto the shoulder. the clavicle (collarbone) is a slender s-shaped bone that connects the sternum to the shoulder blade. because it braces the shoulder, force from a fall on the shoulder or outstretched arm often breaks it. it is part of the appendicular skeleton (pectoral girdle).
tap the long shaft of the bone. the diaphysis is the shaft of a long bone. its walls are thick compact bone around a hollow medullary cavity. the epiphyses are the wider ends.

tap the smooth tissue that covers the end of the bone where it forms a joint. articular cartilage is hyaline cartilage covering the joint surfaces. it is smooth and slippery, so bones glide without grinding. in osteoarthritis this cartilage wears away.

tap the line that marks where the bone grew in length during childhood. before adulthood, the epiphyseal (growth) plate is a band of cartilage that lets the bone lengthen. when growth stops, the plate is replaced by bone and leaves the epiphyseal line. a fracture through a child's growth plate can affect how long the bone grows.

tap the hollow space in the shaft that holds yellow marrow (fat) in an adult. the medullary cavity runs through the diaphysis. in adults it is filled mostly with yellow marrow, which stores fat. red marrow, which makes blood cells, is found mainly in spongy bone.

tap a thin filament, the protein that is pulled toward the center of the sarcomere during contraction. actin forms the thin filaments attached to the z lines. myosin heads grab actin and pull it toward the m line, so the sarcomere shortens. the filaments themselves do not shorten; they slide past each other.

tap one of the lines that mark the two ends of a sarcomere. a sarcomere runs from one z line (z disc) to the next. thin actin filaments are anchored to the z lines. during contraction the z lines are pulled closer together.

click the space filled with the fluid that lubricates the joint and nourishes the cartilage. the joint cavity is the narrow space between the two bone ends. it is filled with synovial fluid, which feels like raw egg white. the fluid reduces friction and carries nutrients to the articular cartilage, which has no blood vessels of its own. the synovial membrane lining the capsule makes the fluid; the cavity holds it.

in osteoarthritis, structure b wears away, so bone rubs on bone. what is structure b? ligament articular cartilage synovial membrane fibrous joint capsule b is the articular cartilage, the smooth, glassy layer of hyaline cartilage capping each bone end. in osteoarthritis it thins and cracks with wear. without it, bone grinds on bone, causing pain, stiffness and bony spurs. rheumatoid arthritis is different: the immune system attacks the synovial membrane (d).

which lettered structures are found in a synovial joint but not in a fibrous joint such as a skull suture? select all that apply. a (bone) b (articular cartilage) c (joint cavity with synovial fluid) d (synovial membrane) a fibrous joint (like a suture) has bones held tightly together by dense connective tissue with no cavity, so it barely moves. synovial joints are the freely movable ones. they are defined by a fluid-filled cavity, lined by a synovial membrane, with cartilage-capped bone ends. both kinds of joint, of course, are made where bones meet.

click the muscle tissue that is striated (striped) but involuntary. cardiac muscle is striated like skeletal muscle, but you can't control it by choice: it is involuntary. look for striated cells that branch, each with one or two central nuclei. dark intercalated discs join neighboring cells end to end. skeletal muscle is striated and voluntary. smooth muscle is involuntary but has no stripes.

which lettered tissue makes up the walls of the stomach, intestines, bladder and blood vessels and moves food along by peristalsis? a b c c is smooth muscle: spindle-shaped cells, each with one central nucleus, and no stripes. smooth muscle lines hollow organs and blood vessels. its slow, involuntary waves of contraction (peristalsis) push food through the gi tract. a (skeletal) has long striated fibers with many nuclei at the edges and moves the skeleton. b (cardiac) is found only in the heart.

the cells of tissue b are joined end to end by intercalated discs, which contain gap junctions. why is this important? it lets the electrical signal pass quickly from cell to cell so the heart contracts as one unit. it stores calcium so the muscle can contract voluntarily. it attaches the muscle to bone so it can move the skeleton. it allows each cell to divide quickly and repair damage. b is cardiac muscle, the only tissue with intercalated discs (they show as faint dark bands across the fibers). gap junctions in the discs let ions flow straight from one cell into the next, so a wave of excitation spreads across the whole heart and it beats in a coordinated way. desmosomes in the discs also hold the cells together so they don't pull apart with every beat. cardiac muscle cells divide very little, which is why heart damage heals with scar tissue.

according to the graph, during which age range do women lose bone mass fastest? 20 to 30 30 to 40 50 to 60 70 to 80 the steepest downward part of the women's line is from 50 to 60: from 92% to 78%, a drop of 14 points. that is the time of menopause. estrogen helps protect bone, so when estrogen falls, bone breakdown by osteoclasts speeds up. this is why osteoporosis is more common in older women.

based on the graph, why do health experts urge teens and young adults to do weight-bearing exercise and get enough calcium? bone mass peaks around age 30, so building more bone early leaves a bigger reserve to lose later. bone stops being remodeled after age 20. bone mass rises again after age 60 if enough calcium is eaten. exercise after age 30 cannot affect bone at all. the graph shows bone mass climbing until about age 30 (peak bone mass), then slowly declining. a person who reaches a higher peak has more bone "in the bank," so it takes longer to fall to the fragile levels where fractures happen. bone is remodeled for life, so exercise and calcium still help later, but the biggest gains come while bone is still building.

which labeled organ filters blood and removes old, worn-out red blood cells? a b c d c is the spleen, in the upper left part of the abdomen (on your right as you face the figure). the spleen filters blood, removes old red blood cells and holds lymphocytes that respond to blood-borne germs. a is the tonsils, b is the thymus, and d is the thoracic duct.

tap the organ where t lymphocytes (t cells) mature. it is large in children and shrinks after puberty. the thymus sits in the upper chest, behind the sternum and above the heart. immature t cells travel from red bone marrow to the thymus, where they mature and learn not to attack the body's own cells. after puberty the thymus slowly shrinks and is replaced by fat.

a patient has an infected cut on the hand. a day later, tender, swollen lumps appear in the armpit. tap the type of structure that is swollen. lymph from the hand and arm drains to the axillary (armpit) lymph nodes. lymph nodes filter lymph. when they trap germs, lymphocytes inside multiply, so the nodes swell and become tender. the spleen filters blood, not lymph, and it is in the abdomen, not the armpit.

what is structure d, and where does it return lymph to the blood? thoracic duct; into the left subclavian vein thoracic duct; directly into the right atrium right lymphatic duct; into the right subclavian vein inferior vena cava; into the right atrium d is the thoracic duct. it starts in the abdomen and runs up through the chest just left of the midline. it drains lymph from about three-fourths of the body and empties into the left subclavian vein near the base of the neck. the right lymphatic duct is much shorter and drains only the upper right part of the body.

put the steps in the path of lymph in order, from first to last. fluid between cells enters lymphatic capillaries lymph flows through lymphatic vessels lymph is filtered in lymph nodes lymph collects in the thoracic duct lymph enters the blood at the left subclavian vein extra tissue fluid enters tiny, blind-ended lymphatic capillaries and is now called lymph. lymph travels through larger lymphatic vessels that pass through lymph nodes, where it is filtered. vessels join into large ducts. the thoracic duct returns lymph to the blood at the left subclavian vein.

which of the following are functions of the lymphatic system? select all that apply. returning excess tissue fluid to the blood absorbing dietary fats from the small intestine carrying oxygen to the tissues housing lymphocytes that fight infection producing bile to digest fats the lymphatic system returns leaked tissue fluid to the blood, which helps prevent swelling (edema). lacteals (lymphatic capillaries in the small intestine) absorb dietary fats. lymph nodes, the spleen, the thymus and the tonsils house lymphocytes. red blood cells carry oxygen, and the liver makes bile.

which labeled structure is a patch of lymphatic tissue in the throat that traps germs entering through the mouth and nose? a b e c a points to the tonsils, at the back of the throat (pharynx). tonsils trap inhaled and swallowed pathogens and start an immune response. b is the thymus, c is the spleen, and e points to lymph nodes.

which of the following is part of the body's first line of defense against pathogens? antibodies made by plasma cells cytotoxic t cells that kill infected cells fever that slows pathogen growth intact skin and mucous membranes the first line of defense consists of physical and chemical barriers that keep pathogens out: skin, mucous membranes, tears, stomach acid. fever and inflammation are part of the second (internal innate) line, and antibodies and t cells are the adaptive third line.

which of the following are part of innate (nonspecific) immunity? select all that apply. inflammation fever phagocytosis by neutrophils antibody production by plasma cells memory t cells innate defenses respond quickly and the same way to many different invaders: inflammation, fever, and phagocytes such as neutrophils. antibodies from plasma cells and memory t cells are adaptive: they target specific antigens and remember them.

which cells produce and secrete antibodies? helper t cells neutrophils plasma cells red blood cells when a b cell is activated by its specific antigen, it multiplies and many of its offspring become plasma cells. plasma cells are antibody factories; helper t cells help activate b cells but do not make antibodies.

hiv damages the immune system mainly by destroying which cells? red blood cells (erythrocytes) helper t cells (cd4⁺ cells) platelets plasma cells (from b cells) hiv infects and destroys cd4⁺ helper t cells. helper t cells coordinate both antibody and cell-mediated responses, so losing them weakens the whole adaptive immune system and leads to opportunistic infections.

which cells directly kill body cells that are infected with a virus? cytotoxic t cells helper t cells b lymphocytes (b cells) basophils cytotoxic (cd8⁺) t cells recognize viral antigens displayed on infected cells and release chemicals that kill those cells. helper t cells coordinate the response, b cells make antibodies (via plasma cells), and basophils release histamine.

which white blood cells are the most abundant in blood and usually the first to arrive at a site of bacterial infection? lymphocytes eosinophils monocytes neutrophils neutrophils make up about 50–70% of white blood cells and quickly leave the blood to phagocytize bacteria. a high neutrophil count often signals a bacterial infection. pus is largely made of dead neutrophils.

which of the following are classic signs of inflammation at an injured site? select all that apply. redness swelling heat paleness (pallor) pain inflammation dilates local blood vessels (redness and heat) and makes them leakier (swelling). swelling and chemicals released by damaged cells cause pain. the area becomes red, not pale, because more blood flows to it.

a nursing student receives the hepatitis b vaccine before starting clinicals. which type of immunity does this produce? passive, artificially acquired active, naturally acquired active, artificially acquired passive, naturally acquired a vaccine exposes the body to antigens, so the student's own immune system makes antibodies and memory cells: active immunity. because it comes from a medical intervention instead of a natural infection, it is artificially acquired.

a newborn receives antibodies from the mother through breast milk. which type of immunity is this? active, naturally acquired passive, naturally acquired passive, artificially acquired active, artificially acquired the infant receives ready-made antibodies rather than making its own, so the immunity is passive (and temporary, with no memory cells). it happens through a normal process (nursing or transfer across the placenta), so it is naturally acquired.

a child who had chickenpox is exposed to the virus again years later and does not get sick. what best explains this? memory b and t cells mount a faster, stronger secondary response the virus can no longer infect skin cells neutrophils permanently surround the virus the first infection destroyed all the body's receptors for the virus during the first infection, some activated lymphocytes became long-lived memory cells. on re-exposure, memory cells respond quickly and produce large amounts of antibody, usually before symptoms develop. this immunological memory is the basis for how vaccines work.

during a throat infection, the lymph nodes in the neck become swollen and tender. why? the nodes are producing extra red blood cells bile is backing up into the lymph vessels the nodes are storing excess dietary fat lymphocytes in the nodes are multiplying lymph nodes filter lymph and are packed with lymphocytes and macrophages. when they encounter antigens from the infection, lymphocytes multiply rapidly, enlarging the nodes.

besides immune defense, what is a major function of the lymphatic system? pumping blood from the heart to the lungs producing digestive enzymes for the intestine returning excess tissue fluid to the blood filtering urea out of the blood into urine some fluid leaks out of capillaries and is not reabsorbed; lymphatic vessels collect this fluid (lymph) and return it to veins near the heart. if lymph vessels are blocked or removed (for example, after some cancer surgeries), fluid builds up and causes swelling (lymphedema). lymphatic vessels in the intestine (lacteals) also absorb dietary fats.

put the steps of phagocytosis by a macrophage in order. the phagocyte recognizes and attaches to the microbe the phagocyte engulfs the microbe, enclosing it in a phagosome a lysosome fuses with the phagosome lysosomal enzymes digest the microbe the phagocyte first binds the microbe (antibodies or complement coating it make this easier). it wraps its membrane around the microbe, forming a vesicle called a phagosome. a lysosome fuses with it, and digestive enzymes destroy the microbe.

in which organ do t lymphocytes mature? thyroid gland thymus spleen tonsils t cells form in red bone marrow, then travel to the thymus (t for thymus) to mature. the thymus is largest in childhood and shrinks with age. the thyroid is an endocrine gland, not a lymphatic organ.

which organ filters blood, removes old and damaged red blood cells, and is located in the left upper quadrant of the abdomen? spleen liver thymus appendix the spleen filters blood, breaks down worn-out red blood cells, and contains lymphocytes that respond to blood-borne pathogens. the liver is mainly in the right upper quadrant, and the thymus is in the chest.

the y-shaped proteins made by plasma cells that bind to specific antigens are called ______. antibodies (immunoglobulins) bind specific antigens. binding can neutralize toxins, clump microbes together, and mark them for destruction by phagocytes.

an antigen is best defined as a y-shaped protein made by plasma cells a type of white blood cell that engulfs and digests bacteria a chemical released by the brain to cause fever a molecule that triggers a specific immune response antigens are usually proteins or large carbohydrates (on microbes, pollen, or transplanted cells) that trigger an immune response. antibodies are the proteins made to bind antigens; do not mix up the two.

during an allergic reaction to almond pollen, mast cells release a chemical that dilates blood vessels and causes itching and a runny nose. which chemical is this? insulin hemoglobin histamine acetylcholine mast cells (and basophils) release histamine, which dilates blood vessels and makes them leaky. this causes redness, swelling, itching, and mucus, which is why antihistamines relieve allergy symptoms.

a patient develops sudden airway swelling, wheezing, and a dangerous drop in blood pressure minutes after a bee sting (anaphylaxis). which medication is given first to reverse these effects? insulin epinephrine an antibiotic a blood thinner anaphylaxis is a whole-body allergic reaction with massive histamine release. epinephrine constricts blood vessels (raising blood pressure) and relaxes bronchiole smooth muscle (opening airways), which is why it is given right away by auto-injector. antibiotics treat bacterial infections and do nothing for an allergic reaction.

which lymphatic tissues, located in the walls of the pharynx, trap pathogens that are inhaled or swallowed? tonsils lymph nodes of the groin thymus spleen the tonsils are clusters of lymphatic tissue around the throat that sample and fight microbes entering through the mouth and nose. inflamed tonsils (tonsillitis) are a common sign of a throat infection. the thymus is in the chest, the spleen is in the abdomen, and the inguinal lymph nodes are in the groin.

which of the following is an autoimmune disease, in which the immune system attacks the body's own tissues? influenza strep throat valley fever (coccidioidomycosis) type 1 diabetes mellitus in type 1 diabetes, the immune system destroys the insulin-producing beta cells of the pancreas. influenza (virus), strep throat (bacterium), and valley fever (a fungus common in central valley soil) are infections caused by outside pathogens.

macrophages, the large phagocytes found in tissues, develop from which type of white blood cell? neutrophils lymphocytes monocytes basophils monocytes circulate in the blood, then leave it and enlarge into macrophages in the tissues. macrophages engulf microbes and debris and present antigens to t cells, linking innate and adaptive immunity.

tap the organ in the upper left abdomen that filters blood and removes old red blood cells. the spleen is the largest lymphatic organ. it removes worn-out red blood cells and holds lymphocytes that respond to germs in the blood. because it is full of blood, a ruptured spleen can cause serious internal bleeding.

tap the lymphatic tissue at the back of the throat that is sometimes removed when it is infected again and again. the tonsils are patches of lymphatic tissue in the throat. they trap germs that enter through the mouth and nose. repeated infections (tonsillitis) can lead to a tonsillectomy.

tap the large vessel that returns lymph from most of the body to the blood. the thoracic duct starts in the abdomen and runs up the chest. it drains lymph from both legs, the abdomen, the left arm and the left side of the head. it empties into the left subclavian vein near the base of the neck.

the graph shows antibody levels after a person is exposed to the same antigen twice. why is the response after the second exposure faster and much larger? memory b cells made during the first exposure quickly make plasma cells that produce antibodies. the antigen is weaker the second time. antibodies from the first exposure have been stored in the liver. red blood cells learned to make antibodies after the first exposure. the first (primary) response is slow because the body must find and activate the few b cells that match the antigen. that response also leaves behind long-lived memory b cells. on a second exposure they quickly turn into plasma cells, so the secondary response is faster, stronger and lasts longer. this is how acquired (adaptive) immunity works, and it is why you usually get chickenpox only once.

a vaccine series gives a first dose, then a booster dose weeks later. which part of the graph best shows why the booster is given? the large, fast rise after day 28 the small rise between days 0 and 14 the drop between days 14 and 28 the flat line at day 0 the first dose causes a small primary response and creates memory cells. the booster acts like a second exposure: memory cells respond fast and strongly, raising antibody levels much higher (the peak after day 28). higher antibody levels and more memory cells give stronger, longer-lasting protection. this is active, artificially acquired immunity.

using the graph, about how many days after the first exposure do antibody levels peak? 7 days 14 days 28 days 42 days find the top of the first, small hump: it is at day 14 (about 10 units). the big peak at day 42 belongs to the second exposure, which happened on day 28.

which class of antibody can cross the placenta to give a fetus temporary protection before birth? iga ige igg igm igg is the only antibody class that crosses the placenta, giving the newborn passive immunity for the first few months. igg is also the most abundant antibody in the blood.

a breastfeeding parent asks how breast milk protects the baby's gut from infection. which antibody class in breast milk mainly protects the lining of the infant's digestive tract? iga igd ige igm iga is the main antibody in body secretions: breast milk (especially colostrum), saliva, tears, and mucus. in the infant's gut, iga binds pathogens on the mucous membranes before they can invade.

which statements about antibody classes are correct? select all that apply. igm is the first antibody made in a primary immune response and is a pentamer. ige binds to mast cells and triggers allergic reactions. igg is the most abundant antibody in the blood. iga is the main antibody that crosses the placenta. ige is the most abundant antibody in the blood. igm (five y-shaped units joined together) appears first in a new infection; igg rises later and becomes the most abundant antibody in blood. ige attaches to mast cells and basophils; when an allergen binds it, they release histamine. igg, not iga, crosses the placenta, and ige is present in only tiny amounts.

an unvaccinated nurse has a needlestick from a patient with hepatitis b. the nurse is given hepatitis b immune globulin (ready-made antibodies) and also starts the hepatitis b vaccine. why is the immune globulin given? it protects right away, but only for a few months. it gives lifelong protection, because the donated antibodies make memory cells. it works more slowly than the vaccine does, but its protection lasts for many years. it replaces the need for the vaccine series. immune globulin is artificially acquired passive immunity: the antibodies work right away, but no memory cells form and they are broken down within weeks to months. the vaccine produces active immunity: the nurse's own b cells make antibodies and memory cells, which takes weeks but lasts much longer.

tap the gland that releases insulin and glucagon to control blood glucose. the pancreas lies behind the stomach, with its head on the body's right and its tail toward the body's left. its islet cells release insulin (lowers blood glucose) and glucagon (raises blood glucose). the adrenal glands sit on top of the kidneys and release cortisol and epinephrine.

tap the gland often called the "master gland." it controls several other glands but is itself controlled by the hypothalamus. the pituitary gland hangs from the base of the brain on a thin stalk, just below the hypothalamus. it releases hormones such as tsh, acth, fsh, lh and growth hormone that control other glands. the hypothalamus sends releasing hormones (and nerve signals) to the pituitary, so it is the pituitary's boss.

a patient's blood calcium level is low. tap the glands that release the hormone that raises blood calcium. (use the thyroid close-up.) low blood calcium triggers the parathyroid glands to release parathyroid hormone (pth). pth raises blood calcium by releasing calcium from bone, reducing calcium loss in the urine and activating vitamin d so the gut absorbs more. the thyroid makes calcitonin, which lowers blood calcium, so tapping the thyroid is the trap answer. the parathyroids are the small glands on the back of the thyroid.

which gland is labeled f, and which hormone does it produce? adrenal gland; cortisol pancreas; insulin adrenal gland; thyroxine kidney; aldosterone f points to the small glands that sit on top of the kidneys. these are the adrenal glands. the adrenal cortex makes cortisol and aldosterone, and the adrenal medulla makes epinephrine. thyroxine comes from the thyroid. the kidney (h) does not make aldosterone, although aldosterone acts on the kidney.

which labeled gland secretes melatonin, which helps regulate the sleep–wake cycle? a b d c c is the pineal gland, a small gland deep in the brain. the pineal gland releases melatonin mostly at night, in darkness, which helps set the sleep–wake (circadian) rhythm. a is the hypothalamus, b is the pituitary, and d is the thyroid.

a patient feels tired and cold. lab results show a high tsh level and a low t4 (thyroxine) level. which labeled gland is most likely underactive? pituitary thyroid hypothalamus parathyroid glands tsh from the pituitary tells the thyroid to make t4. normally, high t4 shuts tsh off (negative feedback). low t4 with high tsh means the pituitary is shouting at the thyroid, but the thyroid is not answering. the thyroid is underactive (primary hypothyroidism). if the pituitary were the problem, tsh would be low, not high. the parathyroids control calcium, not t4.

which of the labeled glands are located inside the skull? select all that apply. hypothalamus thyroid pineal pituitary adrenal glands the hypothalamus and pineal gland are part of the brain, and the pituitary hangs from the base of the brain in a pocket of bone in the skull. the thyroid is in the front of the neck, and the adrenal glands sit on top of the kidneys in the abdomen.

insulin is produced by which cells? beta cells of the pancreatic islets alpha cells of the pancreatic islets cells of the adrenal cortex liver cells (hepatocytes) the pancreatic islets (islets of langerhans) contain beta cells, which secrete insulin, and alpha cells, which secrete glucagon. the liver responds to insulin, but it does not make it.

name the hormone that lowers blood glucose by helping glucose enter body cells. after a meal, rising blood glucose stimulates pancreatic beta cells to release insulin. insulin helps glucose enter muscle and fat cells and signals the liver to store glucose as glycogen.

between meals, blood glucose begins to drop. which hormone is released to raise it, and how does it work? insulin; it signals the liver and muscles to store glucose as glycogen glucagon; it signals muscle cells to absorb more glucose from the blood calcitonin; it releases glucose from bone glucagon; it signals the liver to break down glycogen into glucose pancreatic alpha cells release glucagon when blood glucose falls. glucagon tells the liver to break down stored glycogen and release glucose into the blood. insulin has the opposite effect, lowering blood glucose.

a patient with type 2 diabetes has high blood glucose even though the pancreas is still producing insulin. what is the most likely explanation? the immune system has destroyed all of the beta cells the liver has completely stopped making glucagon body cells have become resistant to insulin's effects the kidneys are secreting too much insulin into the blood in type 2 diabetes, cells respond poorly to insulin (insulin resistance), so glucose stays in the blood. destruction of beta cells by the immune system describes type 1 diabetes. the kidneys do not produce insulin.

which structure releases hormones that directly control secretion by the anterior pituitary gland? thyroid gland hypothalamus adrenal cortex pineal gland the hypothalamus releases releasing and inhibiting hormones that travel through a portal system to the anterior pituitary. because it controls the pituitary, the hypothalamus links the nervous and endocrine systems.

a farmworker in fresno county is becoming dehydrated during a 108 °f afternoon. which hormone increases to help the kidneys conserve water? antidiuretic hormone (adh) insulin (from the pancreas) calcitonin (from the thyroid) melatonin (from the pineal gland) when blood becomes more concentrated, the hypothalamus signals the posterior pituitary to release adh. adh makes the kidney's collecting ducts reabsorb more water, producing a smaller volume of concentrated urine. (aldosterone also helps by retaining sodium, but it was not offered as a choice.)

a patient with hyperthyroidism (too much thyroid hormone) would most likely show which set of signs? weight gain, slow heart rate, and cold intolerance low blood calcium, muscle cramps, and spasms very high blood glucose and frequent urination only weight loss, rapid heart rate, and heat intolerance thyroid hormones (t₃ and t₄) raise the body's metabolic rate. too much speeds everything up: weight loss despite eating, fast heart rate, nervousness, and feeling hot. weight gain, a slow heart rate, and feeling cold describe hypothyroidism.

which mineral must be supplied in the diet for the thyroid gland to make its hormones t₃ and t₄? iron calcium iodine potassium t₃ and t₄ contain iodine atoms (the numbers refer to how many each has). a lack of dietary iodine can cause an enlarged thyroid (goiter); iodized salt prevents this.

blood calcium is too low. which hormone is released, and from which gland, to raise it? calcitonin, from the thyroid gland in the neck parathyroid hormone, from the parathyroids insulin, from the pancreas aldosterone, from the adrenal cortex parathyroid hormone (pth) raises blood calcium by stimulating osteoclasts, increasing calcium reabsorption by the kidneys, and activating vitamin d. calcitonin from the thyroid has the opposite effect and lowers blood calcium.

blood levels of thyroid hormone (t₃ and t₄) rise above normal. through negative feedback, what happens next? trh and tsh secretion decrease trh and tsh secretion increase the thyroid gland releases even more t₃ and t₄ the adrenal medulla releases more tsh high t₃ and t₄ inhibit the hypothalamus (trh) and anterior pituitary (tsh). less tsh means less stimulation of the thyroid, so hormone levels fall back toward normal. tsh comes from the anterior pituitary, not the adrenal medulla.

put these steps of thyroid hormone regulation in order. the hypothalamus releases thyrotropin-releasing hormone (trh) the anterior pituitary releases thyroid-stimulating hormone (tsh) the thyroid gland releases t₃ and t₄ body cells increase their metabolic rate trh from the hypothalamus stimulates the anterior pituitary to release tsh. tsh travels in the blood to the thyroid, which releases t₃ and t₄. these hormones raise cellular metabolism, and high levels feed back to slow trh and tsh release.

which gland secretes epinephrine (adrenaline) during a sudden fight-or-flight emergency? adrenal cortex posterior pituitary thyroid gland adrenal medulla the adrenal medulla, the inner part of each adrenal gland, is stimulated by sympathetic nerves to release epinephrine and norepinephrine. the adrenal cortex (outer part) makes steroid hormones such as cortisol and aldosterone.

aldosterone, from the adrenal cortex, causes the kidneys to excrete more sodium and more water into the urine reabsorb more glucose reabsorb sodium (and water) and excrete potassium produce more red blood cells aldosterone acts on the distal tubules and collecting ducts to reabsorb na⁺ and secrete k⁺. water follows sodium by osmosis, so blood volume and blood pressure increase.

which hormone is released by the adrenal cortex during long-term stress and raises blood glucose while suppressing inflammation? epinephrine cortisol oxytocin calcitonin cortisol, a glucocorticoid, raises blood glucose by promoting glucose formation and breakdown of stored fuels. it also suppresses inflammation and the immune response, which is why cortisol-like drugs (such as prednisone) are used for inflammatory conditions. epinephrine is the short-term stress hormone from the adrenal medulla.

which gland secretes melatonin, a hormone that helps regulate the sleep–wake cycle? pineal gland pituitary gland thymus thyroid gland the pineal gland, deep in the brain, releases melatonin mainly in darkness, helping make you sleepy at night.

which hormones are produced and secreted by the anterior pituitary gland? select all that apply. growth hormone (gh) thyroid-stimulating hormone (tsh) prolactin oxytocin insulin the anterior pituitary makes gh, tsh, prolactin, acth, fsh, and lh. oxytocin (and adh) are made in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary. insulin comes from beta cells of the pancreas.

after childbirth, which hormone stimulates the mammary glands to produce milk? oxytocin estrogen glucagon prolactin prolactin from the anterior pituitary stimulates milk production. oxytocin from the posterior pituitary causes milk ejection ("let-down") from the ducts, not production.

how do endocrine glands deliver their hormones to target cells? they release hormones through ducts onto the skin they empty hormones into the digestive tract they secrete hormones into the bloodstream they pass hormones directly along nerve axons endocrine glands are ductless; their hormones diffuse into nearby capillaries and travel in the blood. exocrine glands (sweat, salivary) use ducts to release secretions onto a surface or into a cavity.

which of the following are endocrine glands? select all that apply. thyroid gland adrenal glands pituitary gland salivary glands sweat glands the thyroid, adrenal glands, and pituitary secrete hormones directly into the blood. salivary and sweat glands are exocrine glands; they release their products through ducts.

steroid hormones such as cortisol and estrogen bind to receptors located inside target cells. why can they reach these receptors? they are pumped in by sodium–potassium pumps they are lipid-soluble and cross the plasma membrane they are large proteins that enter through channels they are carried into cells attached to red blood cells steroid hormones are made from cholesterol, so they are lipid-soluble. they pass through the phospholipid bilayer and bind receptors in the cytoplasm or nucleus, often changing gene expression. water-soluble protein hormones such as insulin cannot cross the membrane; they bind receptors on the cell surface.

a hormone travels in the blood to every part of the body, yet it affects only certain cells. why? only its target cells have receptors for that hormone the hormone is destroyed in all other tissues first only target cells are reached by the blood supply the hormone can only travel in one direction a cell can respond to a hormone only if it has the matching receptor. cells without the receptor are exposed to the hormone but do not respond.

which organ produces most of the testosterone in males? prostate gland adrenal medulla thymus testes interstitial (leydig) cells in the testes produce testosterone, under the control of lh from the anterior pituitary. the prostate makes part of the seminal fluid but does not produce testosterone.

tap the gland in the neck that makes hormones controlling metabolic rate. the thyroid gland is shaped like a butterfly in front of the trachea. its hormones t3 and t4 set how fast cells use energy. it also makes calcitonin, which lowers blood calcium.

tap the glands that release epinephrine (adrenaline) in a 'fight or flight' response. the adrenal glands sit on top of the kidneys. their inner medulla releases epinephrine and norepinephrine, which raise heart rate and blood glucose. their outer cortex makes cortisol and aldosterone.

tap the gland deep in the brain that releases melatonin when it is dark. the pineal gland is a small gland near the center of the brain. it releases melatonin in darkness, which helps regulate the sleep-wake cycle. bright screens at night can suppress melatonin.

tap the part of the brain that releases hormones controlling the pituitary gland and links the nervous and endocrine systems. the hypothalamus sits just above the pituitary gland. it releases hormones that tell the pituitary what to release, and it makes adh and oxytocin. it also controls body temperature, hunger and thirst.

according to the graph, about how long after the meal does insulin reach its highest level? 0 min 30 min 90 min 180 min the dashed blue insulin line peaks at 30 minutes (about 45 µu/ml). that is the same time glucose peaks: rising blood glucose is the signal that makes the pancreas release insulin.

based on the graph, which statement best explains why blood glucose falls between 30 and 120 minutes? insulin helps body cells take in glucose and helps the liver store it as glycogen. glucagon breaks glycogen down into glucose. the kidneys filter all of the glucose into the urine. the stomach stops absorbing glucose because insulin blocks it. insulin is released by beta cells of the pancreas when glucose rises. it lets muscle and fat cells take up glucose and tells the liver to store glucose as glycogen, so blood glucose drops back toward normal. glucagon does the opposite (raises glucose) and is released when glucose is low.

if the same meal were eaten by a person with untreated type 1 diabetes, how would the graph most likely look? glucose would rise higher and stay high, and insulin would stay near zero. glucose and insulin would both rise higher than shown. glucose would stay flat, and insulin would rise sharply. both lines would look the same as in the graph. in type 1 diabetes, the immune system has destroyed the insulin-making beta cells, so insulin stays very low. without insulin, cells can't take in glucose well, so blood glucose climbs higher and stays high for hours. in type 2 diabetes, by contrast, insulin is often present (even high), but the cells respond poorly to it (insulin resistance).

a patient with heart failure has extra fluid that stretches the walls of the atria. the atria respond by releasing atrial natriuretic peptide (anp). what effect does anp have? the kidneys reabsorb more sodium, so blood volume rises. the kidneys excrete more sodium and water. blood vessels constrict, raising blood pressure. the collecting ducts reabsorb more water, making urine more concentrated. anp is released when the atria are stretched by high blood volume. it makes the kidneys excrete more sodium (natriuresis), and water follows the sodium out, so blood volume and blood pressure fall. anp also relaxes blood vessels and works against aldosterone, adh, and the renin–angiotensin system.

a modesto patient with high blood pressure is prescribed an ace inhibitor, which blocks the enzyme that converts angiotensin i to angiotensin ii. why does this lower blood pressure? more renin is made by the kidneys, so the kidneys excrete more salt and water. more adh is released by the pituitary, so the collecting ducts reabsorb less water. less angiotensin ii forms, so vessels relax and less aldosterone is released. less angiotensinogen is made by the liver, so the heart beats more slowly. in the raas, the kidneys release renin, which converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin i; ace then converts angiotensin i to angiotensin ii. angiotensin ii raises blood pressure by constricting arterioles and by triggering aldosterone release, which makes the kidneys retain sodium and water. blocking ace means less angiotensin ii, so vessels relax and less sodium and water are kept: blood pressure drops.

tap the ball of capillaries where blood pressure pushes water and small solutes out of the blood to form filtrate. the glomerulus is a tuft of capillaries inside bowman's capsule. high pressure in the glomerulus forces water, ions, glucose and wastes like urea out of the blood. this is filtration. bowman's (glomerular) capsule is the cup around the glomerulus. its outer layer collects the filtrate; its inner layer of podocytes wraps the capillaries and is part of the filter.

tap the part of the nephron that reabsorbs most of the filtrate: about two-thirds of the water and sodium and nearly all of the glucose. the proximal convoluted tubule (pct) comes right after bowman's capsule, in the cortex. its cells have microvilli, which give a large surface area for reabsorbing water, sodium, glucose and amino acids back into the blood. the loop of henle, dct and collecting duct fine-tune what is left.

put these structures in the order that filtrate flows through them, from first to last. bowman's capsule proximal convoluted tubule loop of henle distal convoluted tubule collecting duct filtrate forms in the glomerulus and is collected by bowman's capsule. it flows through the proximal convoluted tubule, then down and back up the loop of henle in the medulla. next is the distal convoluted tubule, which empties into a collecting duct shared by many nephrons. from there urine drains to the renal pelvis.

adh (antidiuretic hormone) inserts water channels into the tube that receives fluid from many nephrons, so more water is reabsorbed. tap that tube. the collecting duct receives fluid from the distal convoluted tubules of many nephrons and carries it through the medulla toward the renal pelvis. adh from the posterior pituitary makes the collecting duct more permeable to water, so the body keeps water and makes less, more concentrated urine. when a patient is dehydrated, adh goes up and urine becomes darker and more concentrated.

a patient with uncontrolled diabetes has glucose in the urine. normally, filtered glucose is reabsorbed almost completely. in which labeled structure does that reabsorption normally happen? a c e f glucose is filtered at the glomerulus (a) and normally reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule (c). the carriers in the pct can only move so much glucose. when blood glucose is very high, the filtered glucose overwhelms them and the extra spills into the urine. e is the loop of henle and f is the collecting duct. they do not reabsorb glucose.

tap the tube that carries urine from a kidney to the urinary bladder. each kidney has one ureter, a muscular tube that carries urine down to the bladder. the urethra is the single tube that carries urine from the bladder out of the body.

most urinary tract infections start when bacteria enter through the structure labeled e. what is structure e? ureter urinary bladder renal pelvis urethra e is the urethra, the tube that carries urine from the bladder to the outside of the body. bacteria from outside the body can travel up the urethra into the bladder (d). if not treated, the infection can climb the ureters (c) to the kidneys (b).

tap the structure where fertilization of an egg by a sperm usually occurs. after ovulation, the egg is swept into the uterine (fallopian) tube by its finger-like fimbriae. fertilization usually happens in the outer, wider part of the uterine tube. the early embryo then travels to the uterus to implant. the ovary releases the egg, but fertilization does not normally happen there.

an early embryo normally implants in layer d. what is layer d, and what happens to its outer part if pregnancy does not occur? myometrium; it contracts during labor endometrium; it is shed during menstruation cervix; it opens during ovulation endometrium; it stays thick until the next ovulation d is the endometrium, the inner lining of the uterus. it thickens each cycle to prepare for implantation. if no embryo implants, progesterone falls and the outer (functional) layer of the endometrium is shed as the menstrual flow. the myometrium (c) is the smooth muscle wall that contracts during labor.

put these organs in the order urine passes through them, from where it is formed to where it leaves the body. kidney ureter urinary bladder urethra urine forms in the kidneys and flows down the ureters to the urinary bladder, where it is stored. it leaves the body through the urethra.

put these parts of the nephron in the order that filtrate flows through them. glomerular (bowman's) capsule proximal convoluted tubule nephron loop (loop of henle) distal convoluted tubule collecting duct blood is filtered at the glomerulus, and filtrate enters the glomerular capsule. filtrate flows through the proximal convoluted tubule, the nephron loop, and the distal convoluted tubule. several nephrons drain into a collecting duct, where final water reabsorption is adjusted by adh.

what is the functional unit of the kidney, where urine is formed? neuron nephron alveolus renal pelvis each kidney has about a million nephrons, each of which filters blood and processes the filtrate into urine. the glomerulus is only the filtering part of the nephron; neurons and alveoli belong to other systems.

in which part of the nephron does filtration of blood plasma take place? glomerulus nephron loop (loop of henle) collecting duct distal convoluted tubule blood pressure pushes water and small solutes out of the glomerular capillaries into the glomerular capsule. blood cells and large proteins are normally too big to be filtered. the tubules and collecting duct handle reabsorption and secretion.

most reabsorption of water, glucose, amino acids, and sodium from the filtrate occurs in which part of the nephron? collecting duct glomerulus and bowman's capsule ureter and urinary bladder proximal convoluted tubule the proximal convoluted tubule reabsorbs about two-thirds of the filtered water and sodium and normally all of the glucose and amino acids. its cells have microvilli that increase surface area for this work. the collecting duct fine-tunes water reabsorption, and the bladder only stores urine.

which of the following is normally not found in the urine of a healthy person? urea (nitrogen waste) water red blood cells sodium and potassium ions blood cells are too large to pass through a healthy glomerular filter, so red blood cells in urine (hematuria) suggest disease, injury, or infection. urea, water, and sodium ions are normal components of urine.

a routine urinalysis shows glucose in a patient's urine. which condition is this most often associated with? severe dehydration from heat uncontrolled diabetes mellitus kidney stones blocking a ureter eating a high-protein diet normally, all filtered glucose is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule. when blood glucose is very high, the filtrate contains more glucose than the transporters can reabsorb, so glucose spills into the urine (glycosuria). this is why untreated diabetes causes frequent urination and thirst.

a patient with chronic kidney disease often develops anemia. which hormone, normally made by the kidneys, is most likely deficient? erythropoietin renin insulin aldosterone the kidneys release erythropoietin (epo) when blood oxygen is low; epo stimulates red bone marrow to make red blood cells. damaged kidneys make less epo, so fewer red blood cells are made. renin is also made by the kidneys, but it regulates blood pressure, not red blood cell production.

urea, the main nitrogen-containing waste in urine, is produced from the breakdown of fatty acids glucose cholesterol amino acids when amino acids are broken down, their nitrogen-containing amino groups form toxic ammonia. the liver converts ammonia into less toxic urea, which the kidneys excrete. fats and carbohydrates contain no nitrogen, so they do not produce urea.

urinary tract infections are more common in females than in males. what is the main anatomical reason? females have only one kidney the female bladder is lined with skin the female urethra is much shorter females lack ureters the female urethra is only about 4 cm long and opens close to the anus, so bacteria can reach the bladder more easily. the male urethra is about 20 cm long, which makes it harder for bacteria to travel up it.

how do the kidneys help correct blood that has become too acidic? by excreting bicarbonate and reabsorbing h⁺ ions by excreting h⁺ ions and reabsorbing bicarbonate by releasing extra carbon dioxide gas into the urine by producing hydrochloric acid the kidneys secrete hydrogen ions into the urine and return bicarbonate (a base) to the blood. both actions raise blood ph back toward the normal range of about 7.35–7.45. the lungs, not the kidneys, adjust co₂.

drinking alcohol inhibits the release of antidiuretic hormone (adh). what is the expected effect on urine? a larger volume of more dilute urine a smaller volume of more concentrated urine glucose appears in the urine urine production stops completely adh normally tells the collecting ducts to reabsorb water. with less adh, less water is reabsorbed, so more water stays in the urine: more urine, and more dilute. this water loss is one reason alcohol contributes to dehydration.

in which structure does fertilization of an egg by a sperm normally occur? uterus (womb) ovary (follicle) vagina (birth canal) uterine (fallopian) tube after ovulation, the egg is swept into the uterine tube, where it is usually fertilized. the resulting embryo travels to the uterus over several days and implants in the uterine lining.

in a healthy person, which substances are normally reabsorbed from the kidney filtrate back into the blood? select all that apply. water glucose amino acids creatinine excess hydrogen ions (h⁺) most filtered water and essentially all filtered glucose and amino acids are reabsorbed, mainly in the proximal convoluted tubule. creatinine, a muscle waste product, is not reabsorbed and is excreted in urine. excess h⁺ ions are secreted into the filtrate to help control blood ph, not reabsorbed.

put these structures in the order sperm pass through them, from production to exit. seminiferous tubules epididymis ductus (vas) deferens ejaculatory duct urethra sperm form in the seminiferous tubules and mature in the epididymis. during ejaculation they travel through the ductus deferens and ejaculatory duct into the urethra. a vasectomy cuts the ductus deferens, so sperm can no longer reach the urethra.

which event directly triggers ovulation, the release of an egg from the ovary? a sudden drop in estrogen levels a sharp rise in prolactin levels a surge of luteinizing hormone (lh) a surge of insulin from the pancreas as a follicle matures, rising estrogen triggers a sharp lh surge from the anterior pituitary. the lh surge causes the mature follicle to rupture and release the egg, about midway through the cycle. home ovulation tests detect this lh surge.
