the graph shows that atomic radius decreases from sodium (na) to argon (ar). which explanation is best? the number of protons increases, so the nucleus pulls the electrons (in the same energy level) closer. each element adds a new energy level, so atoms get smaller. atoms lose neutrons across a period, so they shrink. metals are always larger than nonmetals because they are heavier. across a period, each element has one more proton, so the nuclear charge grows. the new electrons go into the same energy level (shell 3), so they aren't much farther out. the stronger positive pull draws that shell in, making the atom smaller. going down a group is different: each step adds a new energy level, so atoms get larger.

according to the graph, which element in period 3 has the largest atoms? argon (ar) chlorine (cl) sodium (na) silicon (si) the highest point on the graph is sodium, at 186 pm. this matches the trend: atomic radius is largest at the left of a period (and at the bottom of a group).
using the isotope symbol, how many neutrons are in one atom of carbon-14? neutrons = mass number − atomic number. carbon-14: 14 − 6 = 8 neutrons.

what do carbon-12, carbon-13 and carbon-14 have in common? the same number of protons the same number of neutrons the same mass number the same atomic mass all three have atomic number 6, so all have 6 protons. that's what makes them carbon. they differ only in neutrons (6, 7 and 8), which changes the mass number. atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons are isotopes.

carbon-14 is radioactive. a bone found at a dig site has 25% of its original carbon-14 left. based on the graph, about how old is the bone? 2,865 years 5,730 years 11,460 years 22,920 years the graph halves every 5,730 years: that is carbon-14's half-life. 100% → 50% is one half-life; 50% → 25% is a second. two half-lives = 2 × 5,730 = 11,460 years. a common slip is to think 25% means "one-quarter of a half-life." each half-life cuts what's left in half.

tap the atom that has a full outer shell and is very unreactive (a noble gas). atom d has 18 protons (argon) and 8 electrons in its outer shell, which is a full octet. noble gases (group 18) rarely react because they don't need to gain, lose or share electrons.

tap the atom most likely to lose two electrons and form a 2+ ion. atom b has 12 protons (magnesium) with 2 electrons in its outer shell. losing those 2 electrons leaves a full shell underneath, so magnesium forms mg²⁺. group 2 metals form 2+ ions.

tap the atom that most easily gains one electron to form a 1− ion. atom c has 17 protons (chlorine) and 7 outer electrons. gaining just 1 more completes its octet, so it forms cl⁻. atoms with 1 or 2 outer electrons (a, b) lose them; atoms one short of a full shell (c) gain. argon (d) is already full.

tap the box that shows the reactants. reactants are the substances you start with. they are on the left side of the arrow in an equation, which is the "before" box here. the "after" box shows the product, ammonia (nh₃), which forms when nitrogen (n₂) and hydrogen (h₂) react.

use the particle diagram to balance the equation: __n₂ + __h₂ → __nh₃ using the lowest whole numbers, what coefficient goes in front of h₂? count the molecules. the before box has 2 n₂ and 6 h₂, and the after box has 4 nh₃. that ratio is 2 : 6 : 4. divide each number by 2 to get the lowest whole numbers: 1 : 3 : 2. the balanced equation is n₂ + 3h₂ → 2nh₃. check: n is 2 on the left and 2 × 1 = 2 on the right. h is 3 × 2 = 6 on the left and 2 × 3 = 6 on the right.

which statements are supported by the particle diagram? select all that apply. the number of nitrogen atoms is the same before and after the reaction the number of hydrogen atoms is the same before and after the reaction the number of molecules is the same before and after the reaction this is a synthesis (combination) reaction some mass is destroyed during the reaction atoms before: n = 2 × 2 = 4 and h = 6 × 2 = 12. atoms after: n = 4 × 1 = 4 and h = 4 × 3 = 12. the atoms are the same, so mass is conserved. the number of molecules changes from 8 (2 n₂ + 6 h₂) to 4 (nh₃). atoms are conserved, but molecules do not have to be. two simpler substances join to make one product (a + b → ab), so this is a synthesis reaction.

what type of bond holds the nitrogen and hydrogen atoms together within the molecule labeled c? ionic bond, because electrons are transferred covalent bond, because electrons are shared hydrogen bond, because the molecule contains hydrogen metallic bond, because nitrogen is a metal c is ammonia (nh₃). nitrogen and hydrogen are both nonmetals, and nonmetals bond to each other by sharing electrons. that is a covalent bond (here, a polar covalent bond). ionic bonds form between a metal and a nonmetal, such as na⁺ and cl⁻. a hydrogen bond is a weaker attraction between molecules, not the bond that holds n and h together inside one molecule. nitrogen is a nonmetal.

which type of reaction does the particle diagram show? decomposition single replacement synthesis combustion two reactants (n₂ and h₂) combine to form one product (nh₃). that pattern, a + b → ab, is a synthesis (combination) reaction. decomposition is the reverse (ab → a + b). single replacement swaps one element for another. combustion needs o₂ and usually makes co₂ and h₂o.

which compound is held together by ionic bonds? co₂ h₂o nacl ch₄ ionic bonds form between a metal and a nonmetal when electrons are transferred: na⁺ and cl⁻. co₂, h₂o and ch₄ contain only nonmetals, so they are covalent.

in a covalent bond, atoms transfer electrons from one atom to another share protons form ions with opposite charges share pairs of electrons covalent bonds form when two atoms (usually nonmetals) share one or more pairs of electrons. transferring electrons makes ions and ionic bonds.

the o–h bonds in a water molecule are polar covalent bonds. why? oxygen is more electronegative, so the shared electrons are pulled closer to oxygen. hydrogen is more electronegative, so the electrons are pulled toward hydrogen. oxygen completely transfers its electrons to hydrogen. oxygen and hydrogen share the electrons exactly equally. oxygen pulls on shared electrons more strongly than hydrogen does. this unequal sharing gives oxygen a partial negative charge (δ−) and each hydrogen a partial positive charge (δ+). equal sharing would be nonpolar; full transfer would be ionic.

hydrogen bonds between water molecules are best described as covalent bonds between two h atoms in the same molecule attractions between δ+ h on one molecule and δ− o on another ionic bonds between h⁺ ions and oh⁻ ions in the water shared electron pairs between o atoms of neighboring molecules a hydrogen bond is an attraction between molecules, not a true bond within a molecule. it forms when h bonded to o, n or f is attracted to a lone pair on an o, n or f of a neighboring molecule. hydrogen bonds explain water's high boiling point and surface tension.

in the dna double helix, what holds the two strands together? ionic bonds between sugars peptide bonds between amino acids hydrogen bonds between paired bases covalent bonds between phosphate groups on opposite strands a–t and g–c base pairs are held together by hydrogen bonds (2 for a–t, 3 for g–c). these relatively weak attractions let the strands unzip for replication and transcription. peptide bonds are found in proteins.

what type of reaction is 2h₂ + o₂ → 2h₂o? decomposition (breaking apart) single replacement (swap) double replacement synthesis (combination) two reactants combine into one product: a + b → ab is synthesis. (this reaction is also a combustion of hydrogen.)
what type of reaction is caco₃ → cao + co₂? decomposition synthesis single replacement combustion one reactant breaks into two simpler products: ab → a + b is decomposition.

what type of reaction is zn + 2hcl → zncl₂ + h₂? double replacement single replacement decomposition synthesis one element (zn) replaces another (h) in a compound: a + bc → ac + b. double replacement swaps partners between two compounds.

what type of reaction is agno₃ + nacl → agcl + nano₃? single replacement synthesis double replacement combustion two compounds swap partners: ab + cd → ad + cb. ag⁺ pairs with cl⁻ and na⁺ pairs with no₃⁻; the solid agcl precipitates.

what are the products of the complete combustion of propane (c₃h₈), the fuel in many backyard grills? carbon and hydrogen gas carbon monoxide and oxygen methane and water carbon dioxide and water complete combustion of a hydrocarbon with oxygen always produces co₂ and h₂o (and releases energy). carbon monoxide forms only when oxygen is limited (incomplete combustion), which is why grills shouldn't be used indoors.
balance the equation by finding the missing coefficient: ___ h₂ + n₂ → 2nh₃ right side: 2nh₃ has 2 × 3 = 6 h atoms. each h₂ has 2 h atoms, so 6 ÷ 2 = 3 h₂. check n: 2 on each side. ✓

balance the combustion of propane by finding the missing coefficient: c₃h₈ + ___ o₂ → 3co₂ + 4h₂o count o on the right: 3co₂ has 6 o and 4h₂o has 4 o, for 10 o total. 10 ÷ 2 = 5 o₂. check: c 3 = 3, h 8 = 8, o 10 = 10. ✓

which set of coefficients balances this equation? ___ al + ___ o₂ → ___ al₂o₃ 4, 3, 2 2, 3, 1 1, 3, 2 4, 6, 2 with 4, 3, 2: al 4 = 2 × 2 = 4 ✓; o 3 × 2 = 6 = 2 × 3 = 6 ✓. with 2, 3, 1: o is 6 on the left but only 3 on the right. with 4, 6, 2: o is 12 vs 6.

why must chemical equations be balanced? molecules are not created or destroyed in a chemical reaction. atoms are not created or destroyed in a chemical reaction. the products must always have more mass than the reactants. every reaction must have the same number of reactants and products. the law of conservation of mass: the same atoms are rearranged, so each element must have the same count on both sides. molecules can change in number (2h₂ + o₂ → 2h₂o turns 3 molecules into 2).

how many oxygen atoms are shown in 2al(no₃)₃? 6 9 11 18 one no₃ has 3 o; the subscript 3 outside the parentheses gives 3 × 3 = 9 o per formula unit. the coefficient 2 doubles everything: 2 × 9 = 18 o atoms. 9 forgets the coefficient; 6 or 11 miscount the parentheses.

an instant cold pack gets cold when a salt inside dissolves in water. what does this tell you about the dissolving process? it is exothermic; it releases heat to the surroundings. it is endothermic; it releases cold into the surroundings. it is endothermic; it absorbs heat from the surroundings. it is exothermic; it absorbs heat from the surroundings. the pack feels cold because heat flows from your skin into the pack to drive the process. absorbing heat = endothermic. "releasing cold" isn't a real thing—cold is just less heat.

why does raising the temperature usually make a reaction go faster? particles grow larger when heated, so they are easier to hit. heat lowers the activation energy barrier of the reaction itself. heat adds more reactant particles to the mixture as it warms. particles move faster, so they collide more often and with more energy. higher temperature means higher average kinetic energy, so more collisions have enough energy to react. a catalyst lowers activation energy; heat does not change it.

which of these compounds are covalent (molecular)? select all that apply. co₂ nacl h₂o kbr nh₃ co₂, h₂o and nh₃ are made only of nonmetals that share electrons. nacl and kbr each pair a metal with a nonmetal, so they are ionic.

which changes would usually increase the rate of a chemical reaction? select all that apply. raising the temperature increasing the concentration of a reactant grinding a solid reactant into a fine powder adding a catalyst cooling the reaction mixture more collisions (higher concentration, more surface area) and more energetic collisions (higher temperature) speed up reactions. a catalyst lowers the activation energy. cooling slows reactions—this is why refrigeration slows food spoilage.

put these attractions in order from strongest to weakest. covalent o–h bond inside a water molecule hydrogen bond between two water molecules london dispersion attraction between two helium atoms covalent bonds hold atoms together within a molecule and are much stronger than attractions between molecules. hydrogen bonds are strong intermolecular attractions; london dispersion forces between tiny nonpolar atoms like helium are the weakest.

a student timed how long a fizzing antacid tablet took to dissolve in water at different temperatures. which conclusion do the data support? the reaction is faster at higher temperatures. the reaction is slower at higher temperatures. temperature has no effect on the reaction. the tablet will dissolve instantly at 70 °c. a shorter time means a faster reaction. the time drops from 92 s to 15 s as the water warms up. at higher temperature, particles move faster and collide more often and with more energy, so the reaction speeds up. the data stop at 55 °c. predicting "instantly" at 70 °c goes beyond the data.

in the energy diagram, what does the arrow labeled a represent? the activation energy the energy released by the reaction the energy of the products the amount of catalyst used a is the height of the "hill" from the reactants up to the peak. that is the activation energy, the energy needed to get the reaction started. b shows the overall energy change between reactants and products. a catalyst (such as an enzyme) would lower the hill (a) but not change b.

is the reaction in the diagram endothermic or exothermic, and how can you tell? exothermic, because the products have less energy than the reactants, so energy is released. endothermic, because there is an energy hill to climb. exothermic, because the activation energy is large. endothermic, because the products have less energy than the reactants. compare the starting and ending levels. here the products sit lower than the reactants, so the extra energy was given off: exothermic (δh negative). every reaction has an activation-energy hill, so the hill alone doesn't tell you which type it is. in an endothermic reaction (like a cold pack), the products end higher than the reactants because energy was absorbed.

the diagram shows sodium reacting with chlorine. what happens to form the bond? sodium transfers one electron to chlorine, making oppositely charged ions that attract. sodium and chlorine share one pair of electrons equally. chlorine gives seven electrons to sodium. protons move from sodium's nucleus to chlorine's nucleus. sodium has 1 electron in its outer shell; chlorine has 7. sodium loses its outer electron (orange) and chlorine gains it. now na⁺ (2, 8) and cl⁻ (2, 8, 8) each have a full outer shell. their opposite charges attract: that attraction is an ionic bond. sharing electron pairs would be a covalent bond, which forms between nonmetals. protons never move in a chemical reaction.

after the electron moves, why does the sodium ion have a positive charge? it has 11 protons but only 10 electrons. it gained a proton from chlorine. it has more electrons than protons. its nucleus split in two. a neutral sodium atom has 11 protons (+) and 11 electrons (−). after losing one electron it has 11 protons and 10 electrons, so it has one extra positive charge: na⁺. chloride is the reverse: 17 protons and 18 electrons, so it is cl⁻.

magnesium has 2 outer electrons, and chlorine needs 1 more electron to fill its outer shell. using the same idea as the diagram, write the formula of the ionic compound magnesium chloride. magnesium loses its 2 outer electrons to become mg²⁺. each chlorine can take only 1 electron, becoming cl⁻. it takes two cl⁻ ions to balance one mg²⁺: (+2) + 2(−1) = 0. the formula is mgcl₂.

in the lewis structure of water, tap a pair of electrons that is shared between two atoms (a covalent bond). a covalent bond is a pair of electrons shared between two atoms. in water, each green pair is shared between o and one h. the dot pairs above and below the o belong only to oxygen. they are lone (unshared) pairs.

how many lone (unshared) pairs of electrons does the oxygen atom in water have? oxygen has 6 valence electrons. it uses 2 of them in its two bonds with h (one in each shared pair). the other 4 electrons form 2 lone pairs, shown above and below the o. those lone pairs push the h atoms together, giving water its bent shape.

tap the molecule that is linear (all atoms in a straight line). co₂ has two double bonds and no lone pairs on carbon, so the two o atoms sit on opposite sides: a straight line (180°). water is bent, methane is tetrahedral, and ammonia is a pyramid.

tap the molecule shaped like a pyramid because one lone pair on the central atom pushes three bonded atoms down. ammonia (nh₃) has three n–h bonds and one lone pair on nitrogen. the lone pair takes up space at the top, pushing the three h atoms down into a trigonal pyramid. methane has four bonds and no lone pairs (tetrahedral); water has two bonds and two lone pairs (bent).

molecule b (co₂) has two polar c=o bonds, but the molecule as a whole is nonpolar. what explains this? its linear shape is symmetric, so the two bond polarities cancel out. carbon and oxygen have the same electronegativity. it has lone pairs on the central carbon. it is an ionic compound, not a molecule. co₂ (b) is linear: its two c=o dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel, like two equal tug-of-war teams. (methane, c, is nonpolar too: its c–h bonds are only very slightly polar and are arranged symmetrically.) water (a) and ammonia (d) have lone pairs that make them lopsided, so their bond dipoles don't cancel and the molecules are polar. that's why water dissolves salt and sugar so well.

in the h–cl molecule shown, why does the chlorine end carry a partial negative charge (δ−)? chlorine is more electronegative, so it pulls the shared electrons closer. chlorine has given its electrons to hydrogen. hydrogen has more protons than chlorine. the electrons are shared exactly equally. electronegativity is an atom's pull on shared electrons. chlorine (3.0) pulls harder than hydrogen (2.1). the shared pair spends more time near cl, making that end slightly negative (δ−) and the h end slightly positive (δ+). this is a polar covalent bond. if the electrons were transferred completely, it would be ionic; if shared exactly equally (as in cl–cl), it would be nonpolar.

which balanced equation matches the particle diagram? 2h₂ + o₂ → 2h₂o h₂ + o₂ → h₂o 2h₂ + 2o₂ → 2h₂o h₂ + o → h₂o count molecules: before has two h₂ and one o₂. after has two h₂o. check atoms: 4 h and 2 o on each side. mass is conserved, so the equation is balanced: 2h₂ + o₂ → 2h₂o.

the diagram shows methane burning: ch₄ + __o₂ → co₂ + 2h₂o. count the oxygen atoms in the "after" box. how many o atoms are there in total? co₂ has 2 o atoms, and each of the two h₂o molecules has 1 o atom: 2 + 1 + 1 = 4. that's why the equation needs 2o₂ on the left (2 × 2 = 4 o atoms). the balanced equation is ch₄ + 2o₂ → co₂ + 2h₂o. atoms are rearranged, never created or destroyed.

tap the panel that shows a decomposition reaction. in decomposition, one compound breaks apart into two or more simpler substances: ab → a + b. panel b shows the joined circle-square splitting into a separate circle and square. example: 2h₂o → 2h₂ + o₂ (electrolysis).

zn + 2hcl → zncl₂ + h₂. tap the panel that shows this type of reaction. zinc (one element) replaces hydrogen in hcl. one element swaps into a compound and kicks another element out: a + bc → ac + b. that is a single-replacement reaction, panel c. in double replacement (panel d), two compounds swap partners: ab + cd → ad + cb.

when solutions of silver nitrate and sodium chloride are mixed, a white solid forms: agno₃ + nacl → agcl + nano₃. which panel shows this type of reaction? a b c d two compounds trade partners: ag pairs up with cl, and na pairs up with no₃. that is double replacement, ab + cd → ad + cb (panel d). the solid that forms (agcl) is called a precipitate. many double-replacement reactions in water make a precipitate, a gas or water.

tap the box that shows a pure compound. a compound is made of two or more different elements chemically bonded in a fixed ratio, and a pure compound has only one kind of molecule. the bottom middle box has identical molecules, each made of one red atom bonded to two white atoms. the bottom left box is an element (only one kind of atom). the bottom right box is a mixture (two different kinds of particles). the top boxes all show single atoms of one element.

which description best classifies the contents of box f? a pure compound of two elements a pure element made of two isotopes a mixture of two compounds a mixture of an element and a compound box f has two kinds of particles that are not bonded to each other, so it is a mixture. one kind is a molecule of two identical blue atoms, which is an element. the other is a molecule of red and white atoms bonded together, which is a compound. so box f is a mixture of an element and a compound. a pure substance would have only one kind of particle.

black coffee has a ph of 5. tap the marker for the substance whose hydrogen ion (h⁺) concentration is about 1,000 times greater than that of black coffee. the ph scale is logarithmic: each step of 1 ph unit is a 10-fold change in h⁺ concentration. 1,000 = 10 × 10 × 10, which is 3 ph units. a higher h⁺ concentration means more acidic, so the ph is lower: 5 − 3 = 2. the marker at ph 2 is lemon juice. markers above ph 5, such as baking soda, are less acidic than coffee, not more.

normal human blood has the ph shown on the scale. how is blood best described? slightly acidic strongly basic exactly neutral slightly basic normal blood ph is about 7.35 to 7.45, which is just above 7. a ph above 7 is basic, so blood is slightly basic (alkaline). a blood ph below 7.35 is called acidosis, and a ph above 7.45 is called alkalosis. both can be life-threatening.

a patient with heartburn takes milk of magnesia, an antacid with a ph of about 10.5 (close to the ammonia solution on this scale). based on the scale, what does it do in the stomach? it is a base that neutralizes some stomach acid, raising the ph it is an acid that lowers the ph of the stomach contents it is neutral, so it dilutes the stomach acid without reacting it is a base that lowers the ph of the stomach contents milk of magnesia has a ph of about 10.5, so it is a base. when a base reacts with an acid (neutralization), it uses up h⁺ ions. fewer h⁺ ions means the ph goes up, toward neutral. a base cannot lower the ph. lowering the ph would make the stomach more acidic.

which of the following is a physical change? ice melting into water an iron gate rusting wood burning in a fireplace milk souring in the refrigerator melting changes only the state; it is still h₂o. rusting, burning and souring make new substances, so they are chemical changes.

which observation is the best evidence that a chemical change has occurred? bubbles form in a pot when water is heated until it boils. gas bubbles form when baking soda is mixed with vinegar. sugar disappears when stirred into tea. almonds are chopped and crushed into small pieces. baking soda and vinegar react to make a new substance, carbon dioxide gas. boiling bubbles are just water vapor (a phase change), dissolving is physical, and chopping only changes size.

dry ice (solid co₂) turns directly into a gas without melting. what is this phase change called? deposition evaporation sublimation condensation solid → gas directly is sublimation. deposition is gas → solid, evaporation is liquid → gas, and condensation is gas → liquid.

on a hot fresno afternoon, water droplets form on the outside of a glass of iced tea. what causes this? tea seeps through tiny holes in the glass. ice in the glass melts and seeps out through the glass wall. water vapor in the air sublimes directly onto the cold glass. water vapor in the air cools and condenses into liquid. air touching the cold glass cools, and the water vapor in it changes from gas to liquid: condensation. glass is not porous, and sublimation is solid → gas.

which state of matter has a definite volume but takes the shape of its container? liquid solid gas plasma liquid particles are close together (fixed volume) but can slide past one another (no fixed shape). solids keep both shape and volume; gases fill any container, so they have neither.

normal saline used in iv bags is 0.9% sodium chloride dissolved in water. what is the solvent? sodium chloride water chloride ions the iv bag the solvent is the substance that does the dissolving and is present in the larger amount—water. sodium chloride (and its na⁺ and cl⁻ ions) is the solute.

a pharmacy technician adds water to a concentrated solution to dilute it. which statement is correct? the amount of solute decreases, and the concentration stays the same. the amount of solute increases, and the concentration increases. the amount of solute stays the same, and the concentration decreases. the amount of solute and the concentration both stay the same. adding solvent does not add or remove any solute. the same solute is spread through more volume, so the concentration goes down.

a nurse dilutes 10 ml of a 6% solution by adding water until the total volume is 60 ml. what is the new concentration? use c₁v₁ = c₂v₂: (6%)(10 ml) = c₂(60 ml). c₂ = 60 ÷ 60 = 1%. check: the volume became 6 times larger, so the concentration became 6 times smaller.

a solution has a ph of 3. which description is correct? it is basic, with a lower h⁺ concentration than pure water. it is neutral, like pure water. it is basic, with a higher oh⁻ concentration than pure water. it is acidic, with a higher h⁺ concentration than pure water. ph below 7 = acidic; ph 7 = neutral; ph above 7 = basic. lower ph means more h⁺ ions.

solution a has a ph of 4. solution b has a ph of 6. how does the h⁺ concentration of a compare with b? a has 100 times more h⁺ than b. a has 2 times more h⁺ than b. a has 10 times more h⁺ than b. a has 100 times less h⁺ than b. the ph scale is logarithmic: each 1-unit drop in ph means 10 times more h⁺. from ph 6 to ph 4 is 2 units: 10 × 10 = 100 times more h⁺ in a. "2 times" treats the scale as if it were ordinary subtraction.
what is the ph of pure water at 25 °c? pure water has equal amounts of h⁺ and oh⁻, so it is neutral. neutral = ph 7 at 25 °c.

when hydrochloric acid reacts with sodium hydroxide, hcl + naoh → nacl + h₂o, the products are best described as an acid and a base a salt and water a metal and a gas two new acids acid + base → salt + water is a neutralization reaction. here the salt is nacl and the h⁺ from the acid combines with oh⁻ from the base to make h₂o.

which property is characteristic of bases? they taste sour and turn blue litmus paper red. they have a ph below 7. they feel slippery and turn red litmus paper blue. they release h⁺ ions in water. bases feel slippery (soap), taste bitter, turn red litmus blue, and have ph above 7. sour taste, turning blue litmus red, ph below 7 and releasing h⁺ all describe acids.

why does an antacid tablet containing calcium carbonate relieve heartburn? it is an acid that combines with stomach acid to digest food faster. it coats the stomach with a layer of fat. it kills the bacteria in the stomach that produce extra acid. it is a base that neutralizes excess stomach acid. stomach acid is mostly hcl. calcium carbonate is basic and reacts with it, raising the ph. neutralizing the acid reduces the burning feeling in the esophagus.

normal human blood has a ph of about 7.35–7.45. blood is therefore slightly basic strongly acidic exactly neutral strongly basic a ph just above 7 is slightly basic (alkaline). buffers in the blood keep ph in this narrow range; values outside it cause acidosis or alkalosis.

a warm can of soda goes flat faster than a cold one after it is opened. which explanation is best? gases such as co₂ are more soluble in liquids at higher temperatures. gases such as co₂ are less soluble in liquids at higher temperatures. warm soda contains more sugar, which pushes out the gas. cold temperatures turn co₂ into a liquid inside the can. unlike most solids, gases dissolve less as the temperature rises. so the warm soda can't hold as much dissolved co₂, and it bubbles out faster.

which of these are chemical properties? select all that apply. flammability reactivity with acid ability to rust boiling point density a chemical property can only be observed when a substance changes into a new substance (burning, reacting, rusting). boiling point and density are physical properties: you can measure them without changing the substance's identity.

which of these are mixtures rather than pure substances? select all that apply. salt water air distilled water trail mix sodium chloride mixtures contain two or more substances that are not chemically bonded and can vary in proportion: salt water, air and trail mix. distilled water (h₂o) and sodium chloride (nacl) are each a single compound—pure substances.

put these solutions in order from highest h⁺ concentration to lowest. ph 2 ph 5 ph 7 ph 9 ph 12 lower ph means more h⁺ ions. so the most acidic solution (ph 2) has the highest h⁺, and the most basic (ph 12) has the lowest.

while ice is melting at 0 °c, its temperature stays constant even though heat is still being added. where is that energy going? into making the water molecules move faster into breaking the covalent o–h bonds inside each individual water molecule into breaking the attractions that hold the water molecules in the solid out of the ice and into the surroundings during a phase change, added energy overcomes intermolecular attractions instead of raising kinetic energy (temperature). the covalent o–h bonds inside each molecule stay intact—melted ice is still h₂o.

use the solubility graph. at 0 °c, which statement is correct? more sodium chloride than potassium nitrate dissolves in 100 g of water. more potassium nitrate than sodium chloride dissolves in 100 g of water. equal amounts of the two salts dissolve. neither salt dissolves at 0 °c. at 0 °c, read up from the left edge of the graph: sodium chloride is about 36 g and potassium nitrate is about 13 g. so more sodium chloride dissolves at 0 °c. the lines cross between 20 °c and 40 °c. above that, potassium nitrate is far more soluble.

use the solubility graph. which statement best describes how temperature affects the two salts? heating greatly raises potassium nitrate's solubility but barely changes sodium chloride's. heating lowers the solubility of both salts. heating raises both salts' solubility by about the same amount at every temperature. sodium chloride is more soluble than potassium nitrate at every temperature. potassium nitrate climbs from 13 g to 169 g between 0 °c and 80 °c, a huge increase. sodium chloride stays nearly flat, about 36 to 38 g. for most solid solutes, solubility rises with temperature, but by very different amounts.

ice is heated at a steady rate. what is happening during segment b, where the temperature stays at 0 °c? the ice is melting; the heat is used to change its state, not raise its temperature. the water is boiling, so the heat is turning liquid water into steam. the heat source was turned off, so no new energy is entering the sample. the ice is losing heat to the room faster than the heat source can add it. flat parts of a heating curve are phase changes. at 0 °c, ice melts into liquid water. while it melts, the energy goes into breaking the attractions between water molecules, so the temperature doesn't rise. segment d, the flat part at 100 °c, is boiling. segments a and c are where the temperature rises.

use the table. which substances are acidic? select all that apply. lemon juice stomach acid blood black coffee bleach a ph below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral, and above 7 is basic (alkaline). lemon juice (2), stomach acid (1.5) and black coffee (5) are all below 7. blood (7.4) is slightly basic, and bleach (12.5) is strongly basic.

tap the point on the scale that is neutral. a ph of 7 is neutral. pure water has a ph of 7. below 7 is acidic and above 7 is basic. blood is slightly basic, at about 7.35 to 7.45, and milk is slightly acidic, at about 6.3 to 6.6.

tap the substance on the scale that is the most acidic. the lower the ph, the more acidic the solution. battery acid (sulfuric acid) and hydrochloric acid are at about ph 0, the lowest on this scale. stomach acid is hydrochloric acid at about ph 1.5–3.5. each step down on the ph scale is 10 times more acidic.

the blood's main buffer system is co₂ + h₂o ⇌ h₂co₃ ⇌ h⁺ + hco₃⁻. a patient in diabetic ketoacidosis has excess acid in the blood and breathes very deeply and rapidly. how does this breathing help? it adds co₂ to the blood, and the co₂ then neutralizes the extra h⁺ ions. it blows off co₂, which shifts the reaction left and uses up h⁺. it makes the kidneys release more h⁺ into the blood. it raises the amount of oxygen bound to bicarbonate ions in plasma. ketoacids add h⁺, causing metabolic acidosis; bicarbonate (hco₃⁻) binds some of this h⁺ to form carbonic acid. exhaling more co₂ pulls the equilibrium toward co₂ + h₂o, which uses up h⁺ and raises ph. this is respiratory compensation (kussmaul breathing). the kidneys help more slowly by excreting h⁺ and saving bicarbonate.
as acid was added to the solution without a buffer, the solution became: more acidic more basic neutral unchanged the ph fell from 7.4 to 2.7. a lower ph means more acidic (more hydrogen ions).

by how much did the ph of the buffered solution change from 0 to 20 drops? type your answer as a decimal. buffered solution: 7.4 at 0 drops and 6.9 at 20 drops. 7.4 − 6.9 = 0.5 ph units. without a buffer, the ph dropped 4.7 units from the same amount of acid.

which statement best explains the results? the buffer reacted with the added acid, so the ph changed very little. the buffer diluted the acid with extra water, so it became much weaker. the buffered solution received fewer drops of acid than the water did. the ph meter stopped working partway through the second test. a buffer contains a substance that can react with added acid (h⁺) and another that can react with added base. by using up most of the added h⁺, the buffer kept the ph from falling much. both solutions got the same number of drops, which is what makes the comparison fair.

a patient's blood buffers are overwhelmed and the blood ph falls to 7.1. based on the model, this patient's blood is: too acidic (acidosis) too basic (alkalosis) at a normal ph neutral normal blood ph is about 7.35 to 7.45. a ph of 7.1 is below the normal range, so the blood is too acidic. this is called acidosis . even though 7.1 is above 7 (neutral water), for blood it is dangerously acidic.

why did the core in distilled water gain mass? salt moved into the potato. water moved into the potato cells by osmosis. the potato cells divided and grew during the 2 hours. sugar moved out of the potato. distilled water is hypotonic compared with the potato's cells, so water moves into the cells by osmosis and the core gains mass.
calculate the percent change in mass for the core in the 2.0% solution. (include a negative sign if it lost mass.) change = 4.60 − 5.00 = −0.40 g. percent change = −0.40 ÷ 5.00 × 100 = −8%.

between which two solutions is the potato cells' inside most likely isotonic (no net water movement)? 0% and 0.5% 0.5% and 1.0% 2.0% and 4.0% above 4.0% mass increased at 0.5% (+4%) and decreased at 1.0% (−1%), so the point of no change lies between them, close to 1.0%.

which change would most improve the reliability of these results? test several cores per solution, from several potatoes use a different salt for each solution leave the 4.0% core in for 4 hours instead of 2 weigh the cores only at the end of the 2 hours repeated trials (several cores per solution, from more than one potato) show whether the pattern is consistent and reduce the effect of one unusual core.

a student tests how fertilizer affects bean plant growth. in the drawing of the pots, tap the control group. the control group does not receive the treatment being tested. it is the baseline the other groups are compared to. here the treatment is fertilizer, so the control is the pot that got 0 g of fertilizer. the pots that got 2, 4 and 6 g are experimental groups.

what is the independent variable in this experiment? the average plant height after 21 days the amount of water each pot receives the amount of fertilizer added to each pot the type of lamp used the independent variable is the factor the scientist deliberately changes. here, that is the amount of fertilizer (0, 2, 4 or 6 g). plant height is the dependent variable, because it is measured to see the effect. water and the lamp are kept the same for every group, so they are controlled variables.

which of the following are controlled variables (kept the same for every group) in this experiment? select all that apply. amount of water per day type of soil amount of fertilizer light source plant height after 21 days the box under the pots says that all groups had the same bean variety, soil, water (100 ml/day) and lamp. those are controlled variables. keeping them the same means any difference in height can be blamed on the fertilizer. fertilizer is the independent variable (it is changed on purpose), and plant height is the dependent variable (it is measured).

which conclusion is best supported by the results in the graph? height increased with fertilizer up to 4 g, but 6 g did not give taller plants the more fertilizer is added, the taller the plants always grow fertilizer had no effect, because all of the plants grew 6 g is the best amount of fertilizer, because it is the largest amount tested the average heights were 12 cm (0 g), 18 cm (2 g), 24 cm (4 g) and 22 cm (6 g). height rose from 0 g to 4 g and then dropped slightly at 6 g. so "more is always better" and "6 g is best" do not fit the data. the fertilized groups grew 6 to 12 cm taller than the control, so fertilizer clearly had an effect. a good conclusion matches all the data points, not just the trend in some of them.

tap the graph axis that shows the dependent variable. the dependent variable is what is measured. in this experiment that is the average plant height (cm). by convention, the dependent variable goes on the y-axis (vertical) and the independent variable (fertilizer) goes on the x-axis. so the answer is the y-axis, labeled "avg. height (cm)."

in an experiment, the independent variable is the variable that is measured as the result is kept the same in every group cannot be measured the researcher deliberately changes the independent variable is the "cause" the researcher changes on purpose. the dependent variable is measured; controlled variables are kept the same.

a student gives tomato plants 0, 5, 10 or 15 g of fertilizer and measures each plant's height after 4 weeks. what is the dependent variable? plant height amount of fertilizer number of weeks type of plant the dependent variable is what is measured to see the effect: plant height. the amount of fertilizer is the independent variable; time and plant type are kept constant.

a researcher tests whether the dose of caffeine affects resting heart rate in volunteers. which should be kept the same for all volunteers as a controlled variable? the dose of caffeine each volunteer drinks the time of day the heart rate is measured each volunteer's resting heart rate whether the heart rate increases controlled variables are other factors that could affect heart rate, so they are kept constant—such as time of day, room temperature and activity before measuring. caffeine dose is the independent variable and heart rate is the dependent variable.

in a trial of a new sleep medication, one group of participants receives a sugar pill that looks identical to the real pill. what is this group called? the experimental group the dependent group the control group the independent group the control group gets a placebo (no active drug) and provides a baseline for comparison. the experimental group receives the real medication.

which of the following is a testable hypothesis? studying is the most rewarding part of any college experience. getting enough sleep is important for every student in the world. night-shift nurses are the most caring and dedicated nurses in a hospital. students who sleep 8+ hours score higher than those who sleep under 6. a testable hypothesis predicts a measurable relationship between variables (hours of sleep and exam score). the other statements are opinions or too vague to measure.

which best describes a scientific theory? a well-tested explanation supported by a large body of evidence an educated guess about a result that has not yet been tested an explanation that is promoted to a law once it has been proven the result of a single experiment in science, a theory (such as cell theory or germ theory) explains many observations and has survived repeated testing. a hypothesis is the testable prediction; theories do not "graduate" into laws.

which statement best describes the difference between a scientific law and a scientific theory? a theory becomes a law once enough evidence is collected. a law describes what happens; a theory explains why. a law is a guess, while a theory has been proven true. theories can never be revised, but laws often change. example: the gas laws describe how pressure and volume relate; kinetic molecular theory explains why. laws and theories are different kinds of knowledge, and both can be revised if new evidence requires it.

in a fresno study, ice-cream sales and sunburn cases both rise during the summer months. which conclusion is valid? eating ice cream causes people to get sunburned. getting sunburned causes people to buy ice cream. they are correlated, possibly because of hot weather. there is no relationship of any kind between the two. the data show a correlation (they rise together), but correlation does not prove causation. a third factor—hot, sunny weather—likely drives both.

a student tests a new study method on 3 classmates. which change would most improve the reliability of the results? testing the method only on the student's best friend changing several variables at once reporting only the best result testing the method on many more students larger sample sizes and repeated trials reduce the effect of chance and individual differences. picking certain participants or reporting only the best result introduces bias.

students rubbed bacteria-covered hands, washed with different treatments, and then touched agar plates. the number of bacterial colonies that grew is shown. treatment colonies no washing 120 soap and water 30 sanitizer a 15 sanitizer b 60 which conclusion is supported by the data? in this test, sanitizer a reduced colonies the most. sanitizer b killed all of the bacteria. soap and water worked better than both sanitizers. using sanitizer a will prevent all infections. sanitizer a had the fewest colonies (15), so it reduced bacteria the most in this test. sanitizer b still left 60 colonies, and soap (30) did better than b but not a. the data are about colony counts, not infections, so claims about preventing all infections go beyond the data.

a patient received one iv dose of a drug. the blood level of the drug was then measured every 2 hours. time after dose (h) drug level (mcg/ml) 0 80 2 40 4 20 6 10 if this pattern continues, what drug level should be expected at 8 hours? 10 mcg/ml 0 mcg/ml 2.5 mcg/ml 5 mcg/ml look for the pattern: every 2 hours the level is cut in half (80 → 40 → 20 → 10). continue it 2 more hours: half of 10 is 5 mcg/ml.

a nurse notices that patient falls seem to happen more often on the night shift and wonders why. which step of the scientific method is this? drawing a conclusion from the results analyzing the data that were collected making an observation and asking a question testing a hypothesis with an experiment scientific investigations begin with an observation that leads to a question. no data have been collected or analyzed yet.

put the steps of the scientific method in order from first to last. make an observation and ask a question form a hypothesis design and carry out an experiment analyze the data draw a conclusion and share the results an observation leads to a question, and a hypothesis is a testable prediction about it. the experiment produces data, which are analyzed before a conclusion is drawn and shared.

in a drug study, neither the participants nor the researchers who interact with them know who is receiving the real drug. this design is called single-blind uncontrolled observational double-blind double-blind means both participants and researchers are unaware of group assignments. this reduces bias from expectations on both sides. in a single-blind study, only the participants are unaware.

to test whether music improves memory, group a studies with music in a quiet library in the morning, and group b studies without music in a noisy cafeteria in the evening. what is the biggest problem with this design? several variables differ besides music. there is no dependent variable to measure. the two groups are too similar to each other. music cannot serve as an independent variable. music, location, noise level and time of day all differ between the groups. any difference in memory could be caused by any of these, so the experiment can't show that music was the cause. a fair test changes only the independent variable.

a student tests how water temperature affects the time it takes a sugar cube to dissolve. which should be controlled variables? select all that apply. the volume of water the size of the sugar cube how fast the water is stirred the water temperature the time to dissolve controlled variables are factors that could affect dissolving time and must be kept the same: water volume, cube size and stirring. water temperature is the independent variable; time to dissolve is the dependent variable.

the table shows study time and exam scores for five students. study time (h/week) exam score 2 62 4 70 6 75 8 84 10 90 which conclusions are supported by these data? select all that apply. students who studied more tended to score higher. studying more causes a higher score for every student. the data show a positive correlation. the student who studied 2 hours per week scored the lowest. anyone who studies 12 hours per week will score 100. scores rise as study time rises: a positive correlation. the 2-hour student scored 62, the lowest. five students can't prove cause for everyone, and 12 hours is outside the data, so predicting exactly 100 is not supported.

in a well-designed controlled experiment, how many variables should the researcher change on purpose? (type a number.) only the independent variable should be changed deliberately. changing more than one at a time makes it impossible to tell which one caused the result.

why is it important that other scientists are able to repeat (replicate) an experiment? it lets other scientists share credit for the original discovery. getting the same results again shows they were not due to chance or error. it proves the hypothesis is true forever and can never be revised. it means the original data no longer need to be published. replication checks whether results are reliable. even replicated results support—rather than permanently prove—a conclusion.

which observation is quantitative? the wound looks red and swollen. the patient says the pain feels sharp. the patient's temperature is 38.6 °c. the urine sample is cloudy and dark yellow. quantitative data are numbers with units—measured amounts. the other observations describe qualities (color, appearance, feeling), so they are qualitative.

tap the axis that shows the independent variable. the independent variable is the one the scientist changes on purpose: here, the amount of fertilizer. it goes on the x-axis (horizontal). the dependent variable, plant height, is measured and goes on the y-axis.

a nurse notices that the last 20 patients who received a certain antibiotic developed a rash. she concludes that the antibiotic probably causes rashes. what kind of reasoning is this? inductive reasoning deductive reasoning a controlled experiment a scientific law she moved from many specific observations to a general conclusion; that is inductive reasoning. her conclusion is likely but not certain; a new observation could change it.

"all penicillins are beta-lactam antibiotics. amoxicillin is a penicillin. therefore, amoxicillin is a beta-lactam antibiotic." which best describes this reasoning? inductive, because it moves from specific observations to a general rule inductive, because the conclusion is only probably true deductive, because it builds a general rule from many examples deductive, because it applies a general rule to a specific case the argument starts with a general statement (all penicillins) and applies it to one case (amoxicillin). that is deductive reasoning: if the premises are true, the conclusion must be true.

which statement about inductive and deductive reasoning is correct? inductive reasoning produces conclusions that are certain to be true. deductive reasoning starts with many specific observations. a valid deductive conclusion must be true if its premises are true. scientists use only deductive reasoning when forming a hypothesis. in valid deductive reasoning, true premises guarantee a true conclusion. inductive conclusions are only probable: one new observation can overturn them. scientists use both kinds of reasoning.

a student measured the height of a bean seedling every other day. day height (cm) 2 4.0 4 7.0 6 10.0 8 13.0 what is the best estimate of the seedling's height on day 5? 7.0 cm 10.0 cm 8.5 cm 8.0 cm the seedling grows 3.0 cm every 2 days (1.5 cm per day). day 5 is halfway between day 4 (7.0 cm) and day 6 (10.0 cm): 7.0 + 1.5 = 8.5 cm. this is interpolation.

a nurse records the volume left in a patient's iv bag. time (min) volume left (ml) 0 1,000 30 925 60 850 90 775 if the rate stays the same, how many minutes after the start will the bag contain 500 ml? 200 min 150 min 240 min 180 min the bag loses 75 ml every 30 minutes, which is 2.5 ml per minute. going from 1,000 ml to 500 ml means 500 ml must drip in: 500 ÷ 2.5 = 200 minutes.

what is the independent variable in this experiment? the type of hand treatment the number of bacterial colonies the temperature of the incubator the type of agar the independent variable is the one the experimenter changes on purpose. the student chose four different hand treatments. the number of colonies is the dependent variable (what is measured). temperature and agar were kept the same.

which group serves as the control? none (no washing) soap and water, 20 seconds sanitizer, 60% alcohol sanitizer, 30% alcohol a control group gets no treatment, so the other groups can be compared to it. the no-washing dishes show how many bacteria are on hands to begin with (about 152 colonies).

which conclusion is best supported by the data? soap and water and 60% alcohol sanitizer both removed far more bacteria than 30% alcohol sanitizer. 30% alcohol sanitizer removed about as many bacteria as soap and water did. all three hand treatments removed nearly all of the bacteria from the hands. sanitizer with more alcohol always removes more bacteria than soap and water. soap (23) and 60% sanitizer (18) cut the colonies from about 152 to around 20. the 30% sanitizer still left 97 colonies, so a low-alcohol product removed much less. the study tested only two alcohol levels and one soap method, so "always" goes too far.

which factors were controlled (kept the same) in this experiment? select all that apply. incubation temperature incubation time type of agar hand treatment number of colonies controlled variables are kept the same so they can't affect the results. every dish was kept at 37 °c for 48 hours on the same agar. the hand treatment was changed on purpose (independent variable), and the colonies were measured (dependent variable).

what is the dependent variable in this investigation? heart rate time height of the step speed of stepping the dependent variable is what is measured. it "depends" on the conditions. the student measured her heart rate. time is plotted on the x-axis. the step height and stepping speed were kept steady.

which change would make her conclusions about exercise and heart rate more reliable? repeat the test with many people, several times each. measure her heart rate only once, at the very end of the test. change the step height partway through so she works harder. use a different person for each time point. results from one person on one day might be unusual. repeating trials and testing a larger sample makes the results more reliable. changing the step height partway would add a second variable. measuring only once, or using a different person at each time point, would hide the pattern over time.

which hypothesis was the class most likely testing? if the water temperature changes, then the amount of gas the yeast make will change. if more sugar is added to the bottle, then the yeast will make more gas. yeast are single-celled fungi that can live with or without oxygen. carbon dioxide is the gas that collects in the balloon on each bottle. a hypothesis is a testable prediction about how the independent variable affects the dependent variable. the class changed only the temperature and measured gas, so the hypothesis connects those two. sugar was kept the same. "yeast are fungi" and "carbon dioxide is a gas" are facts, not predictions.

which conclusion is best supported by the graph? of the temperatures tested, the yeast were most active at 40 °c. yeast activity always increases as the water temperature increases. yeast are most active at 60 °c. temperature does not affect yeast. the 40 °c bottle made the most gas (31 ml). activity rose from 10 °c to 40 °c, then fell to almost nothing at 60 °c, so "always increases" is wrong. say "of the temperatures tested": the best temperature could be somewhere between 25 °c and 60 °c.

put the steps of this investigation in the order a scientist would do them. ask whether temperature affects how much gas yeast make predict that yeast will make the most gas in warm water run the bottles at four temperatures and collect the gas graph the volume of gas at each temperature decide whether the results support the prediction the scientific method starts with a question, then a hypothesis (prediction). next comes the experiment, then analyzing the data (the graph), and finally a conclusion about whether the data support the hypothesis.

what is the dependent variable in this experiment? whether the classmates drank coffee reaction time in milliseconds the number of classmates tested the day of the week the dependent variable is what is measured as the result: reaction time.
by how many milliseconds did the mean reaction time change from monday to tuesday? 312 ms − 284 ms = 28 ms faster on tuesday.

which are weaknesses in how this experiment was designed? select all that apply. every person knew when they had coffee. everyone took the test twice, so they may have improved from practice. the reaction-time test was the same both days. there was no group that drank decaf coffee on tuesday. reaction time was measured in milliseconds. knowing about the coffee could change effort (a placebo effect), the second test might be faster from practice alone, and with no decaf comparison the student can't separate caffeine from these other effects. using the same test and precise units are strengths, not weaknesses.

which change would best let the student conclude that caffeine itself caused the change? test the same 20 people again next week with more coffee randomly give half caffeinated and half decaf coffee, without telling anyone which let each classmate choose whether to drink coffee measure reaction time in seconds instead of milliseconds random assignment plus a blind decaf (placebo) group controls for practice and expectations, leaving caffeine as the only difference.

what kind of study is this? a controlled experiment, because the researchers assigned sleep amounts an observational study, because the researchers recorded what students already did a case study of one student a computer simulation the researchers didn't assign anyone a sleep amount; they surveyed habits and compared scores. that makes it observational.

which statement is best supported by the data? sleeping more causes students to earn higher exam scores. more reported sleep went with higher mean scores. every student who slept 8 hours scored 82%. sleep has no relationship to exam scores. the data show an association: groups that reported more sleep had higher average scores.

which could explain the pattern without sleep directly raising scores? select all that apply. students with jobs may sleep less and also have less study time. students who chose to answer may differ from those who didn't. students who are well organized may both sleep more and study more. the final exam was the same for every student. sleep amounts were reported by the students themselves. jobs and organization are confounding variables that could affect both sleep and scores. volunteer response and self-reported sleep add bias and error. using the same exam is a strength of the study.

why is the newsletter's claim not justified? the sample of 300 students is too large to give useful results. it claims cause and effect from an observational study. the scores were reported as percents. the study compared three different sleep groups instead of two. "will raise your grade" claims causation, but this study only shows a correlation. a randomized experiment would be needed to test cause.

tap the instrument used to measure the mass of a sample. mass is measured with a balance. this electronic balance shows the mass in grams on its display. glassware such as beakers, flasks and cylinders measures volume, and a thermometer measures temperature.

a student must measure 45 ml of saline as accurately as possible in a single measurement. the pipette shown holds only 10 ml. tap the best tool for the job. a graduated cylinder has evenly spaced marks along its whole height, so it can measure a volume like 45 ml accurately. the lines on a beaker or an erlenmeyer flask are only rough estimates. those containers are for holding, mixing and heating liquids, not for measuring them accurately. a 10 ml pipette is very accurate, but it would take several transfers to reach 45 ml, and each transfer adds error.

what volume of liquid is in the graduated cylinder? read to the nearest whole milliliter. read a graduated cylinder at eye level, at the bottom of the curved surface (the meniscus). the labeled marks are every 5 ml and the small marks are every 1 ml. the bottom of the meniscus sits on the first small mark above 35. 35 + 1 = 36 ml. reading the edges where the liquid climbs the glass would give a value that is too high (about 37 ml).

a patient's temperature is taken with the thermometer shown. what temperature does it read? the labeled marks are every 1 °c, and there is one small mark halfway between each pair, so each small mark is 0.5 °c. the top of the red column is at the small mark between 38 and 39. so the reading is 38.5 °c. that is a fever, since a fever is usually defined as 38.0 °c (100.4 °f) or higher.

convert the thermometer reading to degrees fahrenheit. use °f = 1.8 × °c + 32. 69.3 °f 126.9 °f 53.4 °f 101.3 °f the thermometer reads 38.5 °c. multiply first: 1.8 × 38.5 = 69.3. then add 32: 69.3 + 32 = 101.3 °f. 69.3 °f is the trap for forgetting to add 32. 126.9 °f comes from adding 32 before multiplying, and 53.4 °f comes from dividing by 1.8 instead of multiplying.

using the graph, how many centimeters taller, on average, were the plants given 4 g of fertilizer than the plants in the control group? the control group (0 g) averaged 12 cm, and the 4 g group averaged 24 cm. 24 − 12 = 12 cm taller.

a student needs to measure 25.0 ml of water as accurately as possible. which piece of glassware listed is the best choice? a beaker an erlenmeyer flask a test tube a graduated cylinder graduated cylinders have fine markings for measuring liquid volume. beakers and flasks have only rough volume marks and are for holding and mixing; test tubes usually have no volume marks.

how should the volume of water in a graduated cylinder be read? at eye level, at the bottom of the curved surface (meniscus) from above, at the top edge of the curved surface from below, at the highest mark on the glass at eye level, at the top edge where water touches the glass water curves down in the middle, forming a meniscus. read the bottom of that curve. keep your eye level with the meniscus to avoid parallax error from viewing at an angle.

the figure shows part of a graduated cylinder. each small mark is 1 ml. what volume should be recorded? 30.3 ml 33.0 ml 33.6 ml 37.0 ml the labeled lines are 30 and 35 ml, and each small mark is 1 ml. the bottom of the meniscus sits on the 3rd mark above 30: 33.0 ml. 33.6 ml comes from reading the top edge where the water climbs the glass; 37.0 ml comes from counting down from 40.

a thermometer has marks every 1 °c. the top of the liquid is exactly halfway between the 36 °c and 37 °c marks. what temperature should be recorded? 35.5 °c 36.0 °c 36.5 °c 37.5 °c the reading is between 36 and 37, halfway: 36 + 0.5 = 36.5 °c. 36.0 °c ignores the half-mark; 35.5 °c and 37.5 °c are outside the 36–37 range.

on a triple-beam balance, the riders are at 100 g on the back beam, 40 g on the middle beam and 3.25 g on the front beam. what is the mass of the object? 43.25 g 140.00 g 143.25 g 1,432.5 g add the readings of all three beams: 100 + 40 + 3.25 = 143.25 g. leaving out a beam gives 43.25 g or 140.00 g.

put these metric units of length in order from largest to smallest. kilometer (km) meter (m) centimeter (cm) millimeter (mm) micrometer (µm) kilo = 1,000; centi = 1/100; milli = 1/1,000; micro = 1/1,000,000. so 1 km = 1,000 m, 1 m = 100 cm, 1 cm = 10 mm, and 1 mm = 1,000 µm.
how many milliliters are in 2.5 liters? 25 ml 250 ml 2,500 ml 25,000 ml 1 l = 1,000 ml. 2.5 × 1,000 = 2,500 ml.
a tablet contains 0.75 g of a drug. how many milligrams is this? 1 g = 1,000 mg. 0.75 × 1,000 = 750 mg.

a student weighs a 50.0 g reference mass three times and gets 45.1 g, 45.2 g and 45.0 g. how would you describe these measurements? accurate but not precise precise but not accurate both accurate and precise neither accurate nor precise precision = how close measurements are to each other. these agree within 0.2 g, so they are precise. accuracy = how close they are to the true value. they are about 5 g too low, so they are not accurate.

a balance was not zeroed and reads 0.5 g even with nothing on it. a student weighs several samples without noticing. what kind of error is this? random error that cancels out when the results are averaged systematic error that makes every measurement 0.5 g too low systematic error that makes every measurement 0.5 g too high no error, because all of the readings are consistent an instrument that is off by the same amount every time causes systematic error. since the empty balance already reads +0.5 g, every mass is 0.5 g too high. averaging does not fix it; zeroing (taring) the balance does. consistent readings can still be inaccurate.

which practice best reduces the effect of random error in an experiment? recording only the first trial changing the independent variable more often using a different instrument for each trial repeating the trials and averaging the results random errors scatter results above and below the true value, so averaging many trials tends to cancel them. using different instruments adds more variation instead of reducing it.

a student timed how long a reaction took in three trials: 12.0 s, 12.4 s and 12.2 s. what is the mean time? add the trials: 12.0 + 12.4 + 12.2 = 36.6 s. divide by the number of trials: 36.6 ÷ 3 = 12.2 s.

a nurse wants to show how a patient's temperature changed over a 24-hour period. which type of graph is best? line graph pie chart bar graph of categories venn diagram line graphs show how a quantity changes over time. pie charts show parts of a whole, and bar graphs compare separate categories.

when graphing experimental results, the independent variable is usually placed on the y-axis (vertical axis) x-axis (horizontal axis) legend only title only convention: independent variable on the x-axis, dependent variable on the y-axis. for example, time goes on the x-axis and temperature on the y-axis.

a patient's temperature was recorded during one day. time temperature (°c) 0800 37.0 1200 37.4 1600 38.5 2000 37.9 between which two back-to-back readings did the temperature increase the most? 0800 and 1200 1600 and 2000 1200 and 1600 it rose by the same amount each time 0800→1200: +0.4 °c; 1200→1600: +1.1 °c; 1600→2000: −0.6 °c (a decrease). the largest increase between two readings is from 1200 to 1600. the changes are not equal, so "the same amount each time" is wrong.

which of these are metric units of volume? select all that apply. milliliter (ml) liter (l) cubic centimeter (cm³) gram (g) meter (m) ml, l and cm³ all measure volume; 1 ml = 1 cm³. grams measure mass and meters measure length.

which practices improve the accuracy of a volume reading in a graduated cylinder? select all that apply. placing the cylinder on a flat, level surface keeping your eyes level with the liquid surface reading the bottom of the meniscus for water holding the cylinder up in the air at an angle reading the top edge of the meniscus for water a level cylinder and eye-level viewing prevent tilt and parallax errors. for water, read the bottom of the meniscus; the top edge gives a reading that is too high.

use °f = (9/5 × °c) + 32. a patient's temperature is 39 °c. what is it in °f? 53.7 °f 70.2 °f 102.2 °f 127.8 °f 9/5 × 39 = 70.2. 70.2 + 32 = 102.2 °f. 70.2 forgets to add 32; 127.8 adds 32 before multiplying.

which of these masses is the largest? 450 g 52,000 mg 4.8 × 10² g 0.5 kg convert everything to grams: 0.5 kg = 500 g; 450 g; 52,000 mg = 52 g; 4.8 × 10² g = 480 g. 500 g is the largest, so 0.5 kg wins.

a lab student must transfer exactly 5.00 ml of a solution. which tool is the best choice? a 5-ml volumetric pipette a 250-ml beaker a 100-ml graduated cylinder an erlenmeyer flask a volumetric pipette is made to deliver one exact volume with high precision. a beaker or flask is too rough, and a 100-ml cylinder's markings are too coarse for 5.00 ml.

tap the piece of equipment used to measure temperature. a thermometer measures temperature, usually in °c in science labs. read it at eye level, at the top of the liquid column. body temperature is about 37 °c.

tap the cone-shaped glassware that is easy to swirl without spilling. an erlenmeyer flask has a wide base and narrow neck. the narrow neck lets you swirl the liquid without it splashing out. like a beaker, its volume markings are only approximate.

each small mark on the thermometer scale is 0.2 °f. what temperature does it show? 101.2 °f 101.4 °f 102.4 °f 101.8 °f the labeled long marks are whole degrees, and each short mark is 0.2 °f. the red column passes 101 and ends 2 short marks later: 101 + 0.4 = 101.4 °f.

on this 5 ml syringe each small line is 0.2 ml. read the dose at the front (needle-side) edge of the black stopper. how much medicine is in the syringe? 3.2 ml 3.4 ml 3.8 ml 4.4 ml find the last whole number the stopper passed: 3 ml. then count small lines: each is 0.2 ml. the front edge sits 2 lines past 3, so the dose is 3 + 0.4 = 3.4 ml.
a pediatric order calls for 0.25 mg of a drug. how many micrograms (mcg) is this? type a whole number. 1 mg = 1,000 mcg. 0.25 × 1,000 = 250 mcg.

how many significant figures are in the measurement 0.00450 g? 2 3 5 6 leading zeros (0.00) only hold the decimal place, so they are not significant. the 4, the 5 and the trailing zero after the decimal point all count: 3 significant figures.

a patient's fluid intake for a shift is recorded as 1200 ml (no decimal point is written). how many significant figures does this measurement have? 4 3 1 2 trailing zeros with no decimal point are not significant; they only show the place value. only the 1 and the 2 count, so 1200 ml has 2 significant figures.

which of these measurements have exactly three significant figures? select all that apply. 0.0305 g 250 ml 4.00 cm 1,010 mg 6.020 l 0.0305: the leading zeros don't count; 3, the zero between 3 and 5, and 5 do → 3. 4.00: zeros after the decimal at the end count → 3. 1,010: the zero between the 1s counts, but the final zero (no decimal point) does not → 3. 250 has only 2, and 6.020 has 4 (zeros between digits and trailing zeros after a decimal both count).

a student measures a rectangular gauze pad as 4.25 cm by 2.1 cm. using the correct number of significant figures, what is its area? 8.925 cm² 8.93 cm² 8.9 cm² 9 cm² 4.25 × 2.1 = 8.925 cm². when multiplying, keep as many significant figures as the least precise measurement. 2.1 has 2, so round to 8.9 cm².

an empty beaker has a mass of 12.51 g on a precise balance. a student adds 3.2 g of salt measured on a less precise balance. reported correctly, what is the total mass? 15.71 g 15.7 g 16 g 15.710 g 12.51 + 3.2 = 15.71 g. when adding or subtracting, round to the fewest decimal places. 3.2 is known only to the tenths place, so report 15.7 g.
how many micrograms (mcg) are in 1 milligram (mg)? 10 100 1,000,000 1,000 each step from gram → milligram → microgram is a factor of 1,000. so 1 mg = 1,000 mcg.

a red blood cell is about 8 µm (micrometers) across. what is this length in millimeters? 0.008 mm 0.08 mm 8,000 mm 0.0008 mm 1 mm = 1,000 µm. going to a larger unit makes the number smaller: 8 ÷ 1,000 = 0.008 mm.
during physical therapy, a patient walks a total of 2.4 km in one week. how many meters is this? type a whole number. 1 km = 1,000 m. 2.4 × 1,000 = 2,400 m.

a liquid medication contains 2 mg of drug in each milliliter. how many micrograms (mcg) of drug are in 0.5 ml? 1 mcg 4,000 mcg 1,000 mcg 100 mcg amount = 2 mg/ml × 0.5 ml = 1 mg. convert: 1 mg × 1,000 = 1,000 mcg.

which of the following is 0.00062 written in scientific notation? 6.2 × 10⁻⁴ 6.2 × 10⁴ 6.2 × 10⁻³ 6.2 × 10⁻⁵ move the decimal point right until one nonzero digit is in front: 0.00062 → 6.2 (4 places). a number smaller than 1 has a negative exponent, so it is 6.2 × 10⁻⁴.

a typical red blood cell count is about 5.0 × 10⁶ cells per microliter of blood. write this count as a standard number (no exponent). 10⁶ means move the decimal point 6 places to the right. 5.0 × 10⁶ = 5,000,000 cells per microliter (5 million).

a bacterial culture contains 4.0 × 10⁵ cells. after treatment with an antibiotic, it contains 4.0 × 10³ cells. the number of cells decreased by a factor of 2 100 1,000 100,000 divide: (4.0 × 10⁵) ÷ (4.0 × 10³) = 1 × 10⁵⁻³ = 10². 10² = 100, so there are 100 times fewer cells.

a student views a cheek-cell slide using a 10× ocular (eyepiece) lens and a 40× objective lens. what is the total magnification? 50× 40× 4,000× 400× total magnification = ocular × objective. 10 × 40 = 400×.

while viewing a blood smear, a student switches from the 10× objective to the 40× objective. compared with the view before, the field of view is smaller, and the image is usually dimmer larger, and the image is usually brighter the same size, but the image is brighter larger, so more cells can be seen higher magnification shows a smaller area of the slide, so fewer cells are visible. less light reaches the eye at high power, so the image looks dimmer and the diaphragm may need to be opened.

put these steps for focusing a prepared slide on a compound light microscope in order, first to last. with the lowest-power objective in place, clip the slide onto the stage. focus with the coarse adjustment knob. center the specimen and switch to a higher-power objective. sharpen the image using only the fine adjustment knob. always start on the lowest-power objective: it has the widest field of view and the most room between lens and slide. use the coarse knob only on low power, then center the specimen, move to higher power, and use only the fine knob so the lens doesn't hit the slide.

at a total magnification of 100×, the diameter of a microscope's field of view is 2.0 mm. what is the approximate diameter of the field of view at 400×? 8.0 mm 0.5 mm 1.5 mm 0.2 mm magnification went up by a factor of 4 (100× → 400×). field of view shrinks by the same factor: 2.0 mm ÷ 4 = 0.5 mm.

a nurse measures a wound with a paper ruler marked in centimeters, with 10 small millimeter marks in each centimeter. the wound starts at 0 and ends at the 4th small mark past the 6 cm line. how long is the wound? 64 cm 6.04 cm 10 cm 6.4 cm each small mark is 1 mm = 0.1 cm. 6 cm + 4 × 0.1 cm = 6.4 cm (64 mm).

in a graduated cylinder, the bottom of the meniscus is 3 small marks above the 20 ml line. each small mark is 0.2 ml. what volume should be recorded? 23 ml 20.3 ml 20.6 ml 19.4 ml 3 small marks × 0.2 ml = 0.6 ml. 20 ml + 0.6 ml = 20.6 ml.

a measuring pipette is marked 0 ml at the top, with numbers increasing downward. before dispensing, the liquid level is at the 2.0 ml mark. after a student lets some liquid drain into a test tube, the level is at the 7.5 ml mark. how many milliliters were dispensed? give your answer to the nearest 0.1 ml. the volume delivered is the difference between the two readings. 7.5 ml − 2.0 ml = 5.5 ml.
by how many beats per minute did her heart rate rise in the first 2 minutes? at minute 0 the heart rate was 72. at minute 2 it was 110. 110 − 72 = 38 beats per minute.

which statement best describes her heart rate from minute 6 to minute 10? it leveled off at about 135 beats per minute. it kept rising quickly by about 10 beats each minute. it dropped back down to her resting heart rate. it changed randomly. from 6 to 10 minutes the readings were 134, 135 and 135. the curve is nearly flat, so the heart rate reached a steady level (a plateau) that met the body's oxygen needs during steady exercise. her heart rate fell only after she stopped at minute 10.
what is the mean boiling point for 20 g of salt, in °c? (101.2 + 101.3 + 101.1) ÷ 3 = 303.6 ÷ 3 = 101.2 °c.

which statement best describes the trend in the data? adding salt lowers the boiling point. each additional 10 g of salt raised the boiling point by about 0.6 °c. the boiling point stayed the same no matter how much salt was added. salt had an effect only above 40 g. 0 g → 100.0, 10 g → 100.6, 20 g → 101.2, 40 g → 102.4. each 10 g adds about 0.6 °c.

why did the class run three trials for each amount of salt? to make the water reach its boiling point faster to check consistency and reduce random error to change the independent variable because the thermometer could only be used three times repeated trials show whether measurements agree (here they're within 0.2 °c) and averaging reduces random error.

using the trend, what is the best prediction for the boiling point with 30 g of salt? 100.8 °c 101.8 °c 102.4 °c 103.0 °c 30 g is halfway between 20 g (101.2 °c) and 40 g (102.4 °c). halfway between those values is 101.8 °c.
whose measurements were both accurate and precise? ana ben chloe dev ana's counts are close to the true value of 80 (accurate) and close to each other (precise).

ben's counts were consistent but always too low. what kind of error does this most likely show? random error that scatters results in both directions systematic error, such as starting late each time no error at all, since his counts agreed with each other an error in the simulator's setting results that are off by about the same amount in the same direction every time point to a systematic error in the method.

what is the mean of chloe's three counts, in beats per minute? round to the nearest whole number. (70 + 88 + 81) ÷ 3 = 239 ÷ 3 = 79.67, which rounds to 80. her average is accurate, but the individual counts are not precise.

which skill would most improve dev's precision? counting for only 15 seconds and multiplying by 4 using the same careful counting method every time estimating the rate from how fast the chest seems to rise recording only one count precision improves when every measurement is taken the same careful way.

click the molecule that is the building block (monomer) of proteins. proteins are long chains of amino acids. molecule b is an amino acid (alanine): it has an amino group (–nh₂), a central carbon, a side chain (here –ch₃) and a carboxyl group (–cooh). a is glucose (a sugar, the monomer of starch and glycogen). c is a nucleotide (monomer of dna and rna). d is a triglyceride (a fat).

click the molecule that is a monomer of dna. (look for a phosphate group, a five-carbon sugar and a nitrogen base.) molecule c is a nucleotide: a phosphate group (p with o's), a five-carbon sugar ring, and a nitrogen-containing base (adenine). nucleotides link sugar-to-phosphate into long chains to make dna and rna. glucose (a) is a six-carbon sugar with no phosphate or base.

click the molecule that is a lipid used for long-term energy storage in fat tissue. molecule d is a triglyceride: a glycerol backbone joined to three long fatty acid chains. triglycerides store about twice as much energy per gram as carbohydrates (about 9 vs 4 calories/gram), so the body uses them for long-term storage in adipose tissue. glucose (a) gives quick energy, and it is stored short-term as glycogen.

the ring-shaped molecule shown contains only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, in about a 1:2:1 ratio. to which class of macromolecules does it belong? carbohydrates proteins nucleic acids lipids this is glucose (c₆h₁₂o₆). a formula with c, h and o in a 1:2:1 ratio, (ch₂o)ₙ, is the signature of a carbohydrate. glucose is a monosaccharide, the monomer for starch, glycogen and cellulose. it is the cell's main quick-energy fuel.

many molecules like the one shown are linked together and stored in the liver and muscles to be used for quick energy later. what is that storage molecule called? glycogen cellulose cholesterol keratin animals store extra glucose as glycogen, a highly branched chain of glucose units, mainly in the liver and skeletal muscle. when blood glucose drops, the hormone glucagon signals the liver to break glycogen back down into glucose. plants store glucose as starch. cellulose is a plant fiber humans cannot digest.

the molecule shown is made from glycerol and three fatty acids. what is it? a triglyceride a phospholipid a polysaccharide a polypeptide tri- means three: a triglyceride has three fatty acid chains attached to one glycerol (the three-carbon backbone on the left). a phospholipid has only two fatty acids; the third position holds a phosphate group.

in the triglyceride shown, which fatty acid chain is unsaturated? the top chain the middle chain the bottom chain none of the chains an unsaturated fatty acid has at least one carbon–carbon double bond (c=c). only the bottom chain has "ch=ch" in it. the top and middle chains are all single bonds, (ch₂)ₙ, so they are saturated (full of hydrogen).
