fatty acid a is saturated and fatty acid b is unsaturated (cis). why are fats made mostly of chains like a (such as butter) usually solid at room temperature, while oils made mostly of chains like b are liquid? straight chains like a pack tightly together, so it takes more heat to melt them. chain a has more double bonds, which hold molecules together. chain b is much longer, so it flows more easily. chain b contains nitrogen, which keeps it liquid. a saturated chain (a) has only single bonds, so it is straight. straight chains stack closely, like pencils in a box, and attract each other strongly, so the fat is solid at room temperature. a cis double bond (b) puts a kink in the chain. kinked chains can't pack tightly, so the attractions are weaker and the oil stays liquid. olive oil, which is mostly unsaturated, is liquid at room temperature. (separately, diets high in saturated fat are linked to higher ldl cholesterol.)

the molecule shown has a polar (water-loving) phosphate head and two nonpolar (water-fearing) fatty acid tails. what is its main job in the body? forming the double layer (bilayer) of cell membranes storing genetic information speeding up chemical reactions carrying oxygen in the blood this is a phospholipid. in water, phospholipids line up in two layers: heads face the watery inside and outside of the cell, and tails hide in the middle. that phospholipid bilayer is the basic structure of every cell membrane.

the molecule shown is cholesterol, a steroid. which of these are made from cholesterol in the body? select all that apply. estrogen testosterone cortisol insulin hemoglobin steroids all share the same four-ring core shown in the figure. cholesterol is the starting material for the steroid hormones: estrogen, testosterone, progesterone, cortisol and aldosterone. cholesterol is also used to make vitamin d and bile salts, and it keeps cell membranes flexible. insulin and hemoglobin are proteins, made from amino acids.

click the part of the amino acid that is different in each of the 20 amino acids. every amino acid has the same backbone: an amino group (–nh₂), a central carbon with an h, and a carboxyl group (–cooh). the r group (side chain) is the only part that changes. it may be as small as an h (glycine) or a large ring, and it gives each amino acid its properties (polar, nonpolar, acidic or basic).

click the carboxyl group, the acidic part of the amino acid. the carboxyl group is –cooh: a carbon double-bonded to one o and single-bonded to an oh. it can give up h⁺, which makes it acidic. the amino group (–nh₂) on the other end can accept h⁺, which makes it basic. when two amino acids join, the carboxyl group of one bonds to the amino group of the next (a peptide bond).

the molecule shown is a tripeptide made of three amino acids. how many peptide bonds hold it together? a peptide bond links the carboxyl carbon of one amino acid to the nitrogen of the next (the c–n bond between a c=o and an n–h). three amino acids in a row need two links: amino acid 1–2 and amino acid 2–3. in general, n amino acids are joined by n − 1 peptide bonds.

when the three amino acids in the figure were joined, what else was produced? two molecules of water three molecules of water one molecule of oxygen two molecules of carbon dioxide each peptide bond forms by dehydration synthesis (condensation): an oh from one amino acid and an h from the next are removed as a water molecule. two peptide bonds → two water molecules. breaking the bonds again (digestion) is hydrolysis, which uses water to split them.

the figure shows a chain of amino acids in a specific order. which level of protein structure is this? primary secondary tertiary quaternary primary structure is the sequence of amino acids in the chain, like letters spelling a word. the dna code determines this order, and the order determines how the chain will fold.

the figure shows a protein made of four separate polypeptide chains fitted together, like hemoglobin. which level of protein structure is this? primary secondary tertiary quaternary quaternary structure exists only when a protein is made of two or more polypeptide chains (subunits). hemoglobin has four: two α and two β chains, each holding an iron-containing heme group (the red squares).

a high fever or a strong acid can denature a protein. which levels of structure are disrupted when a protein is denatured? select all that apply. primary secondary tertiary quaternary (if present) denaturing breaks the weaker attractions (hydrogen bonds, ionic attractions and others) that hold the folded shape, so the protein unfolds and loses its function. the peptide bonds stay intact, so the primary structure (the amino acid sequence) is not changed. cooking an egg white is a familiar example: the proteins unfold and clump, and they can't fold back.

click the part of the nucleotide that pairs with a base on the other strand of dna (a, t, g or c). the nitrogen base carries the genetic "letter." in dna, a pairs with t and g pairs with c, held by hydrogen bonds. the phosphate and sugar alternate to form the backbone (sides of the ladder), and the bases form the rungs.

in the nucleotide shown, carbon 2 of the sugar has only h atoms (no oh group). which nucleic acid would this nucleotide be part of? dna, because the sugar is deoxyribose rna, because the sugar is ribose rna, because the base is adenine dna, because it has a phosphate group de-oxy-ribose means ribose missing an oxygen: it has h instead of oh on carbon 2. that sugar is found in dna. rna's sugar, ribose, has an oh on carbon 2. adenine and phosphate groups are found in both dna and rna, so they don't tell you which one it is.

the top dna strand reads 5′-a-t-g-c-3′. reading the matching (complementary) strand under it from left to right, 3′ to 5′, what is its sequence? 3′-t-a-c-g-5′ 3′-a-t-g-c-5′ 3′-u-a-c-g-5′ 3′-c-g-t-a-5′ in dna, a pairs with t and g pairs with c (as shown on the ladder). so a–t–g–c pairs with t–a–c–g. u (uracil) replaces t only in rna, so u–a–c–g would be the matching rna strand made during transcription.

according to the graph, at about what temperature does this human enzyme work best? 20 °c 37 °c 50 °c 70 °c the highest point of the curve (optimum temperature) is at about 37 °c. that is normal human body temperature, where most human enzymes work best.

based on the graph, why does the enzyme's activity drop so quickly above about 45 °c? heat changes the enzyme's shape (denatures it), so the substrate no longer fits the active site. the enzyme gets used up in each reaction. molecules move more slowly at high temperature. the substrate becomes a different molecule at high temperature. up to the optimum, warmth speeds molecules up and they collide more, so activity rises. past the optimum, heat breaks the bonds holding the enzyme's 3-d shape. the active site changes shape, the substrate no longer fits, and activity crashes. this is one reason a very high fever is dangerous.

pepsin works in the stomach and trypsin works in the small intestine. based on the graph, which statement is best supported? the stomach is strongly acidic, and the small intestine is slightly basic. both organs have the same ph. pepsin works best in a basic environment. trypsin would work well in the stomach. pepsin's activity peaks at ph 2 (strongly acidic). that fits the stomach, where hydrochloric acid keeps the ph around 1.5–3.5. trypsin peaks at about ph 8 (slightly basic). in the small intestine, bicarbonate from the pancreas neutralizes stomach acid. trypsin has almost no activity at ph 2, so it would not work in the stomach.

the diagram shows the same reaction with and without an enzyme. what does the enzyme change? it lowers the activation energy, so the reaction happens faster. it lowers the energy of the products. it adds energy to the reactants. it changes which products are formed. the dashed green curve (with enzyme) has a lower hill. the enzyme lowers the activation energy, so many more molecules can react per second. the starting and ending energy levels are the same on both curves, so the enzyme does not change the overall energy released or the products. enzymes are catalysts: they speed reactions and are not used up.

use the table. which macromolecule class do enzymes, antibodies and hemoglobin belong to? carbohydrates lipids proteins nucleic acids proteins do most of the work in cells: enzymes speed reactions, antibodies defend the body, and hemoglobin carries oxygen. all of them are chains of amino acids folded into specific shapes.

use the table. which macromolecule is not built from a single repeating type of monomer? carbohydrates lipids proteins nucleic acids lipids are a varied group (fats, phospholipids, steroids). fats are built from glycerol plus fatty acids, which are not a single repeating monomer, so lipids aren't true polymers. carbohydrates repeat monosaccharides, proteins repeat amino acids, and nucleic acids repeat nucleotides.

a person with lactose intolerance makes very little lactase. based on the table, what happens when this person drinks milk? lactose isn't split into glucose and galactose, so it reaches the large intestine, where bacteria ferment it and cause gas and cramps. sucrose can't be digested, so table sugar causes the symptoms. milk proteins can't be digested because lactase is needed for proteins. glucose from the milk is absorbed faster than normal. only monosaccharides are absorbed. lactase normally splits lactose into glucose + galactose in the small intestine. without enough lactase, lactose stays whole and moves on to the large intestine. bacteria there ferment it, making gas, and the extra sugar draws in water (bloating, diarrhea). lactase tablets or lactose-free milk (lactose already split) prevent this.

a competitive inhibitor has a shape similar to the substrate and binds the enzyme's active site. based on the graph, how can its effect be overcome? add much more substrate, so substrate molecules win the active sites most of the time. remove most of the substrate. heat the enzyme far above body temperature. nothing can overcome it; the maximum rate is always lower. the inhibitor and substrate compete for the same active site. at low substrate, the inhibitor wins often and the rate is much lower. as substrate concentration rises, substrate molecules outnumber the inhibitor, and the dashed curve climbs toward the same maximum rate. many drugs work this way, for example statins block an enzyme the liver uses to make cholesterol.

in sickle cell disease, a single amino acid in each β chain of hemoglobin is changed (glutamic acid → valine). why can one change in the primary structure alter the whole protein? the amino acid sequence determines how the chains fold, so a different r group can change the shape and how the chains interact. the change removes the iron atoms from hemoglobin. it changes the dna in the red blood cell's nucleus. it turns hemoglobin into a lipid. each chain folds based on the properties of its r groups. valine's r group is nonpolar, while glutamic acid's is charged. the new nonpolar patch makes hemoglobin molecules stick together when oxygen is low, forming long fibers that bend red cells into a sickle shape. this shows the link the teas asks about: dna → amino acid sequence (primary structure) → 3-d shape → function.
